Prólogo al lector

La diversidad de opiniones (Prudente lector) que se halla
en las crónicas del nuevo mundo, y el deseo de inquirir
y apurar la verdad de las causas que en ellas se escriben, fue el prin
cipal motivo que me hizo determinarme a venir a estas Indias.
Porque qualquiera que leyere atentamente los varios escri
tores que han impreso historias destas Indias occidentales
experimentara lo que digo, y en aquellos que mas conforman
entre si en sus escritos, se echara de ver que unos han tomado de
otros lo que dicen; siguiendo a los primeros los que después de
ellos escribieron, fiados en su fe y autoridad sin ponerse a
examinar la verdad de lo que hallaron en ellos. De mane
ra que si los primeros se engañaron en algunos casos, el mismo
engaño fue cundiendo por los que les siguieron. Culpa que
no se puede presumir chibo en los historiadores que en Europa
escribieron, cuya intención fue de acertar, sino en los
que de aca les embiaron los relaciones que compusieron sus historias;
que por la experiencia que yo tengo en tantos años de Indias,
de muchas relaciones que se han hecho de nuevos sucesos,
y descubrimientos de tierras acaecidos en mi tiempo, hallo
que pocas veces van tan fieles como convenía; y si hechas

translation:
Prologue to the Reader

The diversity of opinions, prudent reader, that one finds in the chronicles of the New World, and the desire to inquire into and ascertain the truth of the matters written therein, was the principal motive that led me to decide to come to these Indies. For anyone who reads attentively the various writers who have printed histories of these Western Indies will experience what I say, and in those who agree most closely with one another in their writings, it will be apparent that some have taken from others what they say; those who wrote after the first authors followed them, trusting in their credibility and authority without troubling themselves to examine the truth of what they found in them. So that if the first authors were mistaken in certain cases, the same error spread through those who followed them. This fault cannot be presumed to lie with the historians who wrote in Europe, whose intention was to be accurate, but rather with those who sent them from here the accounts upon which they based their histories; for from the experience I have gained over so many years in the Indies, from the many accounts that have been made of new events and discoveries of lands that occurred in my time, I find that they are seldom as faithful as they ought to be; and if made so sincerely that no passion, flattery, or ambition creeps into them — those who

But I do not wish to dwell further on this particular matter, as it is

having said in one place, as proof of the truth he treats therein,

And so it is that among the historians who wrote in Spain, drawing from what they gathered through particular accounts without firsthand knowledge of some provinces: in both groups I find that they lacked the most solid foundation that a history must have, which is to be supported by the public archives of the republic about which one writes. Beyond this, what is necessarily required for political and ecclesiastical history, and the course of the times and customs that have occurred in the New World since its discovery: regarding the natural soils to be found there, I have not seen that anyone has treated this subject thoroughly. For this reason, wishing to supply, as far as my abilities allow, the said deficiencies, I resolved to write this history in order to serve the common good, and it appears (though not without great labor) that I have succeeded in accomplishing it.

First, because of the many years I have resided in the Indies, which are no fewer than fifty-seven, from the year one thousand five hundred and seventy-six when I went there, until the present year of one thousand six hundred and fifty-three: aided not only by my natural inclination to learn and to probe the secrets of the lands where I have resided, but especially having experienced the diverse climates found throughout both hemispheres of the New World; for I have lived in one and the other for a long time, which has given me the opportunity to inquire into and contemplate at length the ma[tters...]

the nature of the regions, and the rare fruits they produce, which are the things that professors of natural philosophy tend to overlook and conceal.

The Spaniards, because they have been living among the Indians, have arrived at the founding of their settlements, and I can say that they entered them within the first century of the founding of a republic. For although this land was discovered in the year fourteen hundred and ninety-two, and the Spaniards returned a year later to begin its settlement, it was not until the city of Santo Domingo was founded in the year fourteen hundred and ninety-seven, that it newly gained a permanent seat and stability as a new republic. And thus, having arrived myself at the island of Hispaniola in the aforementioned year of ninety-six, within the ninety-ninth year of the founding of the said city of Santo Domingo, it is well verified that I entered among them and among the Indians in the first century of their settlement. For this reason I had the occasion to come to know some of the first settlers, particularly from the kingdom of Peru, which I entered in its sixty-eighth year after its conquest; and nearly all the sons of its conquerors, and not a few from other provinces; and a great number of Indians who remembered when those from Spain entered their land — with whom I conversed at length, and who were able to inform me of much of what they had witnessed; and what they could not reach themselves, they knew from the mouths of the first Spaniards who came.

Beyond this (which is the third reason), I have found many ancient accounts in manuscript papers, such as diaries and relations written by some of the conquistadors, which their descendants now keep. Among these, I consider particularly worthy of full credence a brief account made of the conquest of New Spain by one of its principal conquistadors, called Captain Bernardino Vázquez de Tapia, which he presented to Don Antonio de Mendoza, the first Viceroy thereof. The original of this, written in his own hand by Bernardino Vázquez, was shared with me by one of his grandsons. Regarding those who wrote about the conquest of the kingdom of Peru, one of its first conquistadors, named Pedro Pizarro, resident of the city of Arequipa, gave me his account, which a descendant of his shared with me and which I now hold in my possession.

In addition to these authentic writings, I have made use of many old depositions that the conquistadors made to document their services, with witnesses who were themselves conquistadors, in which particular circumstances are found that never came to the attention of the first chroniclers. Others of these include royal provisions and letters from Viceroys and governors, many of which are kept in the public archives, and others are inserted into depositions authorized by the courts. And finally I have seen and drawn from many

Concluida pues con el fauor diuino esta obra despues de
quarenta años que la comence, me parecio intitularla his
toria del nueuo mundo: por que dexio ndo se a dullarnos
con la uniuersalidad del sugeto, que estodas esta tierra delas
Indias occidentales, y nueuo mundo. Y lo primero, porque en
ella se contienen quantos casos desean saber de la nueua
tierra los aficionados a la uniuerse historia, y erudicion:
pues parte desta escritura pertenece a historia natural, y par
te apolitica, y eclesiastica. Y si bien della ultima habia
hiera justamente intitular historia eclesiastica, y tirar
do la denominacion de su mas noble parte, con todo es por
ser mas general el titulo dicho, y que corresponde mejor
translation:
things from the ecclesiastical and secular archives in the places where
I have been, which, being certain and irrefutable arguments of the truth
of what is written, are scattered throughout this history, particularly
in the second and third parts, with many documents and texts copied
formally from said archives: which in the course of this
writing serve as a guide, just as the markers of posts that
are set up along the roads that are often covered by snow
to direct the travelers. This I do more par
ticularly when it is necessary to clarify
obscure matters, or to refute those things that without foundation of truth
are told in some histories.

Having concluded, then, with divine favor this work after
forty years since I began it, it seemed right to me to entitle it the
History of the New World: because leaving aside being dazzled
by the universality of the subject, which encompasses all this land of the
West Indies and the New World. And first, because in
it are contained all the things that those fond of the new
land wish to know about universal history and erudition:
for part of this writing belongs to natural history, and part
to political and ecclesiastical history. And although from the last of these it would
rightly be called ecclesiastical history, and drawing
its name from its most noble part, nonetheless it is because
the aforementioned title is more general, and corresponds better

Los ocho libros siguientes tratan de las calidades, y temples de
el nuevo mundo, y de todas las cosas naturales que de su te
rra llevan, y hallaron nuestros Españoles quando vinieron a
poblarlo, dispuestos por sus grados, y generos, segun el orden deber
fer ados, y nobleca, que en ellas considerados filosofos, y co
smicos, y delamineros por heftos, como los las inanimados;
siguese en todas las especies de piedras, y metales que ha po
lido alcançar: y prosiguiendo por los linages de plantas, y ani
males, que son natürales, y propios de la tierra, en cuya
historia toca de camino el conocimiento, y usos que dellas te
nian los Indios, que dellos han aprendido los Españoles, asi
en lo tocante a su alimento, en que se sirven dellas, como para
la cura de sus enfermedades, a que los han aplicar los por las
virtudes que en ellos alcançaron a conocer utiles para reme
nellos. En el libro decimo comprehendemos todas las usadas de
ellos predicamentos de plantas, animales, que los Espaüo
les han traydos de España, y de otras regiones a estas Indias
despues que las poblaron, y al presente nacen en ellas con no
menos abundancia que las suyas propias. Los quatro libros ul
timos contienen lo que pertenece a la naturaleca, con di
cion, y costumbres de los Indios, particular mente de los
habitadores de este reyno, con el govierno que sus Reyes
tenian asi en lo tocante a la administracion temporal,
translation:
has had.

The following eight books deal with the qualities and climates of
the New World, and all the natural things that from its land
they took, and our Spaniards found when they came to
settle it, arranged by their degrees and kinds, according to the order of merit
and nobility, as considered by philosophers and
cosmographers, and by miners for these, as well as the inanimate ones;
following through all the species of stones and metals that he has been
able to obtain: and continuing through the lineages of plants and ani
mals, which are native and proper to the land, in whose
history he touches along the way on the knowledge and uses that
the Indians had of them, which the Spaniards have learned from them, both
regarding their sustenance, in which they make use of them, and for
the cure of their illnesses, to which they have applied them for the
virtues they came to know in them as useful for remedy
ing them. In the tenth book we cover all the customary
categories of plants and animals that the Span
iards have brought from Spain, and from other regions to these Indies
since they settled them, and at present grow in them with no
less abundance than their own native ones. The last four books
contain what pertains to the nature, con
dition, and customs of the Indians, particularly those of the
inhabitants of this kingdom, along with the government that their Kings
maintained both in what concerns temporal administration,

Because they treat purposefully of all the other republics of the Indians that were worthy of noting: although in the other two parts of this history, the most notable customs and ways of living of some nations are also touched upon.

The second part consists of fifteen books: the first two deal with the discovery and pacification of the first provinces of the Indies and of the Kingdom of Peru; the third covers the course of the governors and viceroys who have governed it, giving a brief account of the uses and other memorable things that have occurred there from its beginning to the present time; in the fourth and fifth is set out the manner in which the republic of the Spaniards and of the Indians has been planted and established in these Indies, after the latter became Christians, and the form of government observed among them, particularly in the Kingdom of Peru; in the nine following books there is a general description of that same Kingdom of Peru by its bishoprics and provinces, and at great length that of the City of the Kings; and in the last is the description of the remaining provinces of Austral America, which fall outside the boundaries of Peru, together with everything else belonging to what of this New World falls within the Antarctic hemisphere.

Por fin deste prologo me parecio advertir al lector dos auisos, la primera que por haueryo visto de cada region al tiempo que yo residia en ella para mayor verificacion de lo que relato como quien entendia la materia presente, no es que la historia el tiempo en que cada cosa se escriuio, sino que algunos se ponen primero que fueron escritos despues; guardando en esto el orden que las mismas cosas piden, y no el tiempo en que se escriuieron: como se ve en la primera parte que la acabe de perficionar despues de las otras dos, respecto de que el sugeto della pedia mayor experiencia, y noticia de las cosas que contiene.

The third part and volume contains fourteen books: the first two deal with the qualities of New Spain, and its discovery and conquest; the third with the governors and viceroys it has had: from the fourth onward, an account is given of its provinces, and of all the others of North America; and an account is given of the founding and present state of the city of Mexico, and of its settlers and families descended from them: and in the fourteenth and last, the islands of both seas, the North and the South, are described, as far as the Philippines and the Moluccas: and a brief treatise is included on the voyages of all the Indies and the new world.

At the end of this prologue it seemed right to me to offer the reader two advisories. The first is that although I personally observed each region during the time I resided there, for greater verification of what I relate, as one who understood the present matter, it does not mean that the history follows the time in which each thing was written; rather, some things are placed first that were actually written later, following in this the order that the subject matter itself demands, and not the chronological order in which they were written: as can be seen in the first part, which I finished perfecting after the other two, given that its subject required greater experience and knowledge of the matters it contains.

The second advisory is that in describing the city of Mexico I treat of its founders, and I do not return to do the same in the description of Lima, not because the latter is inferior to the former

Chapter 1. Of the Universe.

The ancient philosophers gave various names to this universal machine of the world, calling it at times Heaven, at other times Universe, and at other times World. The first of these is no longer in use in that sense; the other two are used interchangeably; given that "World" is the most frequent and common, by which we mean the gathering and joining together of all created things, which amounts to the same as saying Universe. Aristotle defines it in this manner: the World is a gathering composed of heaven and earth, and of all the natures contained within them. Or in other words: the World is an ordered composition of all the things that God has brought to light, and by which they are animated. It may well be that the philosopher speaks here only of the corporeal world, which consists of the four elements and of heaven; but in the chapter he uses the name in a broader sense, insofar as it encompasses all created things that are contained within the Universe.

Which is one alone, and not many; and its shape is spherical, resembling a perfectly round ball, like the principal parts that compose it, which are the simple bodies of the heavens and elements. In the sacrifices called Orgia, which the ancients performed in honor of the god Bacchus, Macrobius relates that they gave special veneration to the egg, honoring it as

La grandeza deste mundo es tan incomparable, e immen

History of the New World.
In the image and likeness of the world, both in its roundness and principally in its composition: taking the white to represent the sky, the yolk the globe of the earth, and the white the region and element of air. A comparison, though humble and domestic, that well illustrates the figure. Because of the three parts that make up the egg — the white, the shell with its hardness, whiteness, and shining luster — and because it embraces and encloses within itself the other two, it ought to be attributed as the symbol of the celestial sphere. The yolk, which represents the earth, by virtue of its position in the middle and center, surrounded and encircled on all sides by the white and the shell, and because its substance is less transparent than the white, and not so white, and denser than the shell. As for the white — who cannot see how aptly it represents the other two elements, water and air, by its fluidity and transparency? Where one can see how wisely those ancients depicted the form and fabric of the universe in an egg: which figure is all the more fitting when we consider the world in that imperfect and chaotic state it had on the first day of its creation, when, according to the most probable opinion, there existed in it no more than three simple bodies — sky, water, and earth — as we shall see in the following chapter.
The greatness of this world is so incomparable and immense that, although it does have its limits and bounds, as may be inferred from its shape, which it could not have were it not finite and limited, it not only exceeds the faculty of the bodily senses, which are measures far too small and short to measure it,

translation: embrace its extent and circumference: but also the human understanding, which, stretching the sight of the imagination across so vast a magnitude, becomes daunted and surrenders, acknowledging its own limitations. For this reason it is necessary to approach it gradually, part by part, exploring and uncovering it through much reflection in order to come to know it. Just as (to give an example) we behold a towering mountain range, full of the highest peaks, whose length runs for many hundreds of leagues; such as the great cordillera that crosses all of this South America: and from this range the mind rises to consider the great body of the land, which contains within itself many other mountain ranges and peaks of equal magnitude: and when we find ourselves in the middle of a broad and open plain and flatland, which is clear and unobstructed on all sides, giving a free view to the horizon: such as the great plains and flatlands of the provinces of Tucumán and Paraguay; and marveling at such extensive flatlands, we consider that the surface of the earth does not end with them, but rather embraces many others no less spacious than they: which together with the mountains, hills, and valleys make up all that of the whole globe of the earth that lies above the water. So too is the reflection, especially the one we make when, placed in the middle of the open sea, we cast our gaze in all directions and discover nothing but water and sky: and we understand how great a part of the land is covered by the waters of the ocean, and by the many arms and inlets that proceed from it.

Known in this way, the greatness of the element of earth, one must give the imagination to measure it, so that by means of it we may go around circling how great the whole of the universe will be, going around it, and using as our guide the smallest star that our sight can reach, which to the senses appears no more than a tiny point: and persuading ourselves from its rays that it is a greater star than the entire lower globe composed of water and earth: and that just as seen from here below, though it is in itself so large, it appears to us as small as a dot: so also the lower globe, viewed from well before reaching the place where it is, will appear no more than another point; and from the starry heavens all of this can be seen in its entirety — the understanding is left stunned and astonished at the consideration of so immense a greatness: and more so if thought penetrates all the way to placing itself upon the summit and convex surface of the empyrean heaven, reaching so far out that there is no human force sufficient to go around and measure them. There are the final limits and boundary markers of the universe; up to there its domain and jurisdiction extends, and goes no further, because beyond what I have marked there is no longer any structure or building — beyond the outermost heaven is nothingness, where there is no body, no movement, no time: and so the world has no other boundary or border than that which it and the last sphere enclose: from which arises the meaning that the name Universe denotes, as Aristotle holds: coming to understand that, comprehending and enclosing within itself all bodies and giving each its order as its nature requires, it itself is not comprehended by anything else.

Having considered its greatness, it is well worth noting that its marvelous
beauty and capital nature declares to us the name of World, which
the Latins gave it, as Pliny says, for its extreme beauty
and consummate elegance. The Greeks called it cosmos, a name
of order, and taxis, for the singular order with which it is com-
posed of all its parts, which enrich and adorn it.
Plato called it the fullness of forms and species, on account of the many
that are found within it. But since its beautiful composition results
from the admirable parts it contains, and from the connection, order,
and harmony that those parts maintain among themselves: from this it follows that one must not
understand that all its beauty and loveliness is only the exterior kind, which
delights all bodily senses: but rather that the principal beauty is the interior,
which is the object of the understanding, through whose knowledge and
contemplation the soul is calmed and delighted, contemplating
the perfection and essential goodness of the Universe, and of all
its parts: and the order in which they correspond to one another, and all
to their ends: for which reason Saint Dionysius teaches that beauty
and perfection are names that signify one and the same thing, that
there is no distinction between them: that what the understanding
imagines insofar as it considers it under various aspects, and so the
most perfect as such, insofar as it is complete and not lacking
in what its being and essence require: and that which is thus perfect is given the
name of beautiful insofar as through its natural perfection, and the

Plato said that beauty was the luster and splendor of good that those things possess, which are perceived through all the senses and through reflection. This beauty makes the perfection of the Universe consist principally of three things, which we equally find in it. The first is the beauty and perfection of the things of which it is composed; the second, the distinction and variety of its natural elements; and the third, the disposition and order of its parts.

Speaking of the essential perfection of things, which cannot be distinguished from their essences, it is clear and manifest that the world cannot exist without it, since the things that compose and form it cannot lack their own essences. The Universe must also be said to have accidental perfection, which arises from the form of each thing as its inseparable property; and no less certain and notable is the perfection that derives from the variety and distinction of the natures it contains. For it contains all the grades of beings, at least the primary and general ones, as Saint Thomas teaches, for it embraces the supreme genera into which being is immediately divided. Likewise, material and immaterial substances: among the latter, the three Hierarchies of the Angels, which are divided into nine choirs. Those are the classes of sublunary beings, which, as if by degrees, surpass one another in nobility. In the first degree are placed the simple bodies of which the Universe is made, as the foundation and whole of that which

The other creatures are contained and presented in the following order: the second belongs to imperfect mixed things, which are generated in the region of the air from the exhalations and vapors that, rising from the others, ascend from the earth and the water. The third contains the perfect mixed things, which lack life. The fourth contains the plants. In the fifth, irrational animals have their place. And in the sixth and supreme place is man: who, beyond being a sum and cipher of all the perfections shared by all the bodily natures of the other beings, surpasses them so greatly with the faculties proper to the rational part — understanding and will — that on account of these it is said that he was created in the image and likeness of his Creator, and as lord and master of His creatures; capable of free will, virtue, and merit, of praise and reward.

Beyond this, it was fitting that beneath each degree (except the sixth) there should be many species, through which various perfections would be spread and dispersed for the greater abundance and adornment of the world. In these we experience such different effects and properties that, by noting well the diversity of substances from which they flow: in the elements we see some heavy, others light and airy; some high, others low; some dark, others clear; some dry and others wet. But so that the beauty and perfection that flows from this well-ordered arrangement may be more clearly understood, it will be good to explain in greater detail the order and subordination that all things existing in the world maintain among themselves. This order shines forth first in the place and position that each thing occupies, being content with that which best suits its nature; and in it, as in its own homeland, things remain calm and quiet, without desiring any change of place. The second way it appears is in the great subordination and harmony by which lower bodies receive from higher ones their movement and influences, through which they are ruled and governed by them; and the higher ones in turn by spiritual substances: among which there is also their own order and harmony, for the highest and most sublime announce to the others the divine mysteries. The third way this order is known is through the way all things attend to their particular ends, as well as to the end of the Universe.

And coming to man, who is the lesser world, for whose sake the greater was created: all his faculties, senses, and members are arranged with marvelous design and artistry for their operations and ends; down to the very source from which all of them spring, which is the soul. To the soul was given its being on account of the most excellent operations that it achieves with its most noble powers.

For number denotes species: since, according to the doctrine of Aristotle, the species of things are compared to numbers. This admirable order and subordination that shines throughout the Universe, both among its parts with one another and of all of them with their Maker, implies that those parts that compose it must be almost infinite in number, distinct and of measured natures; so that the harmony by which they all agree and are unanimous, and are directed toward the common good of the Universe itself, may be called one. And because by the benefit of order the world is called One, from this arose that illustrious tribute: that without order there would be, and could be, no world.

And let the first be that which says that God, in the formation of the world, did so that its beauty and perfection might better be perceived. For just as an object placed against its opposite stands out more clearly, as white does against black; so by creating the world in darkness, and imagining it anew in his understanding in that darkness without any light, he better knew the great perfection and beauty that he bestowed upon it with the benefit of light. And in the same way, considering the state and condition that it had on each of those days that preceded the sixth; without the perfections that, like vivid tints and colors, were being added to it; the order, brilliance, and perfection with which the wisdom of the divine Architect arranged and adorned it shone forth all the more. Beyond this, it was fitting to the nature of the author of creation that he should maintain the same order and style in fashioning the world and giving being to nature; so that it would be proper and connatural to nature itself.

A estas razones añade San Ambrosio que en producir,
y perficionar Dios el te mundo sucesivamente no quiso ha-
cer sus imitadores; en que guardemos este orden, que
primero demos principio a nuestras casas, haciendolas
en ellos: y despues entendamos es perficionarlas; no
sea que por querer hacerlo todo junto, no salgamos con
nada.

Tres cuerpos juntos vio Dios, de nada el primer dia,
el cielo empireo, la tierra, y el elemento del agua;
la qual produjo entanto grande copia, que ocupaua todo
el espacio que auia en medio entre la tierra, y el mismo
cielo: y della despues fue produciendo los otros cuerpos sim-
ples, a siele los cinco elementares. y en el mismo instan-
te crio junto con el cielo empireo, y en el mismo cielo to-
das las naturalezas de los Angeles, que lo poblaron.
Estos tres cuerpos fueron los cimientos, y con los que
adejo Dios de esta habitacion, y casa del Vniuerso; que
labraua para morada del hombre; fijando primero
el techo, y suelo que sus paredes, y demas partes: porque
translation:
First, for the effect
that it produced: Salt then was the inclination and order that
it imprinted upon nature itself, which in its operations
proceeds from the imperfect to the perfect, and
from the less to the more Substantial.

To these reasons Saint Ambrose adds that in producing
and perfecting the world successively, God did not wish to
make us his imitators in keeping this order, that
we first give beginning to our houses, building them
in stages: and afterwards attend to perfecting them; lest
by wanting to do everything at once, we end up with
nothing.

Three bodies together God created from nothing on the first day:
the empyrean heaven, the earth, and the element of water;
which he produced in such great abundance that it occupied all
the space that lay between the earth and the very
heaven: and from it he afterwards produced the other simple bodies,
seven in all counting the five elementary ones. And in that same
instant he created together with the empyrean heaven, and within that same heaven,
all the natures of the Angels who populated it.
These three bodies were the foundations, and with them
God set out this dwelling and house of the Universe, which
he was fashioning as a home for mankind; fixing first
the roof and floor before its walls and other parts: because

text:
Historia del nuevo mundo
por techo seguro el cielo empíreo, y el elemento de la tierra
por suelo, y fundamento: y todo el demás espacio hinchose de
aguas: de las quales como de primeros materiales fue labran
do después las otras partes del gran edificio.

Fue criada la tierra perfectamente redonda, sin los
altibajos que aora tiene: pura en su sustancia, porque de lo
demas tuvo mezclado, como son piedras, minerales etc.
aunque sin la dureza accidental que su esencia pedia,
por no tener toda su sequedad a causa de estar cubierta de
agua: quadrandole aquellos de el Real Propheta: cubrios
la el abismo como si fuera su vestidura. Y porque carecia
del ornato, y perfeccion que respecia, aun al fin
para que fue criada, dicen las divinas letras que
en aquel estado tosco, y rudo, estava vacia, e imperfec
ta, y tan sin apariencia, y lustre que ann razon se
podia llamar, materia invisible; el qual nombre se le
da en el libro de la sabiduria, donde se dice que lo
mano del Señor fabrico el orbe de la tierra de una ma
teria invisible, o sin forma, y sin perfeccion. Porque es
tando por todas partes cubierta de una immensidad
de aguas, no estava a proposito para ser habitada de hom
bres, y animales, que fue el fin para que fue criada.
Y todo aquel abismo de aguas, que tenia dar el espacio
translation:
History of the New World
The empyrean sky served as its secure roof, and the element of earth as its floor and foundation; and all the remaining space filled with waters, from which, as from primary materials, the other parts of the great edifice were afterward fashioned.

The earth was created perfectly round, without the hills and valleys it now has: pure in its substance, though mixed with other things such as rocks, minerals, etc., yet without the accidental hardness that its essence required, as it lacked full dryness on account of being covered with water. Fitting to it are those words of the Royal Prophet: the deep covered it as if it were its garment. And because it lacked the ornament and perfection that it looked toward, still at the end for which it was created, the divine scriptures say that in that rough and crude state it was empty and imperfect, and so without appearance and luster that with good reason it could be called invisible matter; which name is given to it in the Book of Wisdom, where it is said that the hand of the Lord fashioned the orb of the earth from an invisible matter, or without form and without perfection. For being covered on all sides by an immensity of waters, it was not suited to be inhabited by men and animals, which was the purpose for which it was created. And all that abyss of waters, which was to yield the space

text:
Primera parte. lib. 1.

que auia desde la superficie de la tierra hasta el cielo empireo, estaua en obscuridad, y tinieblas: en la qual obscuridad, y noche tenebrosa estuuo el mundo por tiempo de medio dia natural. Al cabo del qual la primera luz, y perficion que puso Dios en el mundo criado en aquel estado imper fecto, fue saliendo con que se alumbrasen, y manifestasen sus obras; y se commencasen a contar los dias, en que auio Deys produciendo, y perficionando lo que restaua para que el Vniuerso tubiese su deuida perfeccion. No proce Dia ella luz de cuerpo alguno, sino que el mismo Dios in mediatamente la yua produciendo al modo que si ta deriuara de algun cuerpo luminoso, succitamente de un lugar deau a otro por toda la circunferencia del mun do: de suerte que aquellos tres primeros dias del tiem po fueron una continua, y luciente produccion de la luz. La qual alumbraua el un hemisferio del mun do desde la superficie de la tierra hasta la del agua y concabo del cielo Empireo, penetrando toda la profun didad, y multitud de aguas que auia en medio. Y con un mouimiento uniforme yua dexando el hemisferio ori ental, y comunicandose al occidental, al modo que aora hace su curso el Sol; y en el mismo espacio de veyntiqua tro horas daua vuelta al mundo, causando con su presen cia el dia, y con su ausencia la noche; y con tres bueltas
translation:
First Part. Book 1.

that extended from the surface of the earth to the empyrean heaven, was in darkness and shadows: and in this darkness and tenebrous night the world remained for the space of half a natural day. At the end of which, the first light and perfection that God placed in the world he had created in that imperfect state, began to emerge, by which his works were illuminated and made manifest; and the days began to be counted, in which God continued producing and perfecting what remained so that the Universe might attain its proper perfection. This light did not proceed from any body, but rather God himself produced it directly, in the manner in which it might derive from some luminous body, moving swiftly from one place to another across the entire circumference of the world: so that those first three days of time were one continuous and brilliant production of light. This light illuminated one hemisphere of the world from the surface of the earth to that of the water and the vault of the Empyrean heaven, penetrating all the depth and multitude of waters that lay between. And with a uniform motion it went leaving the eastern hemisphere and passing to the western, in the manner that the Sun now runs its course; and in the same space of twenty-four hours it made one circuit of the world, causing by its presence the day, and by its absence the night; and with three turns

text:
Historia del nuevo mundo.
que dio en torno de la tierra viejo, a tras primeros dias, y del
tiempo.

El parage, y punto en que dios crio aquella luz, se coli
ge del sitio de como describe Moises el tiempo; porque ha
blando un los Hebreos lo distribuye, y pinta respeto de la
region, y provincia de Palestina, en cuyo Oriente orien
tal es, y amos probable opinion que fue producida; como
quando aora la amanece el Sol alos de aquella tierra de
manera que algunto de la creacion de la dicha luz, comer
cio a ser de mañana en aquella region: no de otra suerte
que si entonces le naciese el Sol. Aparecio pues el primer
dia doce horas despues de criado el mundo; y asi el primer
dia natural en Palestina fue de veyntiquatro horas,
doce de tinieblas, de noche, desde el punto de la cre
acion hasta que fue producida la luz; y las otras doce
de dia artificial, desde la produccion de la luz, hasta el
ocaso della respeto de la dicha provincia de Palestino.
Y en este sentido por tardarse del primer dia entendio Mo
yses aquel tiempo de tinieblas, que precedioala luz; y
por nombre de Mañana, el dia artificial desde el
nacimiento de la luz, hasta su ocaso.

En el qual sentido tambien es verdad auer criado dios
en el primer dia el cielo, la tierra, y el agua, como dice
la sagrada escritura; pues crio estos tres cuerpos en el
instante indicativo de las doce horas de tinieblas, que

Genesis.
translation:
History of the New World.
which extended around the old earth, in the first days, and of
time.

The place and point at which God created that light can be
gathered from the site as Moses describes the time; because speaking
among the Hebrews he distributes it and depicts it with respect to the
region and province of Palestine, in whose eastern
Orient it is, and it is our probable opinion that it was produced there; just as
when the Sun now dawns upon the people of that land in such
a way that from some point of the creation of the said light, it began
to be morning in that region: no differently
than if the Sun had been born for it at that moment. The first
day therefore appeared twelve hours after the world was created; and so the first
natural day in Palestine was twenty-four hours,
twelve of darkness, of night, from the moment of cre
ation until the light was produced; and the other twelve
of artificial day, from the production of the light until the
sunset thereof with respect to the said province of Palestine.
And in this sense, by the delay from the first day, Moses understood
that period of darkness which preceded the light; and
by the name of Morning, the artificial day from the
birth of the light until its sunset.

In which sense it is also true that God created
on the first day the sky, the earth, and the water, as
Holy Scripture says; for he created these three bodies in the
indicative instant of the twelve hours of darkness, which

Genesis.

text:
Primera parte. Libro 1.
fueron la primera parte del primer dia natural: porque
de la tarde, y mañana de la suerte que ha dicho, se cumplio,
y fue hecho el primer dia del tiempo. el mismo sentido
tiene el estilo que guardo Moises de contar los demas di
as siguientes, comenzando por la tarde, y diciendo que
fue hecha la tarde, y la mañana el segundo dia, el ter
cero, el quarto etc. Porque por auer el tiempo de la tinie
blas precedido al de la luz, y sido la primera parte del
primer dia, comenzo Moises la cuenta de los dias por
la noche, llamando la tarde, y al dia artificial Ma
ñana. lo qual concuerda con el computo, y costumbre
de los Hebreos, que comenzaron a contar los dias desde
la puesta del sol; y lo aprendieron de este lugar, y modo
de contar de Moises los principios, y los fines de los dias
de la creacion del mundo.

el segundo dia hizo Dios de la materia de las aguas,
y en medio de ellas, el firmamento, el ves todos los cu
er pos simples, de que consta el Vniuerso, fuera de los
tres sobredichos que al principio fueron criados de nada.
Porque el buen orden de la fabrica de esta casa del mun
do pedia que primero se hizieran las paredes, que son
los cuerpos simples hendidos con nombre de firma
mento: y despues se le fuere añadiendo lo que tocaua a su
ornato, y al habot: y finalmente entrase en ello
el dueño, que la auia de habitar, y para usos, y uso,
translation:
First Part. Book 1.
were the first part of the first natural day: because from the evening and morning, in the manner described, it was completed, and the first day of time was made. The same meaning is found in the style that Moses kept in counting the remaining days that followed, beginning from the evening, and saying that the evening and the morning were the second day, the third, the fourth, etc. Because the time of darkness had preceded that of light, and had been the first part of the first day, Moses began the count of days from the night, calling the evening, and the artificial day, Morning. This agrees with the reckoning and custom of the Hebrews, who began to count days from sunset; and they learned this from this passage, and from Moses's manner of counting the beginnings and ends of the days of the creation of the world.

On the second day, God made from the matter of the waters, and in the midst of them, the firmament, which are all the simple bodies of which the Universe is composed, apart from the three aforementioned which at the beginning were created from nothing. For the good order of the fabric of this house of the world required that first the walls be made, which are the simple bodies divided under the name of the firmament; and afterward there would be added to it what pertained to its adornment and to its dwelling; and finally the owner who was to inhabit it would enter into it, for its uses and purpose,

comodidad no apariçada. y asi criado que fue el mun
do el primer dia en aquel estado imperfecto, y produ
cida salud; en los siguientes lo fue el hacedor perfi
cionando, y adornando. en orden a lo qual el segu
do dia acabo de fabricar todos los paçios, y partes sir
cunantes del, con produçir todos los çielos que abraça
el empireo, y el elemento del ayre. y con esto dividio
las aguas que quedaron sobre el firmamento, y de bajo de
el çielo empireo de las que estan acabajo entre los elemen
tos de la tierra, y del ayre.

enterado, y compuesto ya el mundo de todas sus partes,
y cuerpos intrinsecos, comenzo el divino artifice el
tercero dia a disponerlo, ya comodarlo para el fin
para que lo havia criado. y como toda via el agua ocu
pase toda la superficie de la tierra, como obediava suna
tural inclinacion, aparto estos dos elementos, recogi
endo las aguas a un lugar para que la tierra quedase
descubierta, ya comodada para la habitacion de los
hombres, y animales, y todo lo demas que rame
netos para el ministerio de los hombres. Para ha
cer esta separacion levanto la tierra por muchas
partes
translation:
History of the New World

convenience not yet apparent. And so, having created the world on the first day in that imperfect state, and having brought forth life, in the following days the Creator proceeded to perfect and adorn it. Toward this end, on the second day He finished fashioning all the spaces and surrounding parts of it, by bringing forth all the heavens that the empyrean embraces, and the element of air. And with this He divided the waters that remained above the firmament from those below the empyrean heaven, between the elements of earth and air.

Chapter 4. How God perfected and populated the world with the innumerable species of things that passed through it.

The world being now fully formed and composed of all its parts and intrinsic bodies, the divine artificer began on the third day to arrange it and accommodate it for the purpose for which He had created it. And since water still covered the entire surface of the earth, following its natural inclination, He separated these two elements, gathering the waters into one place so that the land would be left uncovered and made ready for the habitation of men and animals, and everything else that was necessary for the service of mankind. To bring about this separation He raised the earth in many parts

text:
Bisnaraginte. Libro 1.
partes, desnigualando su superficie, y que hasta entonces estauan
por accidente redonda, y en igual distancia de su centro:
las de fando unas partes mas altas que otras, en las mas hun
didas, y valles formograudes, y capaces concauidades, a
manera de hondas fosos, estanques, y henellas, recogió,
y encerro las aguas. y porque todas las fuentes, y congre
gaciones de ellas llamadas mares, se continuan, y comu
nican entros, como la experiencia de los nauegaciones
modernas lo ha descubierto; pero es contrario dicelo
escritura sagrada, que fueron juntadas las aguas en
un lugar: aunque no es uno solo el mar, ni esta parte que
no, parte de brunidos, y la tierra a otra; sino muchos, y
distribuidos por toda ella. Recogidas desta suerte las aguas
del mar, les mezclo Dios muchas exhalaciones terrestres,
secas, y requemadas, unque las volvio saladas para
su pes, conservacion, y otras abilidades; y lo de uso que
perpetuamente la virtud del sol, y de los talros fuero pro
duciendo la mismas exhalaciones, y retirando en el
agua las partes que dellas por varios casos se van siempre
corrompiendo: porque antes que las aguas se retiraran al
mar, no eran saladas, presupuesto que no auia criado Dios
niño alguno, mas de cuya por impeso, y los elementos por
seu virtuan en su puridad: en este hecho de recoger las aguas
en un lugar no solo atendio el criador a que cobdase de su
esta la tierra, que auia de poblar de hombres, animales,
translation:
Book 1.
parts, making its surface uneven, so that until then it had been by accident round, and at equal distance from its center: leaving some parts higher than others, and in the lowest places forming large and spacious hollows, in the manner of deep ditches, pools, and reservoirs, into which He gathered and enclosed the waters. And because all the springs and gatherings of water called seas are connected and communicate with one another, as the experience of modern navigations has discovered; yet Holy Scripture says the contrary, that the waters were gathered together into one place: although the sea is not just one single body, nor is this part that lies between the dry land and the other part; but rather many, distributed throughout the whole earth. The waters of the sea being gathered together in this manner, God mixed into them many terrestrial exhalations, dry and parched, though He made them salty for their preservation and other purposes; and it is understood that perpetually the power of the sun and of other forces kept producing these same exhalations, and restoring to the water those parts which through various causes continually decay within it: because before the waters retired to the sea, they were not salty, given that God had not yet created any living thing, but all things were in their pure simplicity, and the elements preserved their purity. In this act of gathering the waters into one place, the Creator intended not only that the land should be uncovered, which was to be populated by men, animals,

text:
Historia del nuevo mundo.
plantas; sino tambien el aire por estado, y conservacion
de la misma agua. Porque aviendo de criar el sol, y los
demas astros, si la tienan su superficie descubierta, mas
engendrara el ayre encerrado en las concavidades de la
tanta copia de agua, quanta manan perpetuamente
las fuentes, y por los rios corre al mar, para res
taurar lo que por toda su superficie perpetuamente con su
men el sol, y los otros astros, y convierten en ayre,
y vapores humidos.

Al tiempo que levanto Dios las partes de la tierra, que
estan eminentes sobre el agua, dispuso con tal artificio
y providencia las sierras, montes, valles, y lugares
soterraneos, que a trechos convenientes rrotasen fuentes
de agua; mediante las quales pudiese la tierra habitarse,
y llevar fruto. en que se descubre grandemente la sabi
duria del Criador: la qual no menos resplandece en aver
dado tal postura, y forma a toda la tierra que descu
bierto de agua, que por todas partes este inclinada, y
cutra abaxo haua la mar. Se dendeace que los rios de
cendiendo de todas partes, caminen siempre a ella, dar
lo vueltas, y bordeando las raices de los montes, y sierras,
que poniendoles delante parece les quieren atajar su
curso. y con otros vueltas, y rodeos van abriendo, y
buscando camino; y hazen su canal, y madre cueto
abaxo, corriendo con su movimiento natural, sir
translation:
History of the New World.
plants; but also the air for the state and preservation
of the water itself. Because the sun and the
other stars, if the land had its surface uncovered, would produce
more air enclosed in the cavities of such
a great quantity of water, as much as springs
perpetually give forth, and which flows through rivers to the sea, to restore
what the sun and the other stars perpetually consume
across its entire surface, converting it into air
and moist vapors.

At the time that God raised the parts of the earth that
stand above the water, He arranged with such art
and providence the mountain ranges, mountains, valleys, and underground
places, that at convenient intervals springs of
water would flow; by means of which the land could be inhabited
and bear fruit. In this one can clearly see the wisdom
of the Creator, which shines no less in having given
such a position and form to all the dry
land, uncovered by water, that it slopes on all sides
downward toward the sea. From this it follows that rivers,
descending from all parts, always make their way toward it, turning
and winding around the bases of mountains and ranges,
which, placed before them, seem to want to block their
course. And with other turns and detours they go opening and
finding their way; and they make their channel and bed ever
downward, running with their natural movement, serving

text:
Binreographia. libro 1.
detenerse hasta entrar en lamar. y quando topan al
gun obstaculo, que les ataja el paso, entonces devassar
dose sus aguas, forman las lagunas, y esperos, hasta
que rebosando por lo alto de la tierra, que la sirve, y ro
dea, tornan acorrer para donde yuan. Sin ve es que
vengaya a ser tan poca la cantidad de agua, que se
emboca en la tierra; o por venas ocultas, y subterraneas
corra por debaxo de ella.

Asimismo quando hizo Dios se retiraron las aguas de
mar, levantando la tierra; jundo en el centro della el in
fierno; y otros senos, y concavidades, que creemos que
ay en sus entrañas. con lo qual, vino a haverla dejado
por muchas partes cavernosa, y llena de poros, sin que
llea igual densidad, con que fue criada, sino mucho suel
do, y circunferencia, ocupando mucho mayor lugar
que antes tenia. Asimismo produxo en ella todos los
generos de miños inanimados, que encierra en su se
nos, como son los minerales de piedras, y metales. Por
que aunque de la produccion destos miños, que tambien
eran necesarios para el servicio de los hombres, no se ha
ga especial mencion en el primer capitulo del Genesis: de
vemos conocer averse sido producidos de la tierra en el tercero
dia, primero que las plantas, como inferiores a ellas.

Despues de criados los miños, o cuerpos compuestos in
animados, luego el mismo dia vio Dios la tierra
translation:
Geography. Book 1.
to stop before entering the sea. And when they encounter some obstacle that blocks their path, their waters then overflow and form lakes and marshes, until, spilling over the high ground that serves them and surrounds them, they return to running where they were going. Unless it should happen that the quantity of water that flows into the earth is so small, or that it runs through hidden and subterranean veins beneath it.

Likewise, when God caused the waters of the sea to withdraw, raising up the land, He placed Hell at its center, along with other cavities and hollows that we believe exist within its depths. By this means, the earth came to be left cavernous in many places, and full of pores, no longer of the uniform density with which it was created, but much looser, and in circumference occupying a much greater space than it had before. Likewise, He produced within it all the kinds of inanimate minerals that it encloses in its bosom, such as the minerals of stones and metals. For although the production of these minerals, which were also necessary for the service of mankind, is not specifically mentioned in the first chapter of Genesis, we must understand that they were produced from the earth on the third day, before the plants, as things inferior to them.

After the minerals, or inanimate composite bodies, had been created, later that same day God looked upon the earth

Historia del nuevo mundo.
De todos los generos de plantas, asi para ornamento, y hermosura
de la misma tierra, como, para tener en ellos el mantenimien
to de los animales, que havia de criar los dias siguientes, par
ticularmente el sustento del hombre, y produxolas en el
estado, grandeza, y perfeccion, que requeria la naturaleza
de cada especie, conforme a la calidad de la region, y temple
en que las puso.

Con ocasion del ser que tenian las plantas quando las crio
el señor, disputan en este lugar los Autores de la esfera en
que tiempo del año fue criado el mundo: y aunque con
vinieron casi todos en que fue sin razon en el equinoio, los
mas grandes dellos estan divididos en dos partes. Los unos lle
van que en el equinoio de setiembre, que para los que
viven en el Hemisferio Artico es Autumnal, y Vernal
para los que havemos en este Antartico: y los otros que en el
equinoio de Marzo, que al contrario para nosotros es Au
tumnal, y para los habitadores del otro hemisferio, Ver
nal. el fundamento de los primeros, es porque parecio
mas conveniente que criao Dios las plantas con sus frutos
sazonados, quales estan por aquel tiempo: y el de los se
gundos, porque el equinoio de Marzo es mas aproposito
para la generacion, y aumento de las cosas, que no el se
tiembre, quando todos los frutos, y plantas se desminui
yen por estar el invierno tan vecino. Donde se hade notar
que los unos, y los otros presuponen que produxo Dios las
plantas en el ser, y estado que pedia la naturaleza de cada
translation:
History of the New World.
Of all the kinds of plants, both for the ornamentation and beauty
of the earth itself, and to provide in them the sustenance
of the animals that were to be created in the following days, and
particularly the food of man, He produced them in the
state, greatness, and perfection that the nature
of each species required, according to the quality of the region and climate
in which He placed them.

On the occasion of the state of being that plants had when the Lord
created them, the Authors of the sphere dispute in this place
at what time of year the world was created; and although nearly
all agreed that it was at an equinox, the
greatest among them are divided into two groups. Some hold
that it was at the September equinox, which for those who
live in the Arctic Hemisphere is Autumnal, and Vernal
for those of us in this Antarctic region; and others hold that it was at the
equinox of March, which on the contrary for us is Au
tumnal, and for the inhabitants of the other hemisphere, Ver
nal. The argument of the first group is that it seemed
more fitting that God created the plants with their fruits
ripened, as they are at that time; and that of the se
cond group, because the equinox of March is more suitable
for the generation and increase of things than Sep
tember, when all fruits and plants diminish
because winter is so near. It should be noted here
that both groups presuppose that God produced the
plants in the state and condition that the nature of each

Primera parte. Libro 1.
una atento al calidad, y clima del lugar en que nacieron, sin
hacer nuevo milagro, para que pueblos e frutos fuera de su ti
empo: si bien no dudan algunos de conceder que Dios mila
grosamente, sobre lo que la naturaleza d el traspedia, pro
dujo algunas plantas juntamente con flor, y fruto mo
duro para hermosura del Universo, y sustento del hom
bre, y de muchos animales.
Si en esta contrariedad de opiniones, tengo de decir mi pa
recer, siento que como todos los Autores, que hasta agora
han ventilado, y escrito sobre este particular, son habitado
res del hemisferio Setentrional, y no han tenido e pe
riencia de otros temples mas de los de su region; asi halla

The opinion of the greater part of the saints and Christian philosophers, that the world was created at the equinox of March, is one I also hold, founded principally, along with many of them, on the observation that it pleased God our Redeemer to die at that same equinox. This is no poor argument that it was at that time that our first parents sinned, since our Savior chose that same moment to satisfy the eternal Father through His death for their disobedience, and to obtain pardon for all their children. In keeping with this reckoning, we must say that God made the world four days before the equinox of March: so that the sun, which was created on the fourth day, came into being at that same equinox, at the beginning of the sign of Aries, from which point it immediately began to move by its own motion through the zodiac toward the east.

On the fourth day the divine Artificer produced all the stars and luminaries of the eighth heaven, properly called the firmament, and the Planets of the other lower heavens, upon whose movement and influences the life of animals depends more than that of plants. And so for the preservation of these, the light created on the first day was sufficient for that brief time. La esfera de una parte a otra. De manera que todos los círculos mayores pasan por el centro de la tierra, y los menores cortan la bordura de ella que corresponde en derecho de la superficie del cielo, desde el los se describen. Y conforme a esto todas las divisiones, que hacen del mundo con estos círculos, se hade entender ser hechas no solo en la superficie de la esfera, sino también en su profundidad: de modo, que desde la dicha superficie yendo vamos pando derechos, cortando, y señalando cielos, y elementos, hasta la tierra.
Los círculos de la esfera unos son mayores, y otros menores: mayor es el que la divide en dos partes iguales, o mitades: y menor el que la corta en dos partes desiguales. Aquel a quien de las dos partes iguales, en que el círculo mayor divide la esfera, llaman Hemisferio, porque este nombre que ve decir en griego media esfera, que es lo mismo que la mitad del mundo. Los círculos mayores son seis, equinodial, orizonte, Meridiano, la línea eclíptica del Zodiaco, y los dos círculos llamados colures.
La línea equinocial es un círculo de los mayores de la esfera, dista por todas partes igualmente de los dos Polos del mundo: que son los términos, y puntos, en que se remata el eje de la esfera, y tiene varios nombres: el uno se llama Polo del Norte, o Ártico, Septentrional, Boreal, y Aquilonal: y el otro, Polo del Sur, o Antartico, Austral, y Meridional. Por este círculo se divide la esfera en dos.
translation:

The sphere from one part to another. In such a way that all the great circles pass through the center of the earth, and the lesser ones cut the boundary of it that corresponds directly beneath the surface of the sky, from which they are described. And in accordance with this, all the divisions that the great circles make of the world are to be understood as made not only on the surface of the sphere, but also through its depth: so that starting from the said surface and going straight down, cutting through and marking out the heavens and the elements, all the way to the earth.
The circles of the sphere are some greater and some lesser: a great circle is one that divides it into two equal parts, or halves; and a lesser one is that which cuts it into two unequal parts. That which consists of the two equal parts into which the great circle divides the sphere is called a Hemisphere, because this name, which in Greek means half-sphere, is the same as half of the world. The great circles are six: the equinoctial, the horizon, the meridian, the ecliptic line of the Zodiac, and the two circles called the colures.
The equinoctial line is one of the great circles of the sphere, equidistant on all sides from the two Poles of the world: which are the limits and points at which the axis of the sphere ends. It has various names: one is called the North Pole, or Arctic, Septentrional, Boreal, and Aquilonal; and the other, the South Pole, or Antarctic, Austral, and Meridional. By this circle the sphere is divided into two.

equal parts, or hemispheres; each of which takes its name from the Pole that falls on its side. The one belonging to the North is called the Arctic, or Septentrional, Boreal, or Aquilonal hemisphere; we also call it the Northern part. And that of the South is called the Antarctic, Austral, Meridional, or Southern hemisphere. From the said Poles to the equinoctial line there are ninety degrees of latitude, out of the three hundred and sixty into which these Astronomers divide the entire circumference and circuit of the sphere. These equinoctial circles serve to determine the latitude and longitude of degrees, the equinoxes, the climatic zones, and other effects.

The Horizon is another great circle of the sphere, which divides it equally on all sides from our zenith, which is a point we imagine in the sky directly perpendicular above our heads; and from the Nadir, which is another point corresponding to the zenith directly below our feet on the other part of the sphere that we cannot see. From each of these points to any part of the horizon there are ninety degrees. Each location has its own horizon, which divides the part of the world we can see from the part we cannot: that which we see we call the superior hemisphere, and the other the inferior hemisphere.

The Meridian is the third of the great circles of the sphere, which passes through the North and South poles of the world, and through our zenith and Nadir. When the Sun reaches the feet of this circle, falling into the superior hemisphere, it is midday; and when it crosses through the inferior hemisphere, it is midnight. It divides the world into two halves called hemispheres; they are also

Chapter 6. On Climates.

Some cosmographers use the circles called parallels, while others use them to divide the world into climates. They call these circles parallels because each one runs around the sphere at an equal distance from the equinoctial line on all sides. A climate is the space in which there is a difference of half an hour in the longest day of the year, beginning from the equinoctial line and proceeding toward either pole of the world. And because those who live beneath the equinoctial line have days equal to twelve hours throughout the entire year, and from there the days gradually differentiate by another twelve hours up to the altitude of sixty-six and a half degrees — up to which altitude there is throughout the year a distinction between day and night — they count twenty-four climates in the following manner.

The space from the equinoctial line to eight degrees and three, not four minutes of latitude, where the longest day of the year is twelve and a half hours, is the first climate.

The second climate begins at eight degrees and thirty-four minutes, and ends at sixteen degrees and forty-three minutes; at which altitude the longest day of the year is thirteen hours, and the shortest is eleven.

Hence arises the difference in temperatures that we experience in the regions of this Southern hemisphere, compared to those experienced by other regions that lie at the same polar altitude in the Northern hemisphere.

As proof of this we can give as an example two provinces of equal climates in both hemispheres, from experience: let them be that of Charcas in this Southern hemisphere, in the kingdom of Peru; and that of Mexico in the Northern hemisphere, in the kingdom of New Spain. Both fall under the third climate zone and at the same latitude, yet despite this they are very different in their qualities and products. For the province of Charcas has drier air; its high, cold mountains are bare; and in the deep valleys and ravines where groves of trees grow, they are of very different species from those found in New Spain, such as quinine, soto, villa, and other hardwoods of that same kind. And those same valleys are very well suited for vineyards, and thus a great quantity of excellent wine is harvested there.

On the contrary, the province of Mexico has more humid air, with denser forests, found on the high cold mountains near the snowy peaks, and the trees that grow there are pines, junipers, cypresses, oaks, and other kinds, so that apart from the cedar, which grows in both climates, no other species of the same kind is found in both. And the warm valleys of the province of Mexico, such as those of the Marquesado, are not suited for vineyards, but rather for sugar cane plantations.

The astrologers hold that there are ten of them, which number they have chosen from just as many distinct motions that have been observed in them. In the first eight there are stars; and the last three lack them. All the stars are of the same matter as the heavens, but of a different substantial form; and consequently of a distinct species. The tenth heaven is what the astronomers call the prime mover, because it is the first that moves, and with its movement it carries along and draws after itself those that are beneath it. It completes its movement, which we call diurnal, from East to West over the poles of the world, and in the space of twenty-four hours makes a full revolution, so uniformly and regularly that it never moves at one time more quickly than at another. The speed of this movement at its outermost sphere is so great that it equals thought itself. In the lower heavens it grows greater the more they are separated from the tenth; as we see in any wheel that turns. Each of the ten heavens is attended and moved by an Angel, whom the ancient philosophers called Intelligences.

The empyrean heaven embraces and encompasses within itself all the other heavens, and surpasses them all in greatness, brightness, and beauty; and chiefly in the dignity of its nature; as befitted the office and purpose for which it was made, to be the theater of the celestial court and the dwelling of the blessed. It does not move, because it is a place of quiet and rest; and yet for all that it sends its influence down to the lower heavens; and many learned men are of the opinion that the diversity of conditions seen in some parts of the earth within the same climate arises from the influence of this heaven.

Chapter 8. On the aspect of the Southern sky, and the stars we lose sight of there.

I have not been able to consult with anyone on earth about the observation of this southern hemisphere's sky as much as I would have wished, because very few people devote themselves to its study, from whom one might gather the particular observations there are to be made regarding its appearance, and the many stars that we left behind on the voyage as we came to this southern part of the world, which the inhabitants of Europe do not know. And so what I have been able to learn about the matter has come through my own labor alone; for which reason I do not have the satisfaction I would have had, if what I write in this chapter had passed through the scrutiny of persons knowledgeable in astronomy. This is reason enough for me to be forgiven, if in treating these matters by my judgment alone, I should fall into some errors.

This part of the Southern sky is the most beautiful and clear, not inferior in beauty to the other, that of the North: rather it seems to me that it surpasses it in brightness; as we experience in those lands that enjoy a clear sky, free of clouds; which is the case in part of the plains, which lie away from the sea, at the foot of the mountains; and on the slopes facing the Southern sea of the same mountain range. And of the second, the provinces of the highlands bordering those same plains, such as the city of Arequipa, which lies at sixteen degrees South. In that city, where I resided for three years, I made the observations contained in this chapter, owing to the very great purity and serenity of the sky that city enjoys every night of the year.

The beauty and clarity of the sky are caused, first, by the signs of the Zodiac, which fall nearer to us than to those of Europe. Second, and more principally, by that part of the Milky Way which in this region encompasses two particular constellations, and other large stars, and certain brilliantly shining parts of the sky that we have discovered here.

The Milky Way is a part of the firmament and the eighth heaven, which girds it all around, or from one side to the other, like a sash or band; or, better said, in the manner of a baldric — a splendid band, sparkling with precious stones, which lend it remarkable ornament and beauty. The source of its brightness is a matter of debate among astronomers, whether it comes from a multitude of tiny stars with which it is packed and which our sight cannot reach; or from being

Whether this brightness comes from its own nature or from another source, what we observe is that the part of the Milky Way that falls in the Antarctic hemisphere, with its many more stars and brilliance, exceeds what falls in the northern part. For looking from our zenith toward the southern pole and the other pole, we discover the entire semicircle it makes on the southern side; and on the northern side, just a little past our own zenith, it disappears and we can no longer distinguish it from the rest of the sky. And viewed from the northern hemisphere, as I myself observed many times while residing in New Spain, we experience the same thing: that the part of the Milky Way contained in the Antarctic hemisphere is much brighter than what is included in the Arctic hemisphere. De las dos constelaciones, o figuras notables, que observamos en este hemisferio; la mayor, y mas principales la que llamamos Crucero; la qual consta de quatro Estrellas puestas en figura de una perfecta cruz; la qual se endereza, y levanta quando esta nuestro Meridiano, respeto de estar Norte Sur las dos estrellas que forman el pie, y cabeza de la cruz; las quales distan un poco mas entre si, que las otras dos, de que se forman los brazos: de manera que todas quatro muestran figura de una cruz levantada en alto derecha. La estrella del brazo derecho, y mas oriental esta algo mas apartada de la linea, que imaginamos desde el pie a la cabeza que la del brazo Izquierdo; y asi se mueve el un brazo un poquito mas largo que el otro. La magnitud de estas estrellas parece ser aquesta: la estrella del pie, que es la mayor, y mas proxima al polo Antartico, del qual dista treynta grados, es de segunda magnitud. La de la cabeza, y la del brazo derecho son ambas de tercera magnitud: y la del brazo Izquierdo de la quarta. La estrella, y la del pie se muestra otra estrella de quinta magnitud casi igualmente distante de ambas. Por la estrella del pie de la cruz toman de noche la altura los navegantes con la ballestilla; y ella con la de la cabeza sirve de relox de noche.

Of the two constellations, or notable figures, that we observe in this hemisphere; the greater and most principal is the one we call the Southern Cross; which consists of four stars arranged in the shape of a perfect cross; which straightens and rises when our Meridian is such that the two stars forming the foot and head of the cross stand North to South; these stars are a little farther apart from each other than the other two that form the arms: so that all four display the figure of a cross raised upright. The star of the right arm, being the most easterly, is somewhat farther from the line we imagine running from foot to head than the star of the left arm; and thus one arm is a little longer than the other. The magnitude of these stars appears to be as follows: the star at the foot, which is the largest and closest to the Antarctic Pole — from which it is thirty degrees distant — is of the second magnitude. That of the head and that of the right arm are both of the third magnitude; and that of the left arm is of the fourth. Near the star of the foot another star of the fifth magnitude appears, almost equally distant from both. By the star at the foot of the Cross, navigators take their altitude at night using the cross-staff; and that star together with the one at the head serves as a clock by night.

It has its station in the sign of Scorpio, and the Milky Way is found there; and so the Southern Cross appears to it like a jewel of very fine and circular diamonds, as if hanging from a necklace of precious stones.
Around this constellation one can see certain patches of the Milky Way much brighter than the rest of it; and among them, particularly near the star at the foot of the Cross, two other patches of sky much darker than the rest of the same sky. And accompanying the Cross are principally two very large stars, which follow a little behind it, at nearly equal height, which we call the Guardians of the Cross: the larger appears to be of the first magnitude, lies to the east of the other, thirty degrees distant from the south pole, and falls in the sign of Sagittarius. The smaller, and more westerly, is of the second magnitude, and lies in the sign of Scorpio.
In the aforesaid sign of Sagittarius, a little further to the east and at nearly the same height as the Guardians of the Cross, there are three stars that form a perfect triangular figure: the most easterly of them appears to be of the third magnitude, and the other two of the fourth. To the other constellation they have given the name of Fiduarius. It is composed of four stars arranged in a row running North-Northwest to Southeast, the largest being the most westerly and northerly, positioned on the Meridian. They are not all equally distant from one another, nor are they all the same size. The one farthest from the South Pole, which is the largest, is of the third magnitude; and it is the closest to the second star among the others. The second is as far from the third as the third is from the fourth. The third is of the fifth magnitude, and the other two are of the fourth. They are all close together and unaccompanied by other stars, so that this figure can be seen very distinctly, except that near the sides of the third star some small stars of the fifth and sixth magnitude can be seen. All the stars of this constellation fall in the sign of Aries, between the two white patches of which I shall speak shortly; and the two foremost stars of it serve as a clock by night.

Of all that is contained in the eight chapters, the Indians likewise did not manage to know, nor did they wish to have a name that would signify the universe: nor did they understand anything of its figures, magnitudes, and principal parts. Nor in citing from it, any noted Origin is given, and for all these things in their common language, not that of Peru, they called the sky unan, naming it "which means a high place; they were ignorant of the number of the stars, and the variety of their movements. They only knew and gave names to some of the larger ones, and observed the change of seasons caused by the course of the sun in regard to their farming and festivals.

No nation of Indians so barbarous has been found in this
new world, that they did not make use of fire, though perhaps
in ways more difficult than ours. But they did not
consider it an element of the world, nor did they assign it
a special place. In the two general languages of
Peru, Quechua and Aymara, it has one and the same name,
which is, Nina. As the natives of all these
islands and regions lacked the use of iron, they could not strike fire
from flints, having no steel with which to make
strikers. The method by which they obtained it everywhere
was this: they took a dry stick about two or three finger-widths
thick, and a third of a length more or less, which
they called Mora, and in the middle of it they made a
small hole or cavity, which did not pass through to the other side,
but only reached to the center, in the manner
of a small hollow. They placed this stick on the ground flat; then
the Indian, placing his feet on its ends, held it
very firm. Then taking another dry stick, thinner
than a finger of the hand, and fashioning
one end into a point, he inserted it into the hollow
or hole of the other, loosely fitted;
this he rubbed between his palms very firmly, moving
it to one side and the other without stopping, as one who
twists thread on a spindle; until with so much heat from
one stick upon the other, it began to kindle fire in the

If from the lowest land we climb a great hill, we experience that the air grows sensibly colder, the higher we climb; and if at the summit of the hill there are two or three snowfields, it is intensely cold and dry; the flat lands are dry for many seasons; such as those called the province of the Collao; in the middle of the flat land, we feel the air no less cold than at the top of the hill. From which it may be inferred that if the region of air nearest the earth were warm by reflection of the sun's rays, the surrounding air of the said plains ought to be more temperate than that which is experienced at the heights of the hill, but it is not, being rather of the same quality and intensity of cold as at the beginning of the said plains; even though the air is calm and still, with no wind blowing at all.

It is a property of vapors and exhalations — being warm fumes and warm vapors — to temper and moderate the cold; for rising, as they do, ever higher by means of the heat of the sun, even though some may be cold in themselves, they must at least accidentally and incidentally become so.

The cause of this effect, I can only attribute to the vapors that the sun draws up from the lake itself.
