Storms of downpours and lightning bolts are commonly formed over those low-lying lands in the region of the air that falls far below them, and thus they see the clouds and storms as if from a vantage point, and from above, looking at the backs of the clouds; and the lightning bolts that shoot out of them rise upward in the manner of flying rockets. From this experience one concludes that it is not necessary, in order for these inflamed impressions to be generated, nor for the clouds to churn about in the air, that there be a sufficient region of air — which many philosophers place as warmer than the first and middle regions — nor is there any need to distinguish and mark out other degrees and regions in the air. For as the vapors and exhalations rise up to the point where the cold is sufficient to condense them, they go no further; this being so because the air that lies beyond that point is much colder, as we experience when we find ourselves in places higher than the clouds that cover the low-lying lands of the surrounding area.

We observe it to be established that when it rains gently and to the benefit of the sown fields, the clouds do not rise above the hilltops, but rather keep them covered from their midpoint upward; and such rains bring us new things and please the farmers, because they come soft and quiet, without the noise of thunder and lightning, and they generally last longer. But when the clouds rise above the hills, leaving their peaks free and uncovered, the rains are violent, accompanied by great thundering and lightning; and most commonly in these storms there falls snow or hail. The aforementioned lands of the Collao are very prone to lightning strikes, being, as has been said, very high, though of great flatness. From which one may gather that it is not so certain as some say that tall towers and mountains are struck by lightning more frequently than flat land, on account of the lightning coming at an angle and snaking along. I hold for myself that this happens solely on account of elevation, as we have experienced in the said flat lands of the Collao, which by virtue of being so far raised above the center of the world are the most assailed by lightning of all the Antarctic hemisphere and meridional America.

Chapter 11. On the winds of the Indies.
46

The matter of the winds, which was already discussed in the previous chapter, pertains to these: the winds take on much of the character of the lands and seas through which they pass. Those that blow ordinarily in the region that falls within the tropics and the Torrid Zone are of two kinds: some are common and general throughout the entire year along the sea coasts, and others blow in the interior lands. At sea, and along the coasts, easterly winds blow most frequently, particularly offshore, and these we call Brisas; they are very favorable for sailing from Europe to the Indies, and from here to China, the East Indies, and for returning from there to Europe, because they always travel around the world from East to West, in which they appear to follow the diurnal movement of the heavens. Along the coastal lands, the South wind and the North wind are almost continuous, one on some coasts and the other on others. Along all the coasts of the mainland and of Peru, the South wind — which we call Sur — is the most frequent throughout the year; and sometimes when it ceases, the North wind takes over. When this happens, it is most often at night and in the mornings, and as midday approaches, the South wind rises again from the land.

On the coasts of the northern hemisphere, the North wind is more frequent; and between these two winds one experiences

There are notable differences; the first is that the South wind in the climates of the Southern Hemisphere, which is its native region, is very gentle, pure, and mild; it crosses the equinoctial line, and entering the opposite hemisphere it becomes stormy and hot. On the contrary, the North wind in its Arctic hemisphere is cold; and as it passes beyond its limits and enters the other, it turns either cold or warm depending on the land that tempers it with the great coldness that the ocean water along the coast always holds. The South wind in its hemisphere communicates this to it and makes it unhealthy; and the North wind likewise in its northern region; and the others from the south cause sickness that unsettles the body and causes headaches. Beyond that, the North wind in its hemisphere, particularly in the Sea of the North, tends to be so vehement and furious that it causes terrible storms and shipwrecks; for which reason the fleets of New Spain are compelled to winter in the port of Veracruz from September until February, which are the months when the Nortes reign along those coasts; and even within the port itself the ships need to be well anchored and moored to defend themselves from its fury. But once past the equinoctial line into the other Antarctic hemisphere, the weather becomes well tempered.

In some parts, the southwesterly winds that blow from West to East are far less violent. Sailing from Cartagena to Puerto Belo in a small frigate in the year fifteen hundred and ninety-seven, a Southwesterly rose into such a fierce storm in the vicinity of Nombre de Dios that it forced us to run before the wind, until we found shelter among some fleets, where we stayed until the storm passed.

Inland, far from the sea, the winds are not usually as steady as on the Islands, but blow from all directions, notably from wherever the rains and storms form, which tend to come with winds no less violent than those at sea. And each town takes note of and observes from which direction its winds and downpours come.

Chapter 12. On the element of water.

Water is naturally heavy, though not as much so
as earth; cold and moist. And it is divided into
seas, lakes, bays, springs, and rivers. The sea is the place
where the Creator caused the waters to withdraw and gather,
waters which at the beginning of the world covered the land.
Which land occupies not one side of the world alone, and on the other side the land

Es la mar el principio, fin, y paradero de todas las a-

discovered, but rather that water and land are found everywhere together. Because in the way that God divided the two elements, they remained intermingled equally, with the sea making many inlets with its bays and arms into the land; and the land jutting out into the sea in many places with its shores, promontories, islands, and peninsulas; so that all the uncovered land remains on all sides neighboring the sea, and enjoys its comforts and riches; the winds and tides refresh it; and it is watered by the rains, which originate from its waters.

The sea is the beginning, end, and destination of all waters: because from it come all the rains and springs, and to it, as to a center, they all return. So that although the rivers that flow into the sea are innumerable, and some of prodigious size, as we shall see in this work, the sea neither grows nor overflows, because as much as it receives, it sends back in the form of vapors, which the power of the sun, and of the other stars, constantly draws up from its entire surface: in the same way that, through the heat of fire, the vapors rise from liquids that are distilled. And these vapors that rise from the sea turn into rains; with which the rivers are fed, and the earth, being moistened, generates in its depths and pores the water that flows from springs. The general cordillera of mountain ranges of Peru, which, due to the great amount of water that falls from the sky, springs forth everywhere with fountains and piquios [small irrigation channels or springs]: from which all the rivers that flow from this southern America to the North Sea and the South Sea take their source. And at whatever time it rains, the springs produce more water than in the dry season. And just as the rains are more plentiful, so too are the springs: while on the contrary we see that the lands where it never rains lack springs entirely; as happens in these plains of Peru, which, for lack of rainfall from the sky, have no springs in them, except near the rivers in the valleys that are cultivated and irrigated: for the water there seeps from the rivers themselves and from the water used to irrigate the estates.

We also find by experience that during the season of the garúas [coastal mists and drizzles], which will be discussed in its proper place, in the plains that are watered by them, small springs and fountains tend to appear; and once the garúas have passed they dry up entirely. It is true that in those parts and seasons where that moisture is most abundant, these springs tend to last longer. But in most of the plains, where this rain does not reach, the land is so dry that springs never appear, and for lack of water it is entirely useless, and barren of men and animals.

We give the name Ocean to the sea in general, particularly to the wide and deep gulf that, with its profound bays, touches all parts of the world. And that portion we call the Mediterranean Sea: that arm of the Ocean which, breaking through between Europe and Africa by way of the Strait of Gibraltar, pushes inland to bathe the coasts of Asia. Apart from all these we have the various gulfs and inlets into which the ocean divides and spreads. The most common and well-known division in use today is that which is made of the sea into the North Sea and the South Sea. This division, as befits cosmography, is customarily made along the equinoctial line, so that all that part of the sea lying in the Boreal hemisphere takes the name of the North, and that of the other hemisphere, the Antarctic, takes the name of the South. Geographers and historians do not divide it strictly by that circle, but rather in such a way that a great portion of the sea lying in that hemisphere is counted as the South Sea, and conversely many stretches contained in the Austral hemisphere fall into what is called the North Sea. And there is no fixed mark that defines the limits of each of the seas: some are accustomed to extend them, others to narrow them. The most common way in which this division is made today is this: all the sea that lies to the West of the Americas, and runs from its shores turning westward until

Beyond this, almost all year the current they call self-sustaining, or which it receives from the southern part toward the northern, runs so continuously that sailing in its flow one makes one's way toward the north; and on the contrary it overturns navigation toward the south, so that in less than two hundred leagues between the port of Payta and that of Callao, ships sometimes take five or six months; it being a journey of no more than six to seven days from Callao to Payta. It is a matter very worthy of notice that, although the floods of the rivers on this coast of Peru come in summer, which is the time when it rains in the mountains, from October to March, and these same rivers diminish so greatly in winter that many dry up before reaching the sea — despite all this, the sea shows no change in rising more at one time than at another, but always remains the same. Inquiring into the cause of this admirable constancy, I found it to be the wonderfully ordered arrangement with which God composed the waters of the rivers that feed the sea, so that it might never lack sufficient nourishment: and it is that just as on this southern coast they are the fore-

The nature and properties of the particular springs, rivers, and lakes that we find in this New World are treated in the second and third parts of this history. I think it worth noting here only two things observed in that part of the Indies which falls within the Torrid Zone: the first is that inland one finds very few wells of brackish water, but rather that nearly all those dug yield fresh water, good for drinking. The second is that I have not observed the difference found in Spain in springs and wells with the changes of the seasons of winter and summer — whereby in winter the water flows warm and in summer cold — but rather that here the water is found the same at all times of year.

Chapter 13. On the Element of Earth.

The element of earth is somewhat rough and coarse, it occupies the lowest and central place in the world. Its natural qualities are dry and cold, and whereas the two superior elements are transparent, it is turbid and opaque, unable to be penetrated by light. The earth remains still and immobile by reason of its natural gravity and weight. It and the element of water together form a perfectly round globe, which is suspended on all sides, surrounded by air, and equally distant from the heavens — its properties and attributes being those that Holy Job indicates in those words: qui appendit terram super nihilum: meaning that God placed the globe of the earth in the middle of the universe, and keeps it there fixed and immobile, without resting upon any other body, for its natural weight and inclination — by which it seeks what is lowest and farthest from the heavens — suffices to hold it firm. This inclination is expressed in those words of the Prophet: fundabit terram super stabilitatem suam, nun inclinabitur in seculum seculi: and by this the earth is so still and stable that it never inclines to one side or another, for to do so would be to act against its own nature.

it does not argue against the roundness of the globe of the Sea that the land, being covered by water higher than the plains, has some parts raised into high ridges and mountains, and others low and sunken into valleys and plains. Because these ups and downs in so great a body are of such little consequence, just as a very large ball covered with cordovan leather, with the grain facing outward — the raised and sunken parts that show in the grain would not take away its roundness in that case, even if it would not be as perfect in the strict reckoning of mathematicians as it would be if the surface of such a ball were smooth. The same holds for the globe of the world, which would have a more perfect mathematical roundness if it lacked the high and low places that the land has, and if its surface were so even that all lines drawn from the center were equal — as indeed it was when it was first created. But it suited the purpose of the Lord that it should have mountains and valleys, for the benefits that this unevenness provides to the universe.
For, setting aside the beauty and adornment that the lofty mountains bring to it: from them principally comes the diversity of climates that we experience within a single region, which are so necessary for the production of plants and animals of different natures; in them rivers have their source, and flowing down to the sea they fertilize along the way the plains and valleys,

It is true that the surface of the sea is more perfectly spherical than that of the land, because, being a liquid body, it spreads out evenly, and its surface turns at an equal distance from the center of the world.

This globe, composed of water and land, has a circumference of three hundred and sixty degrees, which by the great circle amounts to six thousand three hundred leagues. Until now it has not been possible to determine what proportion the surface of the water bears to that of the land that lies uncovered, nor which of the two elements occupies the greater part of the terrestrial globe; owing to the scant knowledge we have of that part which falls beneath the poles in the frozen zones. But speaking of what other more learned men have found, the Torrid Zone has no more surface of water than of land that is fertile and habitable; and in the austral regions, from the voyages made in our own times, both in the northern and southern parts, it appears that the ocean occupies the greater part.

Chapter 14. On the division of the earth.

The ancient Geographers divided all the land discovered above the water, of which they had knowledge, into three principal parts, which are Europe, Asia, and Africa. But as soon as these Western Indies were discovered, they were placed as the fourth part of the world under the name of America. And as modern navigations have continued to extend further each day, they have come to find in this Antarctic hemisphere another great portion of land separated from America, and much larger than the other three ancient parts. This land may rightly be considered the fifth part of the world, and as such I believe it should be named the Austral Land, since it encompasses all of it, and its adjacent islands, which

Lo qual decían porque nuestros mapas pintar

Concerning Asia, and the reason I have for trusting the testimony of a natural-born Portuguese cosmographer named N. de Mora, who by order of His Majesty, for this important purpose, which I will shortly explain, sailed around the world twice by sea. The first time sailing from Spain to China through the Eastern hemisphere, and from there returning to Spain by the same route. And the second time making a voyage to the same China through the western hemisphere, within the jurisdiction of Castile. This second voyage he made around the years sixteen thirty-three to thirty-five. I was already living in Mexico when he arrived from Spain, and we lodged him in the professed house of the Society of Jesus in that city, because he carried a letter from our Father General requesting that we house him in our establishments. This gave us a fine opportunity to discuss with him both the outward and return journeys.

And when asked, upon returning from China and the ports of Macao, he brought with him a general map of the entire world. When I noticed how he showed America joined to Asia, and pointed this out to him, he replied that he had done so on the advice of the fathers of the Society of Jesus at Macao, who had been in Tartary bordering Japan, working on the conversion of those peoples. For those peoples reproached the fathers who preached to them, saying that how could they presume to teach them about the things of heaven, if they were ignorant of those of the earth. The task that this man came to undertake on these voyages was to find a way by which degrees of longitude could be measured in voyages made from East to West with the same ease and certainty with which degrees of latitude are obtained by measuring the Sun with the astrolabe; and it truly seems that he succeeded in his scheme, according to the demonstration he gave one day at noon in our house of Tante before all the friars who were there present. Of this scheme I thought it worthwhile to give here a brief account, since it has not yet been published, and in case it should never come to light, some knowledge of it may be preserved. This invention consists in knowing how the meridian is marked on a given day, and from it determining what the compass needle reads in the course of navigation from East to West, or the reverse. For this purpose the author of this device said that the world must be divided by two meridians that cross at the poles into four quarters of ninety degrees each. And that he had found by experience that at these meridians, which divide the world into four quarters, the needle points true north at the pole; and that passing from one meridian to another, the needle goes

translation:
History of the New World

What is properly called palmada is today named Esclavinia, and Salbar
vita is the one that borders it inland. The metropolitan city
of Esclavonia is Ragusa, which maintains its freedom
by paying tribute to the Turk.

Bosnia is separated from Esclavonia by the river Savona; it is
a large and fertile province. Its inhabitants descend from the
Sclatas; they boast of being able to muster thirty thousand cavalry and wage
war against the Turk. Its principal towns are Alasio, Gurago,
and Belona. Between Esclavonia and the Danube lies Bosnia,
a rugged land full of mountains abundant in silver.
To the east of Bosnia lies the province of Serbia, and the
eastern part of it borders Bulgaria, which runs along the
bank of the Danube to the Black Sea.

The province of Macedonia stretches from the Ionian Sea,
where it has the city of Durazzo, to the Aegean Sea, where
Salonika lies. In ancient times it was mistress of many peoples,
but today it is subject to the Turkish yoke.

The province of Greece is full of peninsulas, islands, and sea
inlets. On the eastern side of the Ambracian Gulf lies
Arcadia, and crossing the river Achelous, we enter
Aetolia, whose most famous city is Lepanto.
Next comes Thessaly, surrounded by mountains. The other provinces
are the Morea, Achaia, Messenia, Laconia, and Boeotia,
whose metropolis is Thebes, Demetrias, Negroponte,
and others.

Cap. 16. De la Asia.

La Asia es la mayor parte de las tres del mundo viejo, por
que sola ella es mas grande que juntas Africa, y Europa. Co
mienza su latitud desde la linea equinocial, y va para el
Setentrion hasta los ochenta grados; y asi se comprehende
toda en el hemisferio Artico; de longitud tiene ciento y ve
y nticuatro grados, que por circunferencia mayor hacen dos mil y ci
ento y setenta leguas. Esta por los tres lados cercada del oceano;
y por el occidente se junta con Europa por la Tartaria; y por
el Africa por Egypto. Dividese en siete partes, la primera es la
mas vecina a Europa, desde el oceano Setentrional hasta
el mar Caspio, que antiguamente se llamaua la Sarmatia;
y, aora Moscouia y Moscobia: la segunda, la Tartaria, que
confina con el mar Caspio, con el oceano, y con Moscobia;
la tercera la parte del Turco, que es la parte occidental de
Asia, comprehendida entre el mar caspio, seno Persico,
y rio Tigris: la quarta el reyno de Persia: la quinta la In
dia oriental desde el rio Indo hasta la China: la sexta el gran
reyno de la China; y la setima todos los islas adyacentes a
Asia.
translation:

61
The province of Thrace is very large, and has many very
important cities, but the metropolis of them all is Constan
tinople, situated on the bank of a strait, through which Europe
and Asia meet, which in some places is no wider
than a single stadium.

Chapter 16. On Asia.

Asia is the largest of the three parts of the Old World, for
Asia alone is larger than Africa and Europe combined. Its
latitude begins at the equinoctial line and extends toward
the North as far as eighty degrees; and so the whole of it
falls within the Arctic hemisphere. In longitude it spans one
hundred and twenty-four degrees, which in terms of the
greater circumference amount to two thousand one hundred
and seventy leagues. It is bounded on three sides by the ocean;
and on the west it joins Europe through Tartary, and
Africa through Egypt. It is divided into seven parts: the first is the
one closest to Europe, from the Northern Ocean to
the Caspian Sea, which was formerly called Sarmatia
and is now called Muscovy or Moscobia; the second is Tartary, which
borders the Caspian Sea, the ocean, and Moscobia;
the third is the Turkish territory, which is the western part of
Asia, comprising the region between the Caspian Sea, the Persian Gulf,
and the Tigris River; the fourth is the kingdom of Persia; the fifth is the
East Indies from the Indus River to China; the sixth is the great
kingdom of China; and the seventh comprises all the islands adjacent to
Asia.

text:
Historia del nuevo mundo.

La tierra mas austral de la Asia es una peninsula llamada Arabia, que posee el Tercer; la qual se distribuye a quatro grandes provincias: una se llama Trogloditica, que pertenece a la descripcion de Africa: la segunda, finitima a la Mesopotamia, a la Suria, y a Judea, y se llama Arabia de Serto: la tercera la Petraea: la quarta la felice, que es la mayor, mas abundante, y mas poblada; llena de incienso, mirra, y con precio de insignes provincias; y no son los reynos de portar que, Sael, los Aden: desde Arabia hasta Judea corre la provincia de Idumea, es tierra abundantisima de palmos, y contiene en si a Gaza, ciudad antiquissima, Ascalon, Azoto, y otras.

La provincia de Suria es grandissima, cae entre Arabia, Eufrates, y Cilicia: dividese en estas cinco provincias, Palestina, Fenicia, Celessiria, Suria, y Comageno: la Palestina se divide en tres partes, una que se llama propiamente Judea, otra Samaria, y la tercera Galilea: la cabeza de Judea es Gerusalem ciudad de Dios, mas aventajada que todas las ciudades del mundo. Jamas se vio provincia en todo el universo, que en proporcion fuese tan poblada como Palestina quando estava en su grandeza: porque no teniendo mas que ciento y sesenta millos de largo, y sesenta de ancho, en la muestra que se hizo por mandado del rey David, se empadronaron un millon y trecientos mil hombres de pelea, sin que en ellos se contase el tribue de Levi.
translation:
History of the New World.

The southernmost land of Asia is a peninsula called Arabia, which possesses the Third; it is divided into four great provinces: one is called Trogloditica, which belongs to the description of Africa; the second, bordering Mesopotamia, Syria, and Judea, is called Arabia Deserta; the third is Petraea; the fourth is Felix, which is the largest, most abundant, and most populous; full of incense, myrrh, and of precious and notable provinces; and the kingdoms of Sael and Aden are not without importance: from Arabia to Judea runs the province of Idumea, a land most abundantly rich in palms, and containing within it Gaza, a most ancient city, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and others.

The province of Syria is very large, lying between Arabia, the Euphrates, and Cilicia: it is divided into these five provinces — Palestine, Phoenicia, Coele-Syria, Syria, and Commagene. Palestine is divided into three parts: one properly called Judea, another Samaria, and the third Galilee. The capital of Judea is Jerusalem, the city of God, more exalted than all the cities of the world. Never was there seen a province in the entire universe that was, in proportion, as populous as Palestine when it was at its height: for although it measured no more than one hundred and sixty miles in length and sixty in width, in the census carried out by order of King David, one million three hundred thousand fighting men were registered, not counting among them the tribe of Levi.

Asia Minor is a great peninsula of land between the Black Sea (Pontus Euxinus) and the Sea of Cilicia, which they call Anatolia. It encompasses the following provinces: Cappadocia, which embraces Paphlagonia and Bithynia, while others called by this name Pontus, Thrace, Colchis, Phrygia, Lycia, whose metropolis is Ephesus, Caria, Lycia, Pamphylia, Galatia, Cilicia, Lycaonia, and Lesser Armenia. The provinces of Pamphylia and Cilicia bear the name Iskenderun, and below takes its name Karamania. The capital of Cilicia is Tarsus, birthplace of the Apostle Saint Paul. There were in ancient times very famous kingdoms in Asia Minor, such as that of the Trojans, that of Mithridates, of Croesus, of Antiochus, and others.
The remaining western lands of Asia are all the provinces lying to the west of the river Tigris and the Caspian Sea, namely Mesopotamia, Greater Armenia, the Georgians, Mingrelia, and others encompassed between the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, and the Sea of Azov. The Caspian Sea does not connect with the Ocean; it is eight hundred miles long and six hundred miles wide; and its water is not as salty as that of the other seas.
Mesopotamia lies between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris; it is rich land and of incredible fertility. Its principal cities are Urfa, Caramit, which in former times was called Amida, and Mardin, and Mosul. Further below, where the Tigris and the Euphrates meet, see—

De la Citia.

La que antiguamente rodeava sitios, se llama oy la Tartaria, que tiene largos desiertos. A los Tartaros divididos en parcialidades, que ellos llaman Orde: Los de çarançiudad pueblos sobre el rio Bolga, obedecen al Mosobita; entre el Bolga, y el rio Sur habitan los Nagayos divididos entre tres Ordes, los quales tienen señor propio llamado Can. en la costa occidental de Asia están las islas de Chipre, Rodas, y otras de menor nombre. en lo que llamamos Tartaria se comprehende por o menos dos partes de la Asia; porque se estiende desde la laguna Meotide hasta el mar Hircano Caspio, y hasta los confines de la China.

La Persia se estiende desde los terminos de la Armenia hasta los de Media, que oy se llama Seruan: es tierra calidisima por las partes maritimas. la cabeça de la Persia es Xiras, ciudad puesta sobre las riberas del rio Bendimiro, en que dura docientos mil almas; es de mucho contento de mercaderes. Pertenece a esta provincia la llamada Cuistan, que en otro tiempo se llamo Cusiana, cuya metrópolis es la ciudad de Sustra, que fue la antigua Susa.

Y sobre el reyno de Persia hacia el setentrion yaze la Partia, que oy llaman Strac; su cabeça es la ciudad de Ispaan. Por toda esta tierra se cria gran cantidad de seda. Mas lexos el mar Caspio respeta la provincia de Estraba, la qual habitaron antiguamente los Hircanos.
translation:
History of the New World.

On Scythia.

What in ancient times surrounded those regions is today called Tartary, which has vast deserts. The Tartars are divided into factions which they themselves call Hordes. Those of Sarachinsk, towns along the Volga River, obey the Muscovite; between the Volga and the river Sur live the Nogais, divided among three Hordes, which have their own lord called Khan. On the western coast of Asia lie the islands of Cyprus, Rhodes, and others of lesser name. What we call Tartary encompasses no less than two parts of Asia, for it extends from the Maeotian lake to the Hyrcanian Caspian Sea, and all the way to the borders of China.

Persia extends from the borders of Armenia to those of Media, which today is called Shirvan: it is an extremely hot land along its maritime regions. The capital of Persia is Shiraz, a city situated on the banks of the river Bendimir, which sustains two hundred thousand souls; it is greatly favored by merchants. Belonging to this province is the one called Khuzistan, which in other times was called Cusiana, whose metropolis is the city of Shustar, which was the ancient Susa.

And above the kingdom of Persia toward the north lies Parthia, which today they call Iraq; its capital is the city of Isfahan. Throughout all this land a great quantity of silk is produced. Further away, the Caspian Sea borders the province of Straba, which in ancient times was inhabited by the Hyrcanians.

Near the same Caspian Sea lies Albania, which today they call Seruan, whose metropolis is Tauris, which some maintain to be the ancient seat and court of the old Median kings. The province formerly known as Assyria extends from the Tigris River toward the East for a great distance, and comprised the provinces of Arcurum, Chaldea, and many others; the metropolis of Chaldea is Babylon.
The Eastern India, one of the most celebrated regions of the world, begins on the western side at the Indus River, which separates it from Persia. To the west and south it is bounded by the Ocean, and to the north it borders Tartary. It is divided into two parts: the most western is called Intra Ganges, which is what is properly called India; and the second, to which the name is also applied in a broader sense, is called Extra Ganges. India Intra Ganges is a great point of land in the shape of a pyramid, because its tip extends into the Ocean, whose endpoint is called Cape Comorin. From this cape a great mountain range runs northward for about four hundred leagues, until it reaches Mount Imaus, which is an arm of the Caucasus, a beautiful mountain celebrated since antiquity.

translation:

The kingdom of Ormuz encompasses a good part of Arabia Felix, and the finest islands of the Persian Sea, along with another part of the coast of Persia. The island of Ormuz is the capital of this kingdom, situated at the mouth and entrance of the gulf. The other islands adjacent to Asia are infinite in number; to the Eastern part there is a great Archipelago called San Lazaro; it begins at the islands of Japan at forty degrees north latitude, and runs between West and South until it crosses the equinoctial line, ending at twelve degrees on the southern side. This great archipelago is divided into three parts: the islands of Japan, the Philippines, and the Moluccas; the latter two I shall deal with in detail in the third part of this history, as they belong to the Crown of Spain; and so I move on to the first.
Under the name of Japan are encompassed many large islands, divided from one another by small arms of the sea. The largest is itself divided into fifty-three kingdoms, among which is the one they call Miaco, a great city of three hundred thousand inhabitants, which is the capital of all Japan. The second island is called Gimo, and encompasses nine kingdoms, and the third bears the name Gicoso, and there are in it four kingdoms. The remainder of the other islands are distributed around them, and the one that comes closest to said island lies sixty leagues from it.

Chapter 17. Of Africa.

Almost all of Africa is situated within the tropics, which
was the reason why the ancient scholars had no knowledge of most of it.
Its shape is very close to triangular, and its principal parts are Ethiopia, Caffraria,
the lands of the Negroes, Nubia, Barbary, and

One of the reasons that led our Spaniards to give new names to the lands they came across was that none of the native peoples of those lands had a general name by which they could be called. This was because knowledge extended no further than one's own homeland and province, and those that bordered it; to these they had assigned particular names. And since among the Indians there was in ancient times so little trade and commerce, they not only did not deal with anyone beyond their neighbors and nearby peoples, without venturing to distant lands; from this it followed that they came to know not only not all the land that lay adjacent to their own, but not even the provinces and kingdoms somewhat farther away, of which they had little or no knowledge.

The most general name that they commonly gave to the lands was to signify the district and province that was governed by a lord and cacique. And at most, the inhabitants of islands would name the whole island in which they lived with a single name, even if it encompassed many lordships. But the inhabitants of the mainland named it, as has been said, by small provinces; some of ten leagues in length, and others somewhat more or less, according to the extent of the lordship. The most extensive kingdom we find to have a general name given by its own people is the empire of the Inca kings of Peru, called by them Tahuantinsuyu, which measured some eight hundred leagues in longitude and a certain amount in latitude.

Within which there are many provinces, both small and medium-sized, each with its own particular names.

Four are the names that from the beginning of its discovery were given to this New World, namely: the Islands of the West, the West Indies, the New World, and America. Although when taken in their full breadth and broad meaning, these names all refer indifferently to the same thing — that is, all the land newly found by the Spaniards on this side, in the western hemisphere of the world — yet in their proper and more precise meaning they differ considerably, as I shall explain by going through each one in turn. I will begin with the first name, which is at present the least used, or better said, already entirely out of use and even forgotten: Some called this new land the Islands of the West, because the first part of it to be discovered was the Windward Islands, and for some years no mainland was found. And even after the mainland was found, because it could not be determined for a long time whether it was mainland or a large island, it was also called by the name of Island. And so in those early years, those who came and went from Spain used to say they were coming from and returning to the Islands.

And likewise in letters and public and private documents written at that time, it was given the same name of Islands; as we see was done by the Supreme Pontiff

Chapter 2. On the boundaries, size, and location of America.

Just as the Old World, which is divided into Europe, Asia, and Africa, has its length running from east to west, and its breadth from north to south: so this new world of the Indies, called America, extends and stretches in the opposite direction, from one pole to the other, and its breadth runs from East to West. On the southern side it shares its borders, by way of the Strait of Magellan, with the fifth part of the universe called the Austral Land; on the northern side it borders, and is even joined to, Asia; to the east it faces Africa and Europe, from which it is separated by the North Sea; and toward the west it runs until it meets Asia and approaches the Austral Land, with the South Sea lying between them.

This fourth part of the world begins on the southern side from the aforementioned Strait of Magellan at fifty-two and a half degrees south latitude, and runs northward to seventy degrees north latitude, which is the furthest point that has been discovered on that side. It does not run in a perfectly straight north-south longitude, since the southern part inclines somewhat to the east and the northern part to the west, so that its length runs in a northwest-southeast direction. Taking in this entire great land between two meridian lines, drawn so that the eastern one touches the island that faces east and is closest to it, which is that of Brazil,

Chapter 3. Which gives the reasons why the Torrid Zone
is habitable.

Inasmuch as the greater part of America, which the Spaniards have until now dis
covered and settled, falls within the tropics;
and because of the great variety and difference of climates found
in that middle region called the Torrid Zone, both with respect to Eu
rope and other lands that lie outside the tropics, and among
various provinces and lands within the Torrid Zone itself, one learns
of the strange properties of this region; its nature
and qualities are treated here. But because all the difference and
variety that we see in it is also found in the various
provinces encompassed within this kingdom of Peru, and to speak
of the character of the Torrid Zone, I treat this in the description
of the kingdom itself; referring first in this chapter to some
of the most general reasons why, contrary to the opinion of
most of those great philosophers and learned men of the world, it is
habitable.

The reason that moved Aristotle and the other philosophers
who shared his view to think this was what any
understanding mind would conclude, guided by the general causes and reasons
drawn from the experience of what happens in Europe.

A province of Europe outside the tropics, and at such a distance

This conclusion, which they followed from general causes drawn from
the interior, would have seemed clear and obvious to the ancients,
but we see and experience now that what we who inhabit this land
find is so false that no other argument is needed to refute and undo it
than the experience, so well known, that contradicts it. Those who said

Verdad es que en comun generalmente esta razon en todo el espacio que cae dentro de los tropicos, respecto de faltar en los llanos del reyno del Peru, a donde ni llueve el invierno, ni de verano; y con todo esto no excede su calor al de otras provincias del mismo clima. Por eso digo que no es la lluvia sola por si bastante para templar el encendido calor del sol; Sino que otras juntas con otros particulares obran este efeto. de todas las quales la mas general, y que concurre en toda la region media, es la que diré avro. Heat. In proportion to the amount of water from the sky, the waters of the earth are ordinarily abundant as well: the very copious rains cause there to be so many springs, rivers, lakes, and swamps, that they make the Torrid Zone the most humid, pleasant, and plant-abundant region in the entire world. From this it follows that in this respect it is not uninhabitable; because the great abundance of water it enjoys is one of the causes that notably tempers its heat and makes it very fertile, both for the life of men and animals.

It is true that although this reasoning holds generally throughout the entire space falling within the tropics, it fails with respect to the plains of the kingdom of Peru, where it rains neither in winter nor in summer; and yet for all that, its heat does not exceed that of other provinces in the same climate. For this reason I say that rain alone is not by itself sufficient to temper the fierce heat of the sun; rather, other factors working together with others produce this effect. Of all of these, the most general one, which operates throughout the middle region, is one I will now describe. It has great power to mitigate the terrible heat of the region; which is in itself so excessive that, were it absent along with the other causes that combine to reduce it, the opinion of Aristotle — that the Torrid Zone would be uninhabitable — would undoubtedly prove true.

Chapter 4. In which the same is proved.

From the said reason two others follow, one arising from the other,
which greatly help to make the Torrid Zone temperate and habitable.
The first is that during the time of equal length, when the days
have full daylight, the nights come to be just as long
as the days: so that just as at no time of year in its middle
region are the nights as long as the longest in
Europe; likewise there are none as harsh as
the harshest ones there: and so in the long stretch of the night
the land has the opportunity to become temperate, and to cool from the heat
of the day. The second reason that follows from these is that the nights are cooler
in the middle region than those of summer in
Europe; because this land lies at the center of the shadow
of the night, the sun being so far from it: from which
it also follows that the twilight at sunset
and sunrise is so short that they have barely appeared on the hori-
zon when it is already dark night: and for the same reason
day breaks very shortly before the sun rises: which is seen
most clearly where the view ends at the horizon.

At one and the same time it is hot in some places and cold in others; some here enjoy a perpetual and pleasant spring; others at a short distance from them are stiff with cold, and still others a league away are scorched by heat: it is necessary that we seek other particular causes for this great variety.

Setting aside for another place the inequality that lands of the same climate tend to have — some low and deep, and others high and raised from the center of the world — a matter which I will address when I discuss the discrepancy of temperatures found among them — I will bring forth here only the reason that presents itself to me, by which it happens that in lands of the same polar height, and at equal distance from the sky and the center of the earth, in some parts it is hotter or colder than in others.
The first and most principal cause of this variation I hold with certainty to be the cool winds that blow in some places and not in others, as is seen by experience not only on land but also at sea. And the plains of Peru, with their very great dry sand flats where it never rains, although they should be the hottest and most scorched land in the Indies, nevertheless, on account of the cool south wind that perpetually blows through them, are cold in winter; and the year there is more temperate and pleasant than in any land as low as it.

The following case, which happened to me personally, occurred while on a mule-driving journey. I recall that the lay brother in charge of supplies at the college of the Society of Jesus in the city of Lima used to make very thick woolen leggings for the black muleteers who transported the wine from our vineyard at Ica to the port of Pisco. I asked him why he made such heavily padded garments for them, given that the sand flats between Ica and Pisco are extremely hot. He replied that the cold which sets in there during the winter nights is so intense that the blacks would freeze, and they needed all that warm clothing plus a fire to warm themselves. This was so hard for me to believe that I decided to experience it for myself. And so, after having traveled the road from Pisco to Ica many times, I arranged to go with the muleteers during the month of July, which is the heart of winter. We spent the night in the middle of the road on a broad, flat stretch of ground. The south wind blew so keenly that the muleteers lit a fire, and I myself had to wrap up as best I could. What is more, when we set out at two in the morning in order to arrive early at Ica, the cold I felt was so intense that my hands went numb and I could not bring my fingers together until ten o'clock, when I reached Ica — something that had never happened to me on any of the many high passes and snowfields I had crossed in the kingdom. So let us take as an example the city of Lima itself, or even a single house within it, and we will see this with manifest experience. For within one and the same house, taking a room or chamber that has a door or window facing south with a corresponding opening on the opposite side, the coolness enjoyed in summer is so great that one feels no troublesome heat whatsoever. On the contrary, taking another room in the same house without this correspondence to the south, one suffers such great heat and stuffiness that it causes sweating.

At sea this is even clearer, because as all the vapor rises at an equal distance from the center of the earth, in some places it produces excessive heat throughout the year, in others less. But in our case, as along the coast of Peru, beyond the fact that the summer heat is so temperate — and more so than in the opposite land, which comprises the plains — the water is always so cold that one cannot swim in it; jugs and clay pots are cooled in the sea for drinking water, and it breeds no caimans nor any other creatures that flee cold water. This is so even though the other seas that lie at the same latitude on either side, toward one pole or the other, are of a temperate quality, with temperate water, and more warm than cold. No other cause can be found for this difference than the south wind, which blows along the coast of Peru all year long and not in other seas. Of this I have ample experience from two voyages I have made from Peru along that coast. On the second of these

It happened that while sailing from Nicaragua to the kingdom of Latin Bermillo, six hundred and forty-two passengers were on the ship who had never been to that land; and since the heat of that island was so unbearable, they were all of them eager for the expectation that the heat would soon end, and that we would enjoy the fresh wind of Peru upon reaching the equinoctial line (which according to the general rule should have been the opposite, that the closer we came to the line the more the heat would increase). As they experienced the truth of what I used to say — that upon reaching the line we would begin to enjoy the South wind — the temperature changed in such a way that in the mornings I would see some poor passengers wrapped up in their brocades, who said to me: "Father, this is a fresh wind" — "It is nothing but a very pleasant coolness," I answered. Then I said to them: "Ah, see how easy it is for God to shift the temperature from one extreme to another, for He does it with just a little air." From this we can infer the providence of the Creator in arranging things in such a way that fresh winds would ordinarily blow through the region of the plains, which, due to the scorching sun, being of barren sands and without rain, had more need of them than any other land in the Indies to mitigate the burning rays of the sun.

The reasons given by those of the Mediterranean as to why the islands of the Windward region are more temperate, and the heat is less intense than on the mainland, is because, being surrounded by the Ocean, and all of them being narrow, though some quite long, the sea winds notably cool them, especially the sea breezes and trade winds that blow from midday onward; and not only are they very pleasant and delightful on account of this, as I myself experienced during the year I spent on the island of Hispaniola. Another reason that makes certain lands of the same latitude more temperate and cool than others is the presence nearby of high, snow-capped mountains, from which cold winds ordinarily blow down and refresh them. With all that, I have no doubt that beyond the causes we have traced and identified, there may be other hidden ones, unknown to us, that contribute to such variety and the marvelous difference of climates within the same latitude: or perhaps the particular nature of each land itself, or some particular influence of the Empyrean heaven; regarding which certain philosophers and astrologers, as mentioned above, hold that many natural effects arise that cannot be accounted for by reason — such as the existence of many things in certain lands that are not found in others of the same parallel and climate. This is an opinion I consider very probable, because it satisfies as many doubts as may arise on this subject.

Chapter 5. That the division of the year as practiced in
Europe also holds true in the Torrid
Zone.

The reason why the change and inequality of qualities with the variation of seasons of the year, as experienced in Europe, is not felt in the Torrid Zone is a source of very great discrepancy and confusion among common people regarding how to count and distinguish the seasons. For since the Spaniards are accustomed to the reckoning used in Spain, where winter brings with it cold and wet weather, and summer brings warm and dry weather — not stopping to recognize two qualities but rather their opposites, so that dryness is joined with the cold of winter, and humidity and rains with the heat of summer — some rely on one quality and others on the other to orient themselves and distinguish the seasons of the year. Learned men, guided by the cold and warmth that result from the Sun drawing closer to or moving away from our hemisphere, follow the true reckoning, calling summer the warm period when the Sun moves through our Southern hemisphere, and winter the cold, or less warm period, when the Sun moves away from us and passes to the opposite hemisphere. But common people and those without letters, who are ordinarily the greater part of the republic, guided

Regarding the rainy seasons, and running counter to the standard reckoning, they call the rainy season winter and the dry, clear season summer. In this they are not only plainly mistaken in calling those months winter when the Sun is directly overhead and the heat is at its strongest — simply because the rains come then — but they also call it summer during the cold period when the Sun is farthest from us, merely because it does not rain. From this reckoning many absurdities follow.

The first is that in the Indies, winter ought to be warmer than summer, and summer colder than winter. The second is that in the Kingdom of Peru, at the same latitude and altitude, people call it winter in one place and summer less than four leagues away: because since in the highlands it rains in summer and not in the lowlands, and these two lands of such different character border one another, they say that when it is winter in the mountains it is summer in the lowlands, and vice versa. The third absurdity is that, the year being divided into only two seasons — namely winter and summer — they lengthen one and shorten the other within a single climate according to how much time the rains occupy in one place versus another. For where it rains no more than four months of the year, people call those four months winter and the remaining eight summer. And where the dry, clear months number no more than three or four and the rest are rainy, they make summer no more than three or four months and winter eight or nine. But where

The error is most clearly seen in lands where it rains all year long, where people find themselves stumped by this reckoning, unable to distinguish between winter and summer.
But the truth is that in dividing the year into two seasons, winter and summer, this division and reckoning must be made according to the approach and withdrawal of the sun, calling it winter in the hemisphere when the sun travels on the opposite side, from one equinox to the other; and summer, from when it enters our hemisphere until it leaves it. These seasons are followed, as their proper qualities, by cold, or a more moderate warmth, from the sun's absence; and with its presence, more intense heat. From this it follows that rain or lack of rain, making the weather wet or dry, is something incidental to winter or summer. From which it becomes clear that because it rains in the Torrid Zone when the sun is in our hemisphere and summer arrives, and because the weather turns cold and clear when it is far away and most distant from ours, one must say absolutely that rains and wet weather belong to summer, and drier, clearer weather to winter.
The division that in Europe is made of the year into four seasons — spring, summer, autumn, and winter — also applies to this middle region and Torrid Zone; this division arises from the four notable points that the sun marks for us at the two equinoxes and two solstices in the movement it makes in a year. Because the Sun reaches the equinox on the twenty-ninth of March, the three following months are called spring until the northern solstice, because when it reaches the tropic of Cancer on the twenty-second of June: From here, for the next three months until the equinox of the twenty-third of September — that is, from that point until the Southern solstice of the twenty-third of December — is autumn; and from this solstice and tropic of Capricorn until returning to the equinox of March, is winter. Astrologers and philosophers assign to each of the seasons two qualities, belonging to the two symbols that Aristotle attributes to each of the elements; and they compare these four seasons to the four ages of man, to the four humors of the human body, and to the four elements. Spring they make warm and moist; they compare it to childhood and the flourishing age of youth; among the humors to blood; and among the elements to air. Summer, hot and dry, they attribute to youth, to choler, and to the element of fire. Autumn, cold and dry, they liken to mature age, to melancholy, and to the element of earth. Winter, cold and moist, they compare to old age, to phlegm, and to the element of water.

It is well known that Astrologers begin these four seasons on the above-mentioned days of the equinoxes and solstices, assigning three signs of the zodiac to each season; yet common people generally hold to other starting points. For this reason it seemed to me best to reckon the change from one season to another from the beginning of each month in which the equinoxes and solstices fall; and according to this reckoning, in the Kingdom of Peru spring and summer begin at the start of September and last until the end of November; summer, the three following months of December, January, and February; autumn, March, April, and May; and winter, the last three months of June, July, and August.

It is not as easy here as in Europe to identify the qualities of each of these seasons, because the climates found throughout this land vary greatly even within the same season.

In areas that fall within the same climate zone. But comparing others, the most general ones, which belong to the Torrid Zone, are: namely, the climate of the coastal lowlands (tierra yiuca), of the highlands (sierra), and of the plains (llanos). I found that in summer, the coastal lowlands are hot and humid, reaching the highest degree of such; in the highland regions of the same parallel and polar elevation, it is cold and dry, though less so than usual; and in the plains of Peru at the same parallel as the aforementioned, it is moderately humid and cold to such a mild degree that one can say neither cold nor heat is felt. Summer in the coastal lowlands is the hottest and most humid time of the entire year; in the highlands it is the least cold and dry, because the rains then moderate the great dryness of that region; and in the plains it is the hottest and least humid time of the year, though not so much that one could call it absolutely dry, except for some valleys near the highlands, which share in that dryness. Autumn in the coastal lowlands is humid and warm, though less so than summer; in the highlands, somewhat colder and drier; and in the plains, less warm and somewhat more humid than summer. Winter in the coastal lowlands is the least hot and humid time of the year, due to the absence of rain, but not so much that one could call it cold and dry, because it is absolutely nothing but warm and humid; in the highlands it is cold and dry to a great extreme; and in the plains, moderately cold, and the most humid time of the year, though not to such a degree that

Chapter 6. Why within the tropics the rains come
in summer and not in winter.

The more attentively I have set myself to consider what
causes might account for the rain falling in summer, and the dry season
throughout all the land that lies within the Torrid Zone, contrary
to all other regions of the world that lie
outside the tropics, the greater difficulty I find in
giving a reason for so strange an effect. There have been no shortage of
those who have set themselves to philosophize and investigate the
causes of this; but all the explanations they have brought forward are easily tested
and dismantled. Pardon that it is
far easier to refute the opinions of others than to arrive
at the true one, which satisfies all the doubts
and objections that may be raised. Two are the causes,

I have resided for a long time, especially in the kingdom of Peru. Setting aside that in all those lands there is only one wind that blows throughout the year, we observe that it rains there during one season and thunders in another, as happens in the lowlands of that kingdom, where the rainfall comes in winter and not in summer, with the wind of that name blowing every year across these southern lowlands. In the highlands of my kingdom, and in other areas, it is observed that the rains fall in summer under the same winds that blow in winter, since generally they are stronger in one season than in another. In some of the lowland provinces and in the Andes it rains every month of the year, without the rains depending on which wind blows, whether one or another. And it is certain that in some areas it commonly happens that great downpours arrive with such calm and serenity in the air that they do not stir the leaves of the trees; while others come with such terrible and furious winds that they break and uproot trees. In which case, who could distinguish whether the rains proceed from the winds or not, seeing that it tends to rain both without them and with them? Which does not change the fact that some winds bring more rain than others.

At night the air becomes turbid, the weather closes in, and the sky discharges heavy rains, and especially around midday in autumn those clouds rise and dissolve into rain, since when they withdrew at dawn the horizon remained clear and free of clouds. It seems to me that in what has been said above, the reasons previously given — that some believed the Torrid Zone received its rains in summer and not in winter — are sufficiently refuted and dismissed.

What I feel regarding this difficulty, and others no less significant, which present themselves at every turn when considering the strange and admirable effects of nature that we have experienced in this New World, is that no matter how much the human understanding may toil and exhaust itself in inquiring and tracing their causes, it cannot grasp them all, since many of them are secret and hidden from the senses. I hold it as certain, for instance, regarding those that cause the summer rains: the supreme and lofty wisdom of the sovereign Creator of the world ordained that these should occur in this place, in order to provide for the needs of the Torrid Zone so that it could be habitable — for otherwise it would not be, or would be most uncomfortable for human habitation. The reason is that this entire middle region, as we shall presently see, has on one side iron and sand, which is very vast and hot, and very high mountains, dry and cold; and although between these two extremes there are some intermediate and temperate lands, the southern side

Those that occupy the greater part of what has been seen in the world within the tropics. Of these, some lands were made useless and barren, one by excessive heat and others by their rigorous cold; if in the first the summer heat were not tempered by rains; and in the second, the intemperate and cruel cold of winter were not counteracted by the continuous sunshine and the dry, clear weather that prevails at that season.
In order to understand this better, it should be known that the cold of the lands of Peru is so excessive that, while the valleys formed within them — which, being low and sheltered, are temperate — the remaining terrain cannot be traversed without people placing themselves in the sun during the day and gathering near fires at night. So it is that although the heat of the sun is very great, being so directly overhead, the cold of the land on the other hand is so rigorous that it tempers and mitigates it in such a way that one can walk and work in the sun all day without feeling heat or sweating at any time of year. And it is very common and customary for those who live in the highlands, when the midday sun is at its most intense, to expose themselves to its rays, covering only their heads with some shade so as not to be burned. From this it follows that since the cold of the highlands remains so constant throughout the year, if the rains came in winter, the land would undoubtedly be entirely uninhabitable for many reasons.

The first reason is that whatever fell there would come down frozen in snow, and cold, as experience shows with the snow that sometimes falls at the beginning of the season, or at least surrounding areas at other times, with which men could not endure the terrible cold that would result; nor would the land be cultivated and produce fruits; nor would the livestock have pastures; the cold would be intolerable, because snowing every day, such a quantity of snow would pile up on the land that it would last throughout the entire winter, and with the cold that comes from it increasing, and the icy winds that would blow, to the extreme that I say the region already reaches — who could live there? For even in summer, when the weather is by nature milder and more temperate, though it may be warm during the day, the cold is still distressing; on days when it snows, rains, or is cloudy, because the sun does not warm the earth with its rays, one feels greater cold than in winter; so much so that it is necessary to stay by the fire all day long; but as the weather clears and the sky brightens, and the sun comes out, it becomes notably more temperate. From this one can gather how great a role rains play in refreshing the land.

That during the snow neither would the land be sown, nor would the livestock have anything to eat, is very clear, as we find ample experience of this in the sierra itself.

Because going around toward the south as far as the Strait of Magellan, and already leaving the tropic of Capricorn, those regions in winter have, for six months of the year, such an immense quantity of snow upon them that they are not only uninhabitable by people, but not even by animals or birds. And what is more, the roads that connect the kingdom of Chile to the province of Tucumán cannot be traveled in winter at all, until the sun and clear weather of summer melts the snow from the mountain passes and ravines through which the roads are cut, and it becomes possible to travel them. The second reason why it would be uninhabitable is that even if something were sown, the seeds could not possibly germinate given the intense cold and frosts that occur every night, which scorch and wither the plants. The third reason is that even if winter were past, and there were time at the end of summer, one could not sow crops in the rainy season because there is no water, as is currently done; and even if in some places crops were sown under irrigation, they would wither upon sprouting. For every night of the year, both in winter and in summer, whenever the sky is clear and free of clouds, frosts fall. For this reason God arranged that rains should come in summer, so that through them the earth would be watered and sweetened; and with the mildness of the season, which is not as harsh as winter, the crops could grow.

And what is most important, and in which divine providence shines no less, is how the clouds calmed and prevented the crops from being lost to the frosts: because, even though it may be summer, any night that clears up and the sky becomes serene is likely to bring a frost as a matter of course. To address this danger, the Lord arranged the winds and atmospheric influences in such a way that from December through March inclusive — which is the season when the crops are most at risk — there is scarcely a night when the sky is not covered with clouds, without clearing away entirely. During these months the inhabitants of the land are also so wary of the sky clearing and a frost falling that before going to bed they customarily go out to see whether it is cloudy or clear; and if it happens that on some night the sky clears so thoroughly that no clouds can be seen, a great wailing arises, and the stars shine bright and clear — it is a great pity and sorrow to hear the cries and weeping that rise up in the Indian towns. For, forewarning themselves by these signs that a frost is certain on such nights, they do not wait for daylight to learn of the damage, but go out before dawn. And the damage is truly incomparable, what a single night of frost can do, because when it freezes it is commonly so widespread that it may extend over a hundred leagues or more, destroying many thousands of ducats' worth of crops. Chapter 6: The sierra of Peru depends on having its rains in summer.

It remains now to show how the rains are also the cause of the highland being settled and cultivated. But it is clear enough, and needs no further proof beyond the experience we have had, that in the sierra during the rainy season it is felt to be colder in summer than it normally is in winter. From this we can make the following argument: if the rains in the sierra cause such cold in summer — when it would otherwise be temperate — as great as that brought by winter, then likewise in the hot lands they must have great power to moderate the heat of summer, so that the land is not scorched as it would be without them. And so I conclude this question by saying that I find no other reason for the summer rains in the Torrid Zone than that it is thus fitting so that it may be inhabited, and no less for the health of its inhabitants: because both in the sierra and in the lowlands the rainy season is the healthiest time of the whole year. When the rains are late in coming at their usual time, acute illnesses tend to break out, such as fevers and pleurisy — of which there is experience both in Peru and in New Spain, particularly in the city of Mexico, where when by May the rains do not come —

Chapter 7. On the situation of the Kingdom of Peru.

The Kingdom of Peru runs north to south seven hundred and seventy leagues in length, and in width reaches up to one hundred and thirty leagues at its widest, and about eighty at its narrowest. Its farthest limits are, on the northern side, the province and diocese of Quito, and on the southern side, the Archbishopric of Charcas. Because this region encompasses, and all of America experiences, all the qualities and varieties of cold and temperate climates found in the Torrid Zone of this New World, its consideration is very important, because upon it depends the full understanding of the nature of all these Indies. The diversity of climates in this kingdom proceeds from one of the greatest mountain ranges known in the world, which runs along its length, and which we call the sierra, or the general cordillera of Austral America, or of Peru; because it begins and ends with this southern part of America, from the Strait of Magellan at fifty-two and a half degrees of latitude from the Antarctic pole, and runs to the coasts of the North Sea of the provinces of Santa Marta and Venezuela, where it ends at ten degrees of the Arctic hemisphere, in which span, although by a straight north-to-south line there are no more than one thousand and ninety-four leagues; nevertheless, in all

This great Sierra did not run always in one direction, but rather turns in three directions, and thus its length is more than one thousand five hundred leagues. And there have been no shortage of learned men, moved by its extraordinary height and grandeur, who hold this Cordillera to be the spine of the world, which branches out and joins everything in a circle, so that rising up from the ocean, where it ends to our sight, it continues beneath the water, its height exceeding all the floor of the sea, just as it exceeds all other land beyond it; and that it continues from there to other regions of the world. But this is uncertain, and has no greater foundation than the contemplations and discourses of some philosophers of the Indies. What is established and verified is that it embraces and encircles all of this Southern America, not through its middle, but along its western side, standing no more than about fifty leagues from the South Sea at its farthest, and no more than eight at its closest. And the same distance from the North Sea in the said provinces of Santa Marta and Venezuela.
The two slopes and flanks of this sierra are of a very complex nature in all that falls within the tropics, setting aside the western slope of the kingdom of Peru, which has very particular and strange qualities such as are not found elsewhere in the Indies. For this reason we shall divide the land of Peru into three parts or regions, which are like three narrow strips running the whole length of the kingdom; and each is of such different and contrary qualities from the other, that

By way of introduction: The eastern region and strip embraces the slopes and foothills of the land that face east, which we call the Andes and the yunca lowlands. The second strip is the sierra itself, which by excellence we give the name of sierra, and cordillera in general, to distinguish it from the other mountain ranges found in the land. The third encompasses the western slopes and foothills of the same sierra, and is the region we call the llanos.

These three strips and regions differ from one another in the following ways. The first is that, granted that in all three there is both hilly and flat terrain, the sierra and cordillera still surpasses the other two in height to such a degree that the middle region of the air, and the clouds of both of the others, remain far below its peaks. The second difference is that the yunca lowlands are very hot and humid throughout the year; the sierra very cold and dry; and the llanos moderately warm and humid, with no more notable difference between winter and summer than the other two. The third is that in the yunca it rains in some parts all year, and in others for the greater part of it; in the sierra at set times, which is during the summer; and in the lowlands we have little rain, and in a certain part of them what little there is falls in winter. The fourth difference is that the yunca has many swamps and marshes, great dense forests and woodlands, and resembles the torrid zone in form. The sierra, though it is abundant in rivers and lakes, is bare and treeless and healthier than those parts of the New World that lie within the tropics; and the land of the llanos is dry, without water or forests, and not as healthy as

Chapter 8. On the qualities of the yunca land of Peru.

The Indians of Cuzco and its surroundings called by the name of yuncos those lands that lie on the eastern side of the great cordillera, which are directly opposite that city, being principally the provincial land called Anti; a place of very hot and humid climate. From this, the Spaniards, extending these names to all lands of the same character, call them yuncos, and Andes, a corruption of the name Anti; and they call the natives of those lands Indios yuncos, distinguishing them from those of the sierra, whom they call Serranos. The yunca land, as it falls within the boundaries of Peru, is that which lies at the foot of the great cordillera, on the far side of it; and it begins some five or six leagues below the summits of the cordillera, which space consists of very steep, cold, and bare slopes, like the rest of the sierra in general, until one descends five-sixths of its great height.

For this reason, this first strip is more than fifty leagues shorter than the other two: because Peru does not extend as far south on this side as it does along the highlands and the sea coast.

Coming down from those mountain ranges, the rest is flatland; though there is no shortage, here and there, of some hills and small ridges that cut across wide plains: these parts being highland and lowland; and partly made up of large and spacious savannas and meadows, which the Spaniards name after the flatness they judge them to have, calling them open plains. Some of those savannas are so large that, leaving the boundaries of one, one descends into the interior of the land for more than a hundred leagues without finding any hills to block the view. From what is known through accounts of persons who have entered the lands of the gentiles bordering this territory nearby, the greater part of the plains is occupied by dense woodlands; and where the land is open it still has, at intervals, some patches of highland, which, in relation to the open plains surrounding them, look like islands. In the rest of those open plains free of woodland, there grow in great abundance grasses suitable for large cattle; which the Spaniards call pajunales, because they stand so much taller than other plants, and in such great quantity — because of the lack of animals to graze them — that, the dry growth of one year reaching that of the year before, the amount of dry grass is ordinarily as great as the green. The sierras, or ridges, that rise among those open and highland plains share the same character: part of them are outskirts, and part rocky, though they are generally rough, and more so in their slopes than in the flatlands. carried by the very humid air (for it is from this quality that a region is principally called temperate, humid, or dry), but also because its soil is notably moistened both from above and below: for in some parts it rains all year long, in others more or less, and where the rains are most concentrated they fall in the months of peak season, during which time there are many thunderstorms, lightning, heavy downpours, tempests, whirlwinds of fierce winds, lightning flashes and thunderclaps: never at any time does snow fall, nor hail, nor is there any frost or ice. With the heavy rains the rivers rise continuously, and overflowing their banks and shores they flood much of the land, forming great pools and lagoons because the rainwater cannot drain away in many places. And so there are very large stretches of land covered by lakes, marshes, swamps, bogs, and flooded areas.

The heat of the air is so intense that the natives go about naked and unclothed, having no need of garments to cover themselves by day or by night. The Spaniards go about sweating most of the time; and the heat would be even more unbearable were it not tempered by the fresh breezes that sometimes blow. So that these breezes may circulate and cool their houses, the Indians build them without walls all around, but only on wooden posts, open on all sides to the winds. One can also observe the humidity of this land in the fact that food cannot be kept, as it quickly rots; iron becomes corroded; meat goes bad by the second day; salt in saltshakers dissolves and turns to water; and when goods arrive they can scarcely be lifted in sacks.

It is very unhealthy and sickly land; the Indians have teeth the color of cooked quince, and the Spaniards, even if they arrive there with good complexions, soon lose them and turn yellow, looking like sick men. For this reason it has always been the least populated land among the Indians, as it still is today, both among the natives and the Spaniards. In the end it is better as a place for those who come to live there, because it has a most beautiful appearance, being at all times clothed in greenery and covered with groves of trees, so that one does not know what winter is, which elsewhere strips away their beauty, owing to the continual humidity of the climate. The best and healthiest time of year is winter, because the rains cease, the weather becomes clear and dry, fresher breezes blow, which diminish the excessive humidity of the soil and air, and the heat moderates. With all this it seems that the Creator compensates for the intemperate nature of this region and, together with enriching it with natural goods, grants it favorable winds above all the rest of the new wealth in variety of plants, animals, and abundance of gold mines, which are found throughout it. The Indians had no tame or domestic animals other than guinea pigs and ducks, but this land breeds wild and fierce ones such as tapirs, deer, small cats, wild pigs, armadillos, hares, rabbits, guadatinapos, lions, tigers, bears like those of Europe, and besides those, what we call anteaters, pericuigera, foxes, vicuñas, wildcats, ferrets, weasels, squirrels, innumerable different kinds of monkeys, and many are born
