Animals and venomous creatures: mosquitoes, though smaller in body than all the rest, surpass them in being bothersome and harmful; there are innumerable ones, of four or five species, as well as various kinds of ants, all manner of vipers and snakes, notably those we call "bobas" which are as large as great beams; bees that make honey in the hollows of trees and underground. In the rivers, which are very mighty where they descend from the main mountain range and cross this land, great numbers of fish are found. The variety of birds that inhabit the forests and woodlands is beyond counting, particularly those of beautiful colors, which the native peoples prize most for the fineness of their feathers: some are entirely red, others green, others blue, others yellow, and others of every other color. There is plenty of game birds in the lands: pheasants, parrots, macaws, herons, turtledoves, doves, ducks of various breeds, and others of different kinds. Birds of prey: eagles, condors, hawks, choice falcons of every kind. Finally, so great is the variety of birds found in the mountains and ranges of the Andes that their species and kinds cannot be counted.
Beyond all the fruits of the land found in other parts of the Indies, outside of this territory only a few fruits grow; and there are the various kinds of resins that are brought from the Indies to Europe, such as balsam, liquidambar, dragon's blood, anime, oil of Mary, incense of the land, copal, caraña, rubber, tecomahaca, and many cedars and countless other trees of prized timber, brazilwood, and others.

Lettuces, radishes, and other kinds of garden vegetables like these, although they grow well, never reach the point of going to seed or producing any. Two things that the land produces in great abundance are sugarcane and grapevines, and from both there are large harvests. Of the plants that have been brought from other regions outside of Spain, plantains, ginger, and passion fruit grow very well. The most profitable trades that the Spaniards carry on throughout the warm lowland country are shipments of cattle, from which they extract much leather; also horses and mules; in tobacco, cochineal or carmine dye, indigo, cotton, brazilwood, and other timbers, cacao, sugar, annatto, vanilla, along with some other fruits.
I have spoken so deliberately at length about the animals and plants of the land, both native and Castilian, that grow or do not grow in this poor land, so that it will not be necessary to repeat them many times hereafter, but rather that whenever, in the description of the provinces of the New World — which appears in the second and third parts of this history — we say that all or some of them possess the things found in that singular land, it is understood to mean those items listed in this chapter. Finally, it is also important to note from this point on that the greater part of America that falls under the Torrid Zone is of the same climate and character as what we have described here, with very little variation found in some areas, being somewhat more or less temperate; as are the Windward Islands and all the coasts of the mainland on both seas.

Chapter 9. On the properties of the land of Peru.

Not everything that falls within Peru from the mountain range and general cordillera is of equal width, because in the first third it is narrow, as

To the right of the road will be one range, and to the left will be the other. The coastal mountain range, though from time to time it has very tall and rugged, snow-capped peaks — such as the one that stands directly opposite this city of Lima, which we call Luna, and the range of Pariacaca, named for a great snow-capped peak it has by that name, which can be seen from this city on clear days — in many places it descends and forms wide passes, such that it rarely snows there throughout the seasons, although it is always a very cold highland, and snow-capped peaks are never out of sight. It has many very tall volcanoes that are continuously smoking, and not infrequently launch fire; and when one of them erupts it causes incomparable damage to all the surrounding lands and provinces, as we shall shortly describe.
The Eastern range, or that of the Andes, is higher, with more towering, rugged, and snow-covered peaks. No volcanoes are seen in it, nor is it as broad as the coastal one, since its common width is only six to ten leagues of crossing, whereas the first is fifteen to twenty. In places this eastern range is so tall and snow-covered that seen from afar it looks like nothing but a string of sugar loaves, on account of the many tall, snow-covered peaks it has.

Because this great mountain range is divided throughout, it is the most abundant land in springs and fountains in all of Peru, and indeed in all the Indies. In effect, this is such a folded land that of every eight parts, no more than one should be flat; and this flat land is distributed among certain valleys, which are formed where the mountains open up, between the peaks that surround them: and in spacious plains and plateaus that are also found upon the mountains themselves. The most important valleys are those of Huanca, Cajamarca, Jauja, Sangaro, Andahuaylas, Jaqui, Jaguanal, Yucay, Cochabamba, Cliza, Misque, Tarija, and others of lesser note found in the dioceses of Huamanga, Cusco, Chuquiabo, and Chuquisaca. Of the high and cold plateaus, the most extensive are those of the provinces of the Collao, which run along the length of the mountain range between the two snowy cordilleras for about one hundred and fifty leagues, between the provinces of Cusco and Chuquisaca.

All of the sierra region is in general bare and treeless land, with no woodland except in certain valleys and deep, sheltered ravines. Its climate, generally speaking, is dry and cold throughout the year to an extreme degree, especially during the three winter months. For this reason, fruits and seeds can be kept for a long time without rotting or being eaten by worms; nor does moth damage come as quickly as in humid lands to clothing and books; at least while I was residing in the sierra, having gone through many books, I never found

some eaten by moths. Dead meat keeps without spoiling for two months in winter, and somewhat less in summer. However, throughout the whole year, due to the intense cold and dryness, the pot that is to be eaten at midday must be put on to cook from the night before. The air is so dry that when a person sneezes, and when shaking out the bed blankets, sparks ignite and fly about. And to say mass, one must be very careful in breaking the host, because it is as dry as tinder. And particles are wont to fly off. The salt in the saltcellars never cakes or gets damp. In short, the dryness in winter is so excessive that it makes this season the least healthy of the year, and when some acute illness strikes, everyone hopes the rains will come soon, because with them the severity eases and fewer people are in danger. Thus the healthiest time of the year is summer, or autumn, on account of the rains, which moisten the air and temper its great dryness.

What also helps to make winter less healthy are terrible winds that blow during the months of June, July, and August, which they call throughout the region Tomahelas, because they come from Haina, a village of that name; and in the rest of the land of the province and diocese of Charcas they give them the same name. They are very dry, harsh, and dark; they raise great whirlwinds of dust, with which they notably muddy the air, soil and coat clothes with dust, so much so that one is hard pressed to protect oneself from the dust that this season brings; and with them

winds cling to clothing, and have a very singular property, different from the dust of other regions, because it cannot be removed from garments however freshly washed or cleaned with brushes; rather, it is necessary to dampen them first so that the dust will come off; which is done by watering the ground well and hanging the garments out overnight, and by morning the moisture that has acted on them allows them to be cleaned easily.

But of greater consequence is the harm that the winds cause to human bodies than to the clothing that covers them; because they notably dry out the brain, and kindle the temper in such a way that on the slightest occasion men lose their composure greatly; and so in the highland towns, ringworm is common at certain times, and even more frequent are scabs, and acts of violence; and this harm would be greater were it not somewhat remedied by the sky, through the snows that come in the afternoons, which partly temper and moisten the air. With respect to this extreme dryness, it has been found by experience that the dwellings of houses situated lower are healthier to live in, and whatever vapors come from above; because although the sky is almost always clear, the ground is moist, though not as much as that of the lowland soil, whereby the moisture of the ground in the lower dwelling somewhat repairs the harm of the dryness of the air. From which it is clearly inferred that the temperate quality of a region being humid or not does not arise from whether the soil is so or not, but from the ambient air; because where there is greater humidity than in the water and in all the air, the climate around the highland lakes is as great as that which the land of its shores enjoys; as those who sail the great lake of Chucuito experience, which lies in the coldest and driest part of the land.

Las lluvias no son uniformes, porque en unas partes vienen mas tempranas, y duran mas tiempo que en otras: en la provincia de Quito llueve casi todos los meses del año, sin auer mios que tres o quatro de tiempo enjuto, en que tampoco deja de llover algunos dias; de manera que no ay en todo el año seguridad de gozar un dia sereno. Lo mismo pasa en las cumbres de las dos cordilleras nevadas, que casi no se puede ir sin que nieve, o granice en ellas. Con todo eso lo mas comun, y general en toda la tierra es durar las aguas y temporeros, desde diciembre hasta Marzo, excepto en los valles templados, que suelen comenzar uno, ocho meses antes.

El cielo es extremamente mudable, y vario; porque suele amanecer el dia claro, y sereno, sin que parezca una nube en el cielo, y dentro de unas ocho horas revolverse el tiempo, turbarse el ayre, cubrirse de negras nubes el cielo, y caer furiosos turbiones con gran tempestad de truenos, rayos, y relampagos, que parece rajar se las nubes: y cesar subita mente la tempestad con la presteza que empezo, y volverse a serenar el cielo. Otras veces amanece nevando, arrasado el tiempo por todas partes, y cubiertos de nieve los campos, campos, y quanto alcanza la vista de cerros, y vegas por auer nevado toda la noche, que parece imposible poder se derretir tanta cantidad de nieve sino en muchos dias; y repentinamente aclarar el tiempo, salir el sol, y en unas ocho horas no quedar vna de nieve sobre la tierra, ni parecer cosa blanca en todo el espacio, en que dos horas antes no des cubria la vista mas que nieve.

Son tan ordinarias en el verano estas subitas mudar

The rains are not uniform, because in some places they come earlier and last longer than in others: in the province of Quito it rains almost every month of the year, with no more than three or four dry months, during which it still rains on some days; so that throughout the whole year there is no certainty of enjoying a single clear day. The same happens on the peaks of the two snow-capped mountain ranges, where one can hardly travel without encountering snow or hail. Even so, the most common and general pattern throughout the land is for the rains and seasonal storms to last from December to March, except in the temperate valleys, where they usually begin one or eight months earlier.

The sky is extremely changeable and variable; for the day often dawns clear and calm, without a cloud in the sky, and within about eight hours the weather turns, the air grows troubled, the sky covers itself with dark clouds, and furious downpours fall with great storms of thunder, lightning, and flashes, as if the clouds were splitting apart; and then the storm ceases as suddenly as it began, and the sky clears again. At other times, it dawns snowing, with the weather closed in on all sides, the fields covered in snow, and as far as the eye can see — hills and valleys alike — blanketed from having snowed all night, so that it seems impossible for so much snow to melt except over many days; and then suddenly the weather clears, the sun comes out, and within about eight hours not a trace of snow remains on the ground, nor does anything white appear across the whole expanse that, two hours before, showed nothing but snow to the eye.

Of this diversity, another explanation may be offered beyond that of the coldness of the high region of the air: from this it follows that as we descend from the summits of the high mountain ranges, which are extremely cold, we experience that the climate changes perceptibly the closer we come to the bottom of the valleys that form between the mountains, which are many, and some of them, being very deep, are for that reason very hot; and between these two extremes of the cold of the high places and the heat of the low ones, one finds all the differences in climates that we observe: cold, temperate, and warm.

Taking it from the highest peaks down to the lowest and most sheltered of its valleys, it seems to me that we can divide it into six degrees, orders, or climates, according to the plants that grow, or do not grow, in each climate — which I believe is the best means available for conveying the qualities of each degree and climate. In the first, then, beginning from the high parts of the land, we shall include all the barren and sterile land that is neither cultivated nor sown, on account of its being extremely cold and intemperate plateaus; this is what we call in Peru Puna brava, meaning roughly the coldest and most sterile moorland that exists. Into this degree and climate fall the two snow-covered mountain ranges — that of Lamas and that of the Andes — the peaks of the hills and high ridges of the entire mountain range generally, and certain flat stretches that form on top of them, along with the open slopes and hillsides of the same range, where the same climate and harshness of sterile moorland persists. In the way of game birds, four varieties of doves are found, and as many kinds of partridge native to the land, ostriches, and several types of ducks. Also raised there are very fine sparrowhawks, falcons, and merlins, eagles, kites, kestrels, and condors; these, along with hares and foxes, do great damage to the livestock, because they kill lambs and calves, and sometimes even attack the larger animals. Songbirds and colorful birds do exist, such as the chayños, pichunchayos, chusllunchos, and paracatos, and a few others ranging in size from no larger than a siskin up to the size of a dove. In firewood and timber for construction, the whole puna is very poorly supplied, for it produces only some scrubland and three or four kinds of wild trees, without fruit-bearing ones, in ravines and somewhat sheltered places.
All the land of this first degree and climate is generally cold and dry, even though it is the most abundantly watered by rain and by springs of the entire sierra: because in it are born all the rivers that cross Peru and flow to both seas, the North and the South; it has many very large and deep freshwater lakes, so cold that frogs produce no fish in them. De aqui es ara la solucion de dos dudas, que se les suelen ofrecer a los que experimentan estos grandes frios. La primera, como es tan fria la tierra no se hielan las lagunas, rios: y la segunda, de donde proceda que nevando tanto, que aunque cae nieve sobre la tierra me bien estado, y mas la nieve, no dura mucho tiempo sobre ella sin derretirse, como acaece en Europa. De entrambas se responde ser la causa el gran ardor de los rayos del sol, que en todo el año anda cerca de nuestras cabezas, y pasados veces sobre ellas. Si bien es verdad que ayuda mucho para que no se hiele el agua de los rios, y lagos, ser las noches tan iguales con los dias, y no tan largas en ningun tiempo del año como los de invierno de Europa; aunque son de mayor frio que las mas frias de España, y por consiguiente los dias largos. Con todo eso no deja de haber de mos de los arroyos y los pequeños, y charcos de agua estantia, alguno viachicuelos que llevan bastante agua para moler una, y dos ruedas de molinos; pero no obstante los mos

Running with only the rays it has, which are agitated and vehement, seeming to combat the ardent heat of the sun and the intense cold of the land; from which comes the notion held in Peru that it is something to be feared; and the Sun of the puna is confirmed in this, for although it cannot impart its warmth because of the excessive cold of this region, it is nonetheless harmful, and is wont to cause spotted fevers and other fevers.

From this arises the resolution of two doubts that commonly present themselves to those who experience these great colds. The first, how it is that, the land being so cold, the lakes and rivers do not freeze; and the second, from whence it comes that, though it snows so much, and snow falls well upon the ground, and more snow besides, it does not last long upon the surface without melting, as happens in Europe. To both questions, the answer is that the cause is the great intensity of the sun's rays, which throughout the year remain near our heads, and at times pass directly over them. It is also true that it helps greatly in preventing the water of rivers and lakes from freezing, that the nights are so equal to the days, and not so long at any time of year as winter nights in Europe; although they are colder than the coldest nights in Spain, and the days consequently longer. Nevertheless, it still happens that some of the streams and small pools of standing water, and some little watercourses that carry enough water to turn one or two millwheels, do freeze; but notwithstanding these mills

The air in these high lands is so dry, thin, and
rarefied, that those who come here for the first time, especially if
they ascend from the warm lowlands and the seacoast,
as happens to those who travel from the city of Lima to
the highland towns, find themselves short of breath; and not only men
but also the pack animals. These, climbing the
cold mountain ranges, stop at every step, straining their necks and flanks,
and become sluggish and dull, just as those who
set sail for the first time do at sea; nor can a person
eat a single bite while the nausea and
churning they feel in their stomach lasts, which causes them to vomit up everything
they have inside. Having been well accustomed to this land,
I have made the journey up from the lowlands to the highland provinces three
times, and each time crossing those high
plains I have felt this unsettling of the stomach; and the second time I suffered greatly
with intense retching and vomiting, despite never having been troubled by seasickness
in the many sea voyages I have made. This
happened to me in the year sixteen fifteen, in the month
of December, while crossing the mountain range through the mines of
the new Potosí. There I found myself so exhausted that,
despairing of recovering my health, I begged my companions to leave me

And it is that just as this indisposition is sudden, caused by the thin and intemperate airs of the puna, once one leaves that harsh climate it goes away instantly.
And not only do the highlands so affect men's bodies, but there are places where men are accustomed to die suddenly, pierced by the very cold winds that blow there, as happens in the páramo of the province of Los Lipas, and in that which lies between Quito and the New Kingdom of Granada. The manner in which they remain dead is with the appearance of the living, seated with their eyes open and their teeth showing, always leaning against a rock, so that when people have gone to look for some individuals who had frozen to death while passing through, speaking to them in the manner described, those searching believed them to be alive, and drawing closer and attempting to move them, found them stiff. This is because when the cold and the sinews are gripped by the rigidity of the frost, the lips draw back and they remain with their teeth exposed.
As I was describing to the Archbishop of Nira the great harshness of the high mountain ranges, at the time he was beginning to cross them through the valley of Ica in the year sixteen hundred and twenty-three, he replied that having himself seen and traveled the mountains of Armenia and Persia, he did not believe there could be others in the world more rugged and lofty. And when afterward, upon his entering these plains, I visited him and asked him what

Y lo mismo me han afirmado personas que han visto las altas sierras de Alemania.

Ya que la esterilidad de la puna es tan notable, que no produce ningun genero de plantas, y legumbres para sustento de los hombres, la recompensa el divino repartidor de las riquezas naturales, con criar en ella tan grande abundancia de minas de plata, y otros metales, que casi todos los cerros, y lomas peladas de pedriscos, y rocas de estos yermos paramos, estan lastradas de plata. De donde se ha sacado el insigñable tesoro desta metal, que se ha llevado a España de su reyno del Peru. Y es tan grande el numero de minas que cada dia se descubren en este primer grado, y temple de sierra, que tiene por cierto no faltaran jamas estos ricos metales, en tanto que las Indias duraren. Y cansa asimismo de los paramos el beneficio del azogue, y sobre que se beneficia la plata, y lo que dellos metales, y de ellos rios, y plomo regala en este reyno. It had seemed to him regarding the general mountain range of his kingdom, he responded to me that I had been very right in what I had told him about it: because it far surpasses in height and harshness of climate all those he had seen, both in Asia and in the other parts of the world he had traveled, which was a good portion of it. And the same has been affirmed to me by persons who have seen the high mountains of Germany.

Although the sterility of the puna is so notable that it produces no kind of plants or vegetables for the sustenance of men, the divine distributor of natural riches compensates for this by creating there such great abundance of silver mines and other metals, that almost all the hills and bare slopes of gravel and rocks of these desolate moorlands are laden with silver. From here has been extracted the inestimable treasure of this metal, which has been sent to Spain from its kingdom of Peru. And so great is the number of mines that are discovered every day in this first degree and climate of mountain range, that it is considered certain that these rich metals will never run out, as long as the Indies endure. And likewise from the moorlands comes the benefit of mercury, upon which the silver is refined, and what these metals and rivers, and lead bestow upon this kingdom. Chapter 16. On the other differences of climates

To the second degree of heat, as we go down from
the sierra, belongs the land that lies immediately next to that of
the first, and it is not as barren as that one, for it yields fruits
by which its inhabitants sustain themselves, which are the roots:
potatoes, oca, maize, isanos, and llancos, and the grain called
quinoa; which vegetables grow in this second
climate and serve the Indians: but wheat does not grow there on account of
the great cold, nor barley, nor chickpeas, nor other
seeds and vegetables that require more temperate land.
Nor does any kind of fruit tree grow there, except certain
cactus shrubs that they call pitahayas. It is true that
in the lower places, sheltered by hills, there tend to grow

of the vegetables, greens, and herbs of Spain,
such as lettuces, cabbages, radishes, turnips, carrots, garlic,

But none of those of this kind manage to go to seed and produce grain, except for Clover, Cress, and Chamomile; the last does not wither throughout the year from frosts, as the others do. In the same sheltered places there also grow some stalks of maize, barley, wheat, broad beans, flax, turnips, and almost all the flowers of Spain, such as roses, carnations, lilies, wallflowers, the herb of Saint Mary, and several others. Fine domestic and wild animals thrive there, as do chickens, domestic pigeons, wood pigeons, and many other species of birds. The pastures are better, and so abundant that they do not run dry all year long, since the climate is not so harsh, and for this reason — just as we also call the first zone purea — we turn now to the lands of this second zone, because it does not generally support wheat, nor many other seeds and fruits that grow in temperate lands: and because it has the same character as the first, cold and dry, though to a lesser degree, yet not so much as to prevent it from yielding quite well; and in many hollows the sown fields of quinoa, potatoes, and the other vegetables grown here are affected by frosts.

In this regard a remarkable thing occurs: although the hillsides are colder than the plain lying at their foot by virtue of being higher, nevertheless the crops on the plain are more exposed to frosts than those on the hillsides; and

Reasons why frost settles more when the night is calm and without winds, and while it falls on the flat ground and the slopes of the hills, a continuous wind blows from somewhere, and by means of it the frost on the crops is broken up. The same happens in the flatlands, which are windy with respect to the thickness of the frost, so that although it occurs many times as a second frost there, it does not come in as the first, because the winds do not allow the frost to settle. It also happens that in one year all the plots of a great plain are struck, yet a patch remains in the middle, or survives the frost, because at the moment the frost fell, some cloud had positioned itself over that place, sheltering and protecting it against the frost.
A great deal of land participates in this second highland climate, because the great plains of Collao are included in it, as well as many valleys and hillsides of the same quality; and they are called the Peru region, where men live long, both Spaniards and Indians: because in no part of this kingdom have I seen fewer sick people, nor a greater number of old Indians of more than ten years of age, who remembered the time of the Inca kings and the arrival of the Spaniards in their land. All the animals and birds found in the first and second climate zones are raised here, except for the vicuñas and guanacos, which do not descend from the cold high plains that are their native land. And mares, donkeys, and mules are born here, which cannot be raised beyond this third climate zone going upward. This land differs from that of the second zone in that it is suited for grain-bearing and farming. And it differs from the fourth zone, which will be discussed shortly, in that although it is abundant in wheat and other legumes, it does not produce fruit trees as does the fourth zone that follows this one. For although orange trees, peach trees, and other fruit trees grow here, their fruit does not reach full ripeness and maturity, except for some Castilian grapes that do ripen; and so we say that this third climate zone lacks fruit, because the fruits of trees do not ripen here. The climate is cold and dry to a greater degree than in the second zone; so much so that although the cold does not compel one to sit in the sun at all times, nor to draw close to a fire, one still needs all the warmth one can get, and it is not necessary to change one's habits between winter and summer.    The land of the fourth degree and climate of the sierra is temperate, without notable cold or dryness; the winter cold is mild, and the summer is cool, so that because the heat never reaches a fatiguing level throughout the year, its climate is said to be absolutely cold, or better said, cool. In this fourth region grow all the plants, vegetables, seeds, and animals found in the third; except for llamas, or sheep of the land, which are not found in the valleys and temperate lands, but only in the cold lands of the three preceding degrees. Within this fourth climate fall the best, most fertile, and most well-watered valleys of all the sierra, such as those of Jauja, Andahuaylas, Yucay, Cochabamba, and many others of the same character. There grow in abundance all the fruits of Spain from cold and temperate regions, such as almonds, cherries, plums, peaches, nectarines, apricots, pears, apples, and pippins, and from warm-climate fruits, quinces, pomegranates, and several others.
   The climate of the fifth degree of the sierra we call chaupiyunca, which means "middle yunca," for it is so mild and pleasant that it feels neither cold nor hot. Although it is true that we may say it leans more toward warm than cold, since for a good part of the year a moderate warmth is felt, yet it is not so much that it brings on a chill, nor does the water ever fail to be quite cold at all times. In the fifth zone: all the fruits of Castile that have so far been brought to the Indies, such as figs, grapes, oranges, limes, and all juicy fruits; avocados, pacaes, papayas, and many other local fruits; though dates and some other fruits, both from Europe and from the land, that require a warmer climate do not fully ripen here. Within this fifth zone are found the cities of Arequipa, Guamanga, and Huanuco, along with several other Spanish settlements, and many valleys and mid-level hillsides. The dwelling of this fifth zone, and of the fourth, is the most pleasant, delightful, and comfortable not only in the Indies but in all the world, on account of the perpetual and agreeable spring that prevails here without variation of heat and cold through the changing seasons. Particularly in this fifth zone, many trees never shed their leaves, and what is most remarkable is that in some places they are continually putting forth both flower and fruit, one following the other throughout the entire year. Grapevines and trellises yield grapes at whatever time they are pruned; fig trees never lack both green and ripe figs; and the same holds true for many other fruit trees. These five zones and ranges of the sierra produce very few crawling creatures and venomous animals, such as vipers and other serpents that breed in the lowland yunca lands. The Spanish who live in these zones are healthier than those in the rest of Peru; they never lose the color they brought from Spain, nor do they feel the re-

The sixth and final grade of the Sierra includes the deepest and most profound valleys found within it, and the slopes of the same character, which are extremely hot, as much or more so than the Yunca land, and moderately humid. The reason this region is so hot, and for the air that comes down from the sierra, is because it sits at the same level and height within the sierra as the plains which we shall discuss presently, and the Yunca lands, which are the most base of Peru; because from the valleys of this sixth grade the rivers carry very little current until they enter the Yunca lands. The heat is greatly increased because they are hollow and very deep ravines surrounded by the highest mountains; whereby the rays of the sun have very great intensity there; the winds that blow are few, and not as fresh as those that blow in the high places. And for this reason it is the least healthy land of the sierra. Within this grade fall the valleys and rivers of Vilcas, Auancay, and Apurimac, which we cross when traveling from the city of Lima to that of Cuzco; which travelers endeavor to cross quickly, and in the cool of the morning, because as they come from very cold highlands to enter them, the sudden change from one extreme of cold to another of heat greatly fatigues them, and its excessive heat unsettles them, if they

Although the climate of this last degree of highland is not much like the lowland and the equatorial heat, it differs greatly from it in not being so humid, and in other qualities: and thus there grow abundantly in this region all the fruits, vegetables, and animals as in the fifth: and the plants of the land, and of Castile as in the lowland and equatorial zone, along with the insects and abundance of mosquitoes that are born there: dates ripen perfectly, and wine and sugar are made; only sheep do not breed well. Likewise wheat, maize, rice and plantains, melons, and other similar fruits are harvested in land of this character. In this climate are the towns of Mizque, Palcpaya, Pilaya, Tarija, and other Spanish settlements.

Chapter 12. On the altitude that the

The first observation and argument, which shows its height to be extraordinary, is taken from the slopes that are climbed in many places to reach the top, which are four, six, and more leagues of very steep ascent; and these are where the roads cut through, which ordinarily pass through the gaps and lowest passes: from where, looking up toward the summits of the snow-covered cordillera, one can see that a good stretch of climb still remains. From experience, then, and from what I myself have observed by sight on the occasions when I have stood upon its summits and looked downward along the straight slopes and combed hillsides, and from what knowledgeable persons have made known to us about its difficulty, I conclude that this mountain range has a height, measured by a perpendicular line, of a league and a half from its highest peaks down to the base, which comes to stand at almost the same level as the banks of the sea. Dividing this league and a half of altitude into the six degrees or tiers into which we have divided it, the first zone of exposed, barren páramo heights must be given half a league by perpendicular measure, and the second degree a quarter of a league; so that the first three quarters of a league of this inaccessible mountain range consist of extremely cold páramo, where no fruit trees grow, nor is wheat cultivated, nor other Castilian crops. The other three quarters of a league are fertile land for grain and cultivation, which is tilled and sown, and these are distributed across the four remaining degrees and terraces in the following manner: to the third, fourth, and fifth degrees the half league shall be apportioned in equal parts, so that each of the three degrees and climate zones comes to hold one eighth of a league. From which it follows that this general sierra of Peru is, out of six parts, five parts higher than the land on either side of it, which forms the two strips of the three into which Peru is divided.

Beyond this division, in which we have assigned to each of the six degrees and regions of the sierra the height they possess — measured vertically and by perpendicular lines — it remains for us now to divide the surface and floor of the said sierra across those same six degrees, and to see how much space belongs to each. To do this, the entire sierra must be divided into four parts: two of those parts belong to the first degree and region of the punas, which are barren moorlands; another quarter belongs to the second degree; and the last remaining quarter, which is the fertile land suitable for grain-bearing crops, is divided equally among the remaining four degrees. It should be noted, first, that much of this last quarter has not been cultivated, since roughly half of it remains unworked — partly due to lack of people, and partly because much of it is very rugged terrain, full of rubble and rock. As a result, of all the land in the sierra, no more than one-eighth part is currently cultivated and sown with wheat, maize, and other seeds and fruit-bearing plants. The second point is that when the sierra is divided into six degrees and regions, one should not understand the sierra of each one to be joined and continuous, but rather interrupted and broken up among itself, according to the arrangement of the hills and ridges. De las tres regiones, y fajas en que diuidimos el Peru, es la tercera, y occidental la maritima llamada, llanos, que cae entre la mar, y la sierra general. diosele este nombre no porque toda la tierra que se comprehende en ella, sea llana; sino porque los españoles, que descubrieron, y conquistaron el reyno, entraron en el, y menpeçaron su pacificacion por la costa septentrional de la prouincia de Piuro diocesi de Trugillo, que es de mui grandes llamadas de arenales secos; a los quales llamaron llanos. y despues se fue estendiendo este nombre hasta venir a comprehender el toda la costa del Peru, que participa del mismo temperamento que los dichos arenales; aunque la mayor parte de esta region es tierra doblada. de setecientas leguas poco mas o menos que tiene de costa este reyno, las primeras ciento hauan el Norte son de tierra y toca de las mismas qualidades, que deximos tener la primera faja.

The third and final point is that the climate of each zone is of such a nature that what we call cold is to be understood as cold throughout the entire year, and the same applies to the warm zones; and no less so for those we designate as temperate. For throughout the entire highlands there is no variation of heat and cold with the changes of winter and summer that one experiences in Spain and in the other lands that lie outside the torrid zone.

Chapter 13. On the third belt or strip of Peru, which is the region we call the lowlands.

Of the three regions and strips into which we divide Peru, the third and westernmost is the maritime one called the lowlands, which lies between the sea and the main mountain range. This name was not given to it because all the land it encompasses is flat; rather, it was because the Spaniards who discovered and conquered the kingdom entered it and began its pacification along the northern coast of the province of Piura, in the diocese of Trujillo, which has very large stretches of dry sandy wastes, which they called llanos. Afterward this name spread until it came to encompass the entire coast of Peru, which shares the same climate as those sandy wastes; although the greater part of this region is hilly country. Of the roughly seven hundred leagues of coastline that this kingdom has, the first hundred toward the North are land of the same character and qualities that we said the first belt possesses.

This is not found in any other part of the middle region that lies within the tropics, because all the other provinces of it maintain throughout the year a uniformity with only a perceptible variety; in such a way that what is cold is always cold, and what is warm is always warm, having no other variation with the changing seasons except that the cold regions ease their coldness, and their dryness, in summer; and their heat and humidity in winter.

Secondly, encompassing the whole Torrid Zone, which abounds with waters from above and below, and with moist soil: on the contrary, these plains are by their nature so dry that, were it not for the rivers that come down from the main mountain range, they would be entirely barren and uninhabitable; because they have no other water from the sky or from the earth except what those rivers supply them. For it never rains there, nor for more than ten leagues inland along its entire coast: nor are there any thunder, lightning, or flashes; and its soil is extremely dry, with no wells, lakes, or springs. I say it does not rain on these plains, for this is the general rule, though in certain parts of them there falls a kind of dew, which we call in this land garúa, of which I will speak presently: which is yet another wonder no less remarkable than those of this land, in which it also differs from the rest of the Torrid Zone; for whereas in that zone the rains come in summer, here the dew comes in winter: it differs from all other regions of the world in that, being made of barren sands and lying beneath the Torrid Zone, without rains to temper the heat of the sun, which strikes it with direct rays, and

Toward the eastern part, where the plains border the sierra and a general district, one can observe that their limits begin to rise along the lofty slopes and hillsides, reaching as far as to surpass the greatest height of the hills found in the plains. By which they reach no further than level with that part of the height of the general sierra. And from here the land already rises with grass and vegetation, covered with thickets, and one begins to feel some cold: these are the signs and indications by which we know, when in winter we go up to the sierra, that we are leaving the temperate zone and departing from the plains. Because in summer there are other signs more perceptible and notable; which are the terrible thunderclaps and heavy downpours that we experience upon reaching the boundary and temperate zone of the sierra. So much so that those who travel from the plains to the sierra at this time of year find that on the very first day's journey out from the lowlands, where it never rains nor thunders, within just a few hours of travel they find themselves in the territory of the sierra, which is a land of heavy rains and terrible thunder and lightning. It is very difficult and troublesome to descend from them, and it is considered prudent to dismount, and it is regarded as recklessness not to do so, because many misfortunes and dreadful deaths have occurred. And it is an amusing thing, and one I will not pass over: when travelers come through here, they mock us for calling a land of so many hills and steep crags "the plains." But this name is already established, not because all the land it encompasses is flat, but to signify what its character and climate are like, as has been noted above. Traveling through these plains is more customary in winter than in summer, on account of the cold weather, and the mists and drizzles found there, which do not cause as much discomfort as the summer sun; for in summer the sandy wastes are intolerable, and for this reason those who travel in summer make their journeys by night or at dawn, for fear that the full force of the sun will overtake them on the road.

Short, and running from east to west from their headwaters until they enter the Southern Sea, spanning twenty to thirty leagues, depending on how wide or narrow the lowlands are, and the rivers run straight or winding. Where the main mountain range is closest to the sea, the rivers are smaller but carry more water than where the range is farther away. In winter they carry nine-thirds less water than in summer, because the heavy rains that fall upon the main mountain range during that season cause them to swell considerably. They come with great current and are very turbid, and for this reason they cannot be forded. Their nature is not to run clear water, and they are all crossed by ford. Some, having run not a few leagues, sink into the sandy ground before reaching the sea, especially in winter. All of them make a great noise on account of the rocky and gravelly ground. And even though they are the lifeblood and soul of the lowlands, they do not fail to cause great damage with their swift current, carrying away with their floods and freshets a large portion of the cultivated lands of the valleys that are irrigated by them. They do not breed caimans as do the other rivers of the northern coast of Peru and those of the rest of the Torrid Zone, which is a very great blessing. The fish caught in them are pejeyes, bagres, cachuelos, shrimp, carachás, and others of their kind.

The valleys of the lowlands are separated from one another according to the rivers, some by four, eight, or ten leagues, and others by fifteen, twenty, forty, or more leagues; and the space in between consists of barren sandy stretches and hills of rubble and crags. Not all of these valleys run lengthwise along the rivers from the seacoast to the mountains; what happens is that the reed beds open up and give way to the formation of valleys a few leagues before the sea, as we see in this great valley of Lima, which is one of the largest and most fertile of the lowlands. There are also rivers that in their course form other valleys, opening up and narrowing between the mountains and hills that surround them, and it is through these narrows that the valleys are divided from one another. The most common situation is that the valleys lying away from the sea are long — from three to six leagues along the rivers — and wide from a musket-shot to one, two, four, or more leagues, as we see in the valley of Ica. And those that lie along the coast are the opposite, having their length extended along the seashore and their width running inland. All of these said valleys constitute the farmland of the lowlands; and reckoning proportionally, according to their number and size, it seems to me that they occupy a tenth part of the lowlands, and that the other nine-tenths are barren and uncultivated land. And even though the fertile land is so much less than the barren land, not even half of it is cultivated, for lack of water and people; because not all the rivers carry enough water to irrigate the valleys that are formed along them.

These plains extending to a latitude of twenty-five degrees South, we must distinguish the climate of those lying outside the Tropic, which is temperate, from that which covers the greater part of this region of plains, which falls within the Torrid Zone. The climate outside the Tropic of Capricorn differs from that which lies within the Torrid Zone in that it is uniform and mild throughout the year; one feels neither cold nor heat, nor is it excessively humid or dry, but rather of a marvelous temperance; so that if the land were not almost entirely barren and dry, these would be among the most agreeable climates in this new world for human habitation; as those who live in the province of Atacama, which occupies this stretch of land, can attest.

The remainder of the plains is, generally speaking, of a somewhat humid and cold climate in winter, and warm and less humid in summer. This does not contradict what has already been said about the land being very dry overall; for the climate is determined by the quality of the air and sky, and that of the plains inclines more toward humidity than dryness: yet so great is the dryness of the soil that it tempers this humidity to such a degree that this region is not nearly so humid as the lowland coastal territory. For this reason, the dwellings and lodgings of the valleys are just as healthful as those of the highlands.

The cold that comes in winter on these plains, though it calls for
more covering, and warmer clothing and bedding than in summer,
is nonetheless not of such a nature as to freeze, nor does it oblige one

likewise mild, owing to the south wind, which all

The nights of summer are cool and pleasant, and most

Finally, the climate of the lowlands is such that it can be called
absolutely healthy, although the highlands have some advantage in this regard; but it surpasses the highland lands by a great deal
in being much more healthful than they are; and in the fertility of its
valleys it surpasses all the rest of the Indies. The Spaniards bring good
airs, neither as broken as in the hot lands,
nor as intense as in the highlands. The dwelling
of the lowlands is the most pleasant and comfortable in the Indies, owing to
its uniform mildness and reliable skies, where
one knows today with certainty what the weather will be tomor

or from working in town or outside it. Chiefly

the sea, from its shore until one moves four
or five leagues away from it, are more humid and subject to more continual mists:

The entire lowland territory is very free of vermin and poisonous animals: so much so that travelers, growing tired at night, lie down to sleep and rest on the sandy shores of the ports, safe in the knowledge that no animal of the kind that is dangerous in other regions will trouble them, for not even a mosquito or an ant is to be found there.
All the fruits, seeds, and vegetables of Castile and of this land that grow in the highlands and in the yunca regions are produced here in great abundance: except that among the native fruits of hot lands, coconuts, pineapples, and some others requiring a very hot and humid climate do not grow here; and from those that belong to the highlands, the lowlands produce almonds and plums of Castile. But all the other fruits of this land and of Europe are produced in great abundance, and are of better flavor and quality than those of the highlands, inasmuch as there they ripen in the rainy season, while here, where it never rains, the pears are more — we see this advantage in the pears, quinces,

Chapter 15. On the Garúas, and the highland ridge that in the lowlands we call Lomas.

We have said how in a certain part of the lowlands there falls a fine drizzle, or mist, which in Spain we call mollina, and in this land garúa: which, both because of the place where it falls and because of other properties it has, causes greater wonder than if it had rained fully there during those months. Regarding the length, which we have seen the lowlands of Peru to have, from the port of Tumbes to that of Copiapó, it should be known that although the hills and ridge found within them run from the sea along the entire coast inland until they join the main sierra and cordillera, still in the first hundred leagues from Tumbes, going toward Trujillo, they lie at a distance of eight to twelve leagues from the sea: however, from the boundaries of the said city of Trujillo as far as Copiapó they continue along the entire coast, except that at intervals they are broken by the valleys and flat lands that form along the banks

From the sea, then, among the hills and the maritime land stretching inland one league, or lacking three or four leagues of width from the seashore toward the interior; and the garúa from where it begins near Trujillo, two hundred leagues remain before the cape and end of the plains, where only the garúas fall. The seasons in which these occur we call in this kingdom lomas; and the time in which this dew falls we call the season of lomas, because during it one lives amidst greenery and abundant pastures are raised. So the lomas, and the land of garúas, extend some three hundred leagues more or less in length, and no more than three or four in width. For this reason it is generally said that it does not rain in the plains of this kingdom of Peru; partly because the rains, or garúas, of the lomas are very scarce in comparison to what falls in the climates of the Torrid Zone; and principally because, falling only in this narrow strip running along the coast of the sea, the greater part of the plains receives no rain at all — those being the two extremes, where there are three hundred leagues of coast at their greatest width; and the range, or turning sierra, that lies between the lomas themselves and the main cordillera.

The garúas usually begin around the month of May and last six months more or less. They fall very unevenly, because in the valleys that form between the lomas, and in the sandy flats along the seashore, they are thinner and scarcer than in the hills and lomas, where they are all the heavier and more abundant as the hills are higher; as we see in the sierra of the sand, which lies six leagues from the city of Lima, on whose summit the garúas are most copious and greatly grown

The grass that grows on these hills: on the slopes of the same mountain range, and even from halfway down it, as we described going down to the plain, the rains are so scarce that they do not provide enough moisture to sustain the grass; and so the slopes of the said mountain range closest to the plain remain bare of it. Although it is true that in many low and flat ravines that open up in the midst of the ridges, it tends to rain as much as elsewhere, and the grass grows no less thickly, as we see on the ridges of La Chay and La Chacama in this diocese of Lima.
This rain is not as fine as some who write about it describe; rather it is so abundant in some places that in them alone grass grows so tall that it hides the cattle within it; and in others not so much, and in those where it is least, still sufficient for the livestock to graze; and it lasts long enough for many kinds of flowers and wild herbs to grow, mature, and produce seed, which falling on dry ground sprouts and grows the following season. There also grow some thickets, which are plants that require more plentiful watering than the grasses; and they serve for firewood and fodder. During the time that the garúas last, these hillsides appear green, flowering, and delightful, clothing themselves in new livery; for I have not seen, in all my travels through the Indies, nor even in Spain, more pleasant fields and meadows. In the midst of them there are some valleys and lowlands with such abundant and tall pastures that they look like barley gardens. During the time of the lomas, springs and freshwater sources appear in many places, which last throughout the winter, from which the livestock drink; but once the garúas end and summer arrives, they dry up at once. It is true that some of those springs last for several months after the garúas have ended, the longer in proportion as the rains were more abundant, for they are not the same every year nor equal in every place. The most abundant lomas, and best pasture of all the coast, where the most rain falls, where it is most plentiful and lasts longest, are in the diocese of Arequipa, the hills of Ilo, Atico, and Atiquipa; and in the diocese of Lima, the sierra de la Arena, and the lomas of Pachacama, and La Chay. The pastures in those lomas begin one or two months after the garúas have set in, and they last as long as those rains do, and a little beyond, which is until November and December, rarely failing to appear.

El tiempo que duran los lomas traen apacer a ellas
translation:
History of the New World.
In summer they dry out and wither in less than two months, and the hills return to their natural dryness and barrenness; so that whoever saw them during the season of garúas so clothed in green and in bloom, and comes back through them within two months, does not know what to marvel at more: whether at how hills so dry and barren, and largely covered in sandy wastes, could produce such abundance of grass and pasture as they had before; or at how in so short a time so much greenery and flowering growth has dried up and withered as there once was on them. Truly both things are admirable; the first being that, since almost all of them are flat, dead sandy wastes, wherever they are reached by old water, or from the sky, or from rivers, the dry sandy wastes are made so fertile that abundant pastures grow in them, vineyards and olive groves are planted, and all kinds of vegetables are sown and cultivated. The second is that the dryness of the soil is so extreme that within two months of lacking irrigation, so much and such tall grass withers away as the garúas had produced on the hills, leaving nothing but a few dry scrubby pastures; this being so even though in the sierra, where it rains no more than four months, the grass stays green all year long without any irrigation for the other eight months: which indicates the great moisture and richness of the soil of that region, and the remarkable dryness of the soil of the coastal plains.

The livestock fatten greatly in those rivers for six months, and when the highland rains come to an end, with this abundance of food and range they maintain many large herds, estimated as the greater livestock found on the plains. And if the pastures of the plains were to last for the months they endure, they would last the whole year, and would be an inestimable wealth for the inhabitants of those plains. In the most abundant lowlands, such as those of the bishopric of Arequipa, though it is true that the pastures dry out once the sea mists pass, still so much dry straw remains that everything is clearly laid out for some tame livestock, and a good number of mares, donkeys, and mixed mules, and their owners, which are found there.

The sea mists that fall in the coastal valleys, set back a little from the hills and ridges, are very fine and so brief that they are not sufficient to produce grass; nor do the houses need rooftops. The Indians therefore make the roofs of their houses flat, without slope, and covered with a mat of woven reed with a layer of earth placed on top, which is the Indian custom. The Spaniards at first followed their example and used this same manner of roofing, but since then, as the buildings have continued to improve day by day in refinement and strength of construction, and also because in some years when the winter brings heavy rains these flat roofs leak badly — not being suited to the houses they were using — they have gradually introduced the practice of replacing them with well-timbered plank roofs, and with Florentine-style tiled roofing.

The ordinary thing was that nothing prevented people from traveling outside the town, nor from walking through the streets, and frequenting the plazas and markets, as if it were not raining. Although it rains in the valleys very lightly, these rains are most beneficial for the crops, and when they do not come, or are delayed, they are notably missed: for which reason processions and prayers have been held in Lima, though in other parts they are not usually held for the rains. Because given that the planted fields are irrigated, the garúas (coastal mists) are still so important, that by means of them the crops sprout and ripen until harvest with only two or so waterings; and without them, many more would be needed; as we see happens in the valleys that lie outside the hills, for which there would not be sufficient water in the rivers, since many yield little at planting time. And in the times of the Inca kings, much more land was irrigated than now with the same water, because the Indians did not then have the farms and gardens that the Spaniards now have, in which much water is consumed; besides sugarcane fields, olive groves, plantain groves, and alfalfa fields. And also because, in towns where one can plant at all times of the year in the lowlands, the Indians used to sow in summer when the rivers ran full and flooded; despite all this, the Spaniards generally sow in winter because the labor is more temperate, and to enjoy the benefit of the garúas, which not only fertilize the land with the water that they

As I have said before. At that time I was residing in the city of Arequipa, where some residents of it told me that, having gone at that time to the coastal hills by the sea toward the right side of the olive groves, they found themselves present at a great storm. And a gentleman who had observed with care and curiosity the behavior of the weather and the gathering of the storm, told me that beforehand, to his great wonder, he had noticed that the clouds were rising much higher than they usually stand in that area, and that with that storm of thunder and lightning there fell such a great rain that streams of water rushed down in disarray.

The garúas are more frequent at night and in the mornings than in the afternoons; they fall very gently, without storms or violent whirlwinds of wind; carried only by the soft south wind, which blows throughout the year across those plains, and which also serves many uses worthy of admiration. Among the things that occur with these garúas, one is particularly worth noting: they only gather over the hills of the sea coast, and not over those that continue inland from them, even though all of them are of equal height, and the inland ones are even higher. The dew and mists so well known, which fall in the morning hours of the coastal plains; and beyond them all the land is dry, with no rain whatsoever. Since the Spaniards settled this land, it has happened that it rained a few times on the plains, and it has always been considered unusual and outside the ordinary course of things. The second was in the year fifteen hundred and seventy-eight, when it rained in the valleys of the bishopric of Trujillo. A dark and heavily laden cloud broke near the royal road and unleashed a great downpour over the small area below it; it served to wash some things that had remained there for several days; and as I myself passed along that same road a few days later, it was as if it had never rained.

Also, in the year sixteen hundred and twenty-four, it rained prodigiously in the town of Jaño, and in other parts of the diocese of Trujillo; and afterward it rained in those same valleys two more times. Most recently, in the present year of sixteen hundred and fifty-two, on the third of February, a great downpour fell upon this city of Lima, and because of the damage feared from it, the archbishop ordered all the churches of the city to ring their bells in supplication, asking God to stop the rain, because since the rooftops of the houses are not built to withstand downpours, the water caused no small damage to the houses it soaked, and the damage would have been far greater had the rain continued. These rains that fall on the plains tend to come with lightning that ignites, descending from the sky while it rains, thanks to the season.

We were going very slowly, and night was drawing near, with nowhere to shelter ourselves; I persuaded my companions to quicken our pace in order to get out of the coastal hills before nightfall, and to reach dry ground. We did so, and before the sun had set we came out of the hills and the thick cover of mists, arriving at the high ground, which was the top of the slope we had been climbing, and which in that area is very flat. Likewise upon reaching it, we lifted our heads above the clouds that had been covering us; and we noticed that the clouds had their upper surface level and even with that great plain, so that it seemed the flat land continued right into the high surface of the clouds. The air from there upward was clear and calm; the sky open and cheerful; and the ground of that plain dry and parched — for although it was raining right alongside it, the garúas did not cross the boundary and limits of their district. And we resolved to spend that night there, and we slept on that plain under the open sky, with as little fear of getting wet as if we had slept under a roof. And we lay the whole night under a clear, starlit sky, at less than a musket-shot's distance from the clouds or mists, which were rolling over the coastal hills all night long.

Thus, because of their great dryness, the vapors that rise from the land are very thin and fine; along the sea coast of that region I see no sound reason — for I ask myself — why it never rains there. Setting that aside, it is well known that clouds not only water the lands from which the moist vapors rose, but also, after condensing in the middle region of the air, the winds carry them from one place to another, watering different lands. According to this reasoning, the rains that formed from the sea vapors could well fall on the nearby shores, just as we see them moving inland from the sea, passing beyond it toward the sierra, which is the origin of the plains. I myself observed this one year when there was a great deal of rain in the sierra, while I was visiting the town of Pisco: each morning I would see great quantities of vapors rising from the sea in the form of mists, rushing swiftly toward the sierra, and upon reaching it they would condense into thick clouds, so that by two in the afternoon one could already see from the coast itself that it was raining in the sierra.
    Others also wish to give as a reason the lack of winds to press and squeeze the vapors and resolve them into rains, on account of the shelter that the main mountain range provides to the lowlands. The closer the mountain range runs to the sea, and the greater shelter it provides to the plains, the more people live on the coast of the dioceses of Lima and Trujillo. And where the main mountain range most distances itself from the sea — a stretch of thirty to fifty leagues — the garúas are entirely absent, and the land is the driest and most barren of all the plains. This can be seen in the districts of Porta in the diocese of Trujillo, and Atacama in that of the Charcas, which are the extremes of the plains. From this one may conclude that the lack of rain on the plains, and the falling of garúas only along the strip or belt of the lomas, and not in the rest of them, is one of the greatest secrets of nature that we humans have experienced, whose causes we cannot comprehend; and thus we must place it in the catalogue of the other marvels of nature that we have found in the New World.
Chapter 17. On the Huyas and Mahamaes of the Plains.
Another particularity no less marvelous than those mentioned in the preceding chapters is what we find in the history of the plains — namely, the method the Indians used to make productive for their crops land that was by nature barren and fruitless. They did this in two ways: the first by digging and opening large holes; and the second by making use of humid places, either by means of some river's flow, or by having water within themselves very near the surface:

The lowlands of Villauiri in the province of Ica, no less famous than those of Chilea, are the most inland of any I know of; because they are four to five leagues from the sea, in which case there is greater reason to doubt whether the moisture they receive comes from the sea or from elsewhere. An argument that it comes from the sea could be that they produce, as they do, saltpeter on the surface of the earth, as do those of Chilea and the other coastal lowlands. But it seems to me, with all due respect to better judgment, that such moisture does not come from the sea; first because these lowlands are so far from it; and second because they are not on the same level as the sea itself, but rather considerably higher, as one can verify by experience, in that traveling from the sea toward them, one is always going uphill somewhat, though gradually. Therefore I maintain that all the moisture of the lowlands of Villauiri, and much of that of those situated on the coast, comes from rivers that descend from the mountains; because all of them, from the moment they reach the dry flatlands, steadily diminish, owing to the fact that their water is being absorbed and seeping through the sand and gravel that form the riverbeds, so that many of those that are not very powerful sink into the ground and disappear before reaching the sea, whose water

The same fruits grow there as in the rest of these valleys, and all the fruit of the low-lying hollows ripens well enough to supply the irrigated orchards. Dates in particular, and the wine from these hollows, are preferred above others. And although the hollows have the depth we have described, travelers cannot make out from a distance what lies within them, and so those who do not know them assume that everything stretching before them is sandy flatland, like the surrounding terrain, until, upon reaching these hollows, they find in the midst of such solitude one of these groves and lush depressions, so green and beautiful, with such abundance of trees and pleasant greenery. In the hollows that are not cultivated, much grass grows, which serves as pasture for the animals of travelers, and is no small help to the muleteers.

And because it seems that the excessive moisture, both in the hoyas and in the Mahamues, would have hindered the ripening and seasoning of the fruits; the most wise maker of all things provided that in winter, when the plants require more moisture, and the rivers of the plains carry less water, the hoyas and Mahamues retain so much humidity that they seem to be springing with water. Chapter 18. On the Volcanoes that exist in Peru,
and the great damage they are accustomed to cause.

The two largest and principal parts of Peru, which are
the lowlands and the highlands, are subject to two plagues and
hardships most burdensome, which tend to bring notable
damage to their inhabitants. Both arise from one and the same
principle, which are the mouths of fire, or volcanoes, found along
the main mountain range: which cause very frequent earth-
quakes. And when they erupt, releasing from their
entrails an immense quantity of fire, ash, and
boulders, they tend to devastate and destroy the lands around
them, and even those quite distant and far away. Those
who suffer most from these hardships are the inhabitants of
the lowlands; although the people of the high-
lands do not fail to receive their share, especially
during the eruptions of the volca-
noes. There are a great number of these throughout all the Indies: they are
mountains of admirable size, which dominate
the highest ranges: nearly all of them have their peaks perpetually
covered with snow, and in them a great
mouth, or opening, that descends to the depths of the.

Those who were then navigating on it were forced to jettison the residue of the great quantity of ash that had fallen inside their vessels. A great number of livestock perished throughout the whole province, for lack of fodder. This same thing has happened in the province of Quito several other times before and after, though not with such force and power as this.

The other volcano, which most recently erupted in the year sixteen hundred, caused such great ruin and destruction throughout all of Peru, and beyond, with swift damage across two hundred provinces according to their distance; that one cannot find recorded in the ancient or modern histories anything that occurred anywhere in the world that was more fierce and terrifying. For this reason, having been present myself at the time of this event, and having been an eyewitness to part of that terrible tempest — even though I was more than one hundred and seventy leagues distant from the volcano — I will take it upon myself to give some account of it; and it happened in the following manner.

The general mountain range enters on the eastern side, one of which is ten or sixteen leagues from that city, which is the day of Pinate, named after a village of that name that stood on the slope before it erupted. Five leagues from there, further inland, and behind the said city, stands the second volcano, which we call that of the Ucinas, also taking its name from the nearest village to it, called the first, which is the one that erupted in the aforementioned year of sixteen hundred. It is not a single peak, but a long mountain range of seven leagues, which, although not of excessive height, has such a great base that it spans thirty leagues. Its summit ends in several peaks which, seen from outside, have the form of a crown; the one in the middle is smaller than the others, and in it is the vent. It is considered very probable that underground this volcano communicates with that of the Ucinas, and that the ash, rock, and fire that it cast through this opening or vent came from the interior of both. The indications that persuade one that this is so are two: the first is the infinite quantity of ash and rock that came out of it, for it seems a prodigious thing, exceeding the natural course, that it should have had within itself so much material as it vomited forth, and that if it were gathered and piled up it would without doubt form a mountain two or three times greater than that of the volcano itself. The second, and more certain indication, is to see that after this one erupted, the other did not emit smoke for some years.

The volcano of the Voinas, having previously been continuously smoking, the Spanish settlement closest to the volcano of Omate is the city of Arequipa; and for that reason its inhabitants received the greatest blow of this calamity: although because of the darkness and shadows with which it came upon them, they did not know for several days where it was coming from. Those who witnessed it and experienced most closely all the miseries and damages that occurred were the ones who noted it with the greatest detail and wrote down this torment as it unfolded, and it happened thus.

On the eighteenth day of the month of February, a Friday of the first week of Lent in the year sixteen hundred, at around nine o'clock at night, some tremors of the earth began to be felt in that city, which lasted until the following Sunday. From the hour they began they grew more rapid and stronger, so that they not only increased in number but also in force. Everyone from that hour abandoned their houses, because some were falling. Shortly afterward there were heard very large and frightful sounds, as if they were being fired from within the city, and in such rapid succession that one overtook the next. So it was that at two in the afternoon the day was so dark that no one could recognize anyone they met; and to remedy this, large men walked through the streets carrying torches. At four o'clock the sky cleared somewhat, and ash began to fall again, lasting three hours. Twenty-one days later the ice was entirely covered with mounds, raised and protruding, which were horrifying to look upon; because of this it was necessary to carry lights for any task whatsoever. That day the sky darkened again, though not as much as before, and ash fell for another three hours. A few days later the dawn came with the lost color and hue it had before, and ash began to fall again from nine until three in the afternoon, in the manner of a white powder that made the hair and beard rough, as if it were ground pumice stone. The following two days, although they were not very dark, the sun was not seen at all. On Friday the twenty-first, the air became turbid again and a hot wind came in, around the hour when dusk falls at the end of twilight, and the closer it came to night, the greater the darkness grew, with some thunder and tremors. On the twenty-sixth there was no day at all, for the entire day was as dark as night; a bolt of lightning struck, and so much ash fell in the manner described that it was necessary to clear the rooftops frequently, lighting torches in order to do so. It began to rain ash, the cause being, as people said, some volcano within their district. For the first two days it was thought to come from a very large one that lay six leagues from the city, but they soon realized this was not the case. They suspected it must be the one called Obinas. In the end they could not determine with certainty where the harm was coming from, until after ten or twelve days had passed, when the weather cleared somewhat, and some Indians came to the city — those who had saved themselves from six towns that had been destroyed by being closer to the volcano — and from these, as well as from many other persons, both Indians and Spaniards, who had been at a distance of six to twelve leagues from the volcano and had witnessed the eruption from afar, it became known that it was the volcano of Oñate that had erupted. This caused little surprise at first, because no one had ever been wary of it, since it had never been seen to emit fire or smoke, and also because it was so many leagues distant from the city.

And it was learned that on the first afternoon of the storm, upon erupting, it sent forth such a quantity of black smoke together with the crashes and thunderings already mentioned, that it darkened the sky and plunged ten or twelve leagues around it into profound darkness, which lasted fifteen days, during which one could not distinguish day from night. A stone of great size split open at the foot of the hill, and from it burst forth a great and furious river of fire, which ran for about a league and a half, burning everything it touched, so that it turned all the trees to charcoal and the ground over which it passed was left smooth and as hard as bare rock. There were about seventy Indians at work in those fields gathering their harvest, and most of them were burned by the stones, which, even buried in the ash, came out as glowing coals, looking like balls of fire. They were of different sizes: some like medium-sized jars, others as large as two Peruvian wine jars, others like a man's head, others like large balls, others like a fist, and so on in all sizes down to a dust so fine it barely had substance. They fell at different distances, some farther than others, with tremendous force: at one league from the volcano they were the size of two wine jars, at two leagues about one, and progressively smaller the farther they fell. So great was the quantity of burning stones, and so high did they rise, that looking at the sky it seemed as though the whole of it were ablaze, turned into a sea of the innumerable stones flying through the air. For the fifteen days that the eruption lasted, the volcano did not cease roaring day and night, throwing out ash and stones, and the earth shook frequently. Chapter 19. Which continues the same subject as the previous one.

The confusion and astonishment of the people while these things were happening was so extraordinary that it cannot be expressed in words. From the moment the storm began with such tremendous roaring and trembling of the earth, everyone ran to the churches, dumbstruck and pale, to beg for mercy from God and to implore His forgiveness for their sins and wrongdoings. No one gave a thought to their estates and riches, nor paid them any mind, believing that the end of the world had come and that their days were numbered. Persuaded of this, some Indians, forgetting their Christian obligations, sat down at their leisure to eat and drink until they were drunk, in accordance with the barbarous custom they had practiced in their pagan days; eating, even though it was Lent, the chickens and sheep they owned, saying that since they were going to die anyway, there was no point in saving them. Others among the inhabitants of the villages near the volcano hanged themselves, to be free from the ash and from a more painful death. But the residents of Arequipa

text:

134

Españoles, y gran parte de los Indios se dispusieron para morir como cristianos, recibiendo con gran dolor, y lagrimas los santos sacramentos de la penitencia, y comunion. Estubieron las iglesias abiertas de dia, y de noche, y en ellas descubierto el santisimo sacramento. Cesaron todos los tratos, y oficios de la republica, sin atender grandes, y pequeños a otros de que ahacerle garias a nuestro Señor, y procesiones todos los dias, y algunas dellas de sangre. Andaban los hombres en un perpetuo sobresalto, por no darles lugar a tomar reposo de noche los continuos terremotos, y el halli del volcan, tan afligidos, y quebrantados, que tubian por mejor suerte acabar de una vez la vida, que dilatarla, y para atormentar mas sus almas con la vista de tan lastimosos, y prodigiosos sucesos.

Los daños, y calamidades, que causo esta tan terrible tormenta, fueron de inestimable valor, si bien es verdad que lo que de ella menos daño hizo fue lo que paso mayor bacor, y espanto a las gentes, y eso fueron los horribles truenos, bramidos del volcan, los continuos, y presurosos terremotos, las tinieblas, y relampagos del ayre. Fueron los bramidos tan diformes, y tan horrosos, que los que se han hallado en alguna fortaleza, como la de Malta, o en la batalla naval no pudieron ser mas ofendidos del impetuoso estrepito de la artilleria, que lo fueron los vecinos de Arequi
translation:
First Part. Book 2.
