Spaniards, and a great part of the Indians prepared themselves to die as Christians, receiving with great sorrow and tears the holy sacraments of penance and communion. The churches remained open day and night, with the Blessed Sacrament exposed within them. All commerce and public offices ceased, as both great and small attended to nothing other than offering prayers to our Lord, and to processions every day, some of them bloody. The people walked in a state of perpetual alarm, for the continuous earthquakes gave them no chance to rest at night, and those near the volcano were so afflicted and broken that they considered it a better fate to end their lives at once than to prolong them, and to torment their souls further with the sight of such pitiful and extraordinary events.

The damages and calamities caused by this terrible storm were of inestimable worth, although it is true that what caused the least physical destruction was what produced the greatest dread and terror among the people, namely the horrible thunder, the roaring of the volcano, the continuous and rapid earthquakes, the darkness, and the lightning in the air. The roaring was so monstrous and so horrifying that those who had been present at some great fortress, such as that of Malta, or in a naval battle, could not have been more assailed by the furious noise of artillery than were the residents of Arequi

The sounds were heard two hundred leagues away, and in the city of Lima, which is one hundred and seventy-four leagues from the volcano, we heard them so clearly — being there at the time — that we were certain that the Royal Armada, which had set sail from the port of Callao a few days before in pursuit of a pirate who had entered the South Sea through the Strait of Magellan, had encountered him, and that the thunder we heard was from the artillery being fired in battle.

Many buildings in the city of Arequipa and in other Indian towns in the area collapsed from the earthquakes, and those that remained standing were badly damaged. Hills and slopes crumbled, blocking the flow of several rivers. But the greatest harm — or rather, all of the harm — came from the enormous quantity of pumice stone and ash that poured out of the volcano. This fell over three or four leagues in every direction, and rose as high again. Six Indian towns were buried beneath it, under a thick layer of ash covering the houses. These towns were called Omate, Ubque, Tarata, Tolana, Checa, and Quinistaca; the last of these was about a league and a half from the volcano. La tierra mas molestada de terremotos de toda la America son los llanos, y costas del reyno del Peru, adonde se experimenta una muy biennotable, y porque ocasionandose los frequentes temblos de tierra que aqui suceden, segun la mas comun opinion, de los muchos bolcanes que ay en la sierra, y de la bleraga general de herrervio, con ellas rios de ciados de llamas la Pittoman querella resporia la cordillera occidental, como que da dicho arriba, y estar mucho mas cercanos a la sierra, que cae al oriente de la misma cordillera, que no a los tierros mo vitima de los llanos, con todo eso son sin comparacion mas suge tos a temblos estos llanos, y usila de la mas que las provincias de la sierra. It is impossible to count the great damages and losses that resulted from the terrible and lamentable storm caused by the ash fall from the volcano, which without doubt destroyed some ten or more settlements, of which only something can be said from what has survived: in the valley of Vitor alone, where the residents of Arequipa held the greater part of their vineyards, more than one hundred thousand barrels of wine were produced each year, worth three pesos each, amounting to three hundred thousand; and because of this terrible calamity, no wine was seen in the following six years, from which one can draw good conclusions about the great ruin and damage that the volcano caused.

Chapter 20, On the Earthquakes of Peru.

The land most troubled by earthquakes in all of America is the coastal plain and coast of the kingdom of Peru, where a very remarkable phenomenon is experienced. The frequent tremors that occur here are caused, according to the most common opinion, by the many volcanoes in the highlands and by the general turmoil of subterranean fire, whose flames run beneath the western mountain range, as said above, and being much closer to the highlands than to the far side of the same mountain range, these coastal plains are nonetheless incomparably more subject to tremors than the provinces of the highlands. Paraguay, which is free from the torments of thunder and lightning that afflict the inhabitants of the highlands, does not spare its own residents

text:
Historia del nuevo mundo.
que temer, y donde quiera que gamos ante los ojos alguaciles y executores de la divina justicia: comparados entre si a todos los generos de tempestades, por la que yo se experimentado de entram bos los años que he residido en la sierra, y en los llanos: yo go por mas formidable la tempestad, y persecucion del viento que la de la tierra. Porque para salvar la vida de aquella señora la v remedio, saliendose la gente a lugares descubiertos, apartados de cerros, y edificios; y para la tormenta de rayos no ay lugar seguro en poblado, ni fuera del: la qual se hace mas horrible por ser su golpe tan repentino, que primero se siente el daño que llega al oidos el ruido; lo qual no acor tece en los temblores: si bien es verdad que son mayores los daños, y perdidas de hazienda, que causan estos que no los rayos.
Son tan frequentes, y ordinarios los temblores en las costas del Peru, y del reyno de chile, que corrienmas de ocho cienetas leguas Norte Sur, que no se pasa ningun año que dege de auer algunos: los quales van corriendo por su orden en todo este espacio unos tras otros; alcanzando los menores a cien leguas de costa, y de veinte a treinta la tierra adentro: y los generales, y famosos, que suelen venir mas tarde en tarde, a quatro cientos, y quinientas en fuego de la mar, y de tri quinta a ochenta por la tierra a dentro; que todo este gran pedazo de tierra se mueve, y ondea con un temblor agitado de las olas del mar embravecido, y tempestuoso.
Despues que poblaron esta tierra los Españoles han avisado ser
translation:
History of the New World.
to fear, and wherever we turn our eyes there are officers and executors of divine justice: compared among themselves to all types of storms, of which I have had experience of both during the years I have resided in the highlands and on the plains. I consider more formidable the storm and pursuit of the wind than that of the earth. Because to save life from that threat, the remedy is for people to go out to open places, away from hills and buildings; but from the storm of lightning there is no safe place in a town or outside of it: which is made all the more horrible by its blow being so sudden, that the harm is felt before the sound reaches the ears; which does not occur with earthquakes: although it is true that the damage and loss of property caused by these is greater than from lightning.
Earthquakes are so frequent and common along the coasts of Peru and the kingdom of Chile, running more than eight hundred leagues from north to south, that not a single year passes without several occurring: which follow one after another in sequence throughout this whole expanse; the smaller ones reaching a hundred leagues along the coast, and twenty to thirty leagues inland; and the general and notable ones, which tend to come less frequently, four to five hundred leagues along the sea, and from fifty to eighty leagues inland; such that this entire vast tract of land moves and undulates with a trembling agitated by the waves of the enraged and tempestuous sea.

There have been some very notable earthquakes, worthy of memory, beyond what occurred in the kingdom of Chile in past years, which was so terrible that, overturning and joining two mountains together, it dammed and blocked the river of Valdivia, which had been a mighty river; as the floodwaters rose, the stopped trees were held back for many days, coming to burst forth, and the rains swept away the rivers — admired by all who witnessed them — causing notable harm to towns and people alike, flooding settlements and lands, causing the sea to rise and overflow its boundaries by a great distance, pushing back far from where its waters had been. In many other such instances similar events occurred.

Then followed, in the year fifteen hundred and sixty-two, the earthquake of Arequipa, which completely leveled that city. And then, four years later, came that great earthquake of the city. The tremor of the year fifteen hundred and eighty-six, on the ninth of July, struck — whose damage was beyond reckoning — yet it was fortunate in that not many people perished, owing to the earthquake not catching them asleep, and the noise having given them warning as it approached, so that they fled into the open plazas, streets, gardens, and away from the houses; and thus no more than thirteen to fifteen persons died. But its force and great fury were so terrible that it greatly ruined the city, bringing down many buildings, and obliging the citizens to set up tents and pavilions in the plazas to keep away from the walls and roofs of the houses; and there they remained for many days without daring to trust the shattered supports.

avia visto en este reyno, y aun es reputado en musi cali

sucedido en el mundo. su extencion fue tan grande, que
aun mismio tiempo levanto mas de trecientas leguas de tierra
en longitud, que corre Norte Sur por la vela de la mar, y entro

del Callao, que dista sesenta de la mar, llego con tanta fuerza,
que no se podian tener en pie los hombres, y remecio fuerte men

tan pequeño que no huviese temor. Salimos con este temor

The sea, on the contrary, made the same movement it had made in Chile, attacked the land, and going beyond itself entered far inland, covering the fields and estates with great fear and harm to their owners.

All these torments and calamities were forgotten because of the terrifying earthquake that occurred on the twenty-fourth day of November of sixteen hundred and four, at around one-thirty in the afternoon, which was without doubt the greatest that had ever been seen in this kingdom, and is still regarded as one of the rarest and most prodigious that is known to have occurred in the world. Its extent was so great that at the very same time it shook more than three hundred leagues of land in length, running North to South along the coast of the sea, and entered inland in its width more than seventy leagues. To the city of Callao, which is sixty leagues from the sea, it arrived with such force that men could not remain standing, and it shook the buildings violently, though they did not fall because they were strong and well-founded; only the outer wall of the church of the Company of Jesus fell to the ground. Its duration was more or less, according to the force with which it struck each place. Here in this city of Lima, where I happened to be at the time, in the church of our house with some other religious men, it lasted about four or five — it was not very great here, nor yet so small as to cause no fear. We came out with this fear

fleeing to their patios, as soon as they saw the walls of the church beginning to shake, and the roof timbers cracking loudly. Although it caused fear in Lima in this manner, there was no damage there, but we all feared that the force had gone elsewhere, and consequently the damage as well, as indeed it had.

In the city of Arequipa it lasted half a quarter of an hour, and altogether it went on for half an hour; though, as commonly happens with large earthquakes, many smaller ones followed it, which continued for the next ten days or so. It was all the stronger the further one went from Lima toward the south, as far as the port and city of Arica, where, as in Arequipa, it had its greatest force and violence. The residents of Arequipa had suffered, since the volcano erupted, almost continuous years of harsh calamities from ash and sterility, great want and poverty. But as the ash diminished — for the constant winds, since it was so light, had carried it from one place to another, and a great part of it had blown out to sea — the sun began to show itself more clearly, and with its rays more unobstructed, it warmed the earth more, and through its heat and influence began to fertilize it again. The land enjoyed this benefit, so long denied to it by the heavy, dusty ash clouds, so that it seemed the fields, vineyards, and other properties were coming back to life; and the people, with these good hopes, began to recover

they caught some breath, and gathered together lamenting their past hardships and losses, when there came upon them the fearful and tremendous earthquake, which began to shake the entire city from one hour to the next, and caused as great a devastation in the towns and fields of its surroundings as the eruption of the volcano.

It began gently, and with little noise, which, together with its occurring during the day, was the reason it did not kill many people, as it would have done had it struck at night. It kept growing in such a way that men, thrown to their knees and clinging to one another, could still not hold themselves upright. The fields began to resound with a deep rumbling that gave warning: the mountains moved so violently that they seemed to be crashing into one another; the houses were so shaken and battered by the waves and shuddering of the earth, as ships are by a stormy sea; collapsing, they broke apart, and the force of the tremor hurled their ruins aloft with a horrible roar, as much from the buildings as from the mountains that were crumbling. Such a thick cloud of dust rose up that it darkened the sun, leaving everyone buried in a narrow and dark space, with no one daring to move from the spot where they stood, for fear of falling into greater danger. In all of Arequipa, within half a quarter of an hour, not a building remained standing except the churches of Saint Francis and Saint Augustine. Many came out of the ruins with broken legs, battered heads, and mutilated and crushed bodies; besides those who

were buried, and hearing their voices and cries, many were pulled out alive. The dead were little more than forty, who were gradually discovered on the surface after several days.

Many Indian villages of the diocese of Arobiopa were destroyed, and of the province of Annacocha, which belongs to the district of Guatanga: in this area the village of Pausa was ruined in such a manner that of six hundred houses it had, no more than fourteen or fifteen were left standing, and it was so badly damaged that they were of no use: thirty people died crushed and from lack of food. The earth moved and shook as if it were a piece of sea, and caused springs to burst forth in many places, leaving some elevated areas: from these springs came black and foul-smelling water, which was of no use to anyone, and fields and properties were ruined; what everyone generally feared was that one night the earth opened up, and as indeed happened in many places it opened into great chasms, which with great terror would open wide and then close again. Some people, fearing being swallowed by these crevices, tied themselves firmly to trees. There were some mouths and openings in the earth so large that they swallowed for several days very full rivers; many roads and irrigation channels fell into them; they were four varas wide and one or two hundred paces long, some more and some less. In the valley of Moquegua the earthquake caused no less

Chapter 21. Continuing the same subject

There was the same earthquake within the sea along this entire coast,
which those who happened to be sailing along it did not survive well,
and they were terrified by the great roar; but it was the waters
on the shores that did as much damage as everything
caused by the ruin of mountains, buildings, and river dams.
The sea rose up in a strange manner, and bursting beyond its shores
with terrifying force, made three assaults upon the land, and
just as many retreats, flooding the ravines and low-lying
valleys to the uttermost, spreading through them for half a league
or a full league, destroying the farms and estates, and carrying away
with it the men and livestock that were there, leaving them in such a place

At its retreat, a great quantity of dried fish was left behind, and a large part of its region was exposed. Although the tremors reached the city of Lima with little force, and although the sea likewise left the port and went beyond its banks, it went only a very short distance and not with as much fury as in other places. Only one surge of water entered the town of Callao without fully flooding it, but made it into an island, so that for several days one could not travel from Lima to the port of Callao without crossing a great pool of water, which remained there because the land is low-lying.

What happened at the port of Pisco, thirty-six leagues from Callao, was a great wonder. Pisco is a Spanish settlement founded on the shore of the sea, where it came to pass that when the sea withdrew for the first time, all its inhabitants went out to the beach, drawn by the novelty of such a rare prodigy, quite heedless and unaware of what was soon to follow. The sea then swelled up, enormous and furious, against them; seized with terror at the prospect of being drowned by its swelling waves, they cried out to heaven begging God for mercy. Marvelously, the sea parted its waters to either side of the town, rushing far inland on both sides; and on the side where it was about to crash into and flood the houses with all the people — since the land lay on the same level — the water in front of the town stopped, to everyone's astonishment, without overstepping its bounds. And as the waters that had spread out to the sides withdrew,

En la villa de Camana de la diuision de Arequipa hizo la mar sus tres aumetidos, y retiradas subiendo por el valle mas la mitad de media legua. Destruyo quanto hallo en aquellos poblados, que fueron muchas viñas, bodegas, y cañaverales de azucar, asolo el pueblo, y recogió de caida quarenta personas del ahogado, y una manada de mulos con sus harrieros, y por restituidos a lo mucho que auia robado, dejo al ultimo no retirada tumbando por el valle mas de treynta mil arrobas de pescado, y en ellas de exquisitas generaciones de peces no vistos antes en estos valles. En el valle, y puerto de Ilo salio la mar casi media legua el valle arriba, arcano muchas fumos antiguos y no queriente otredidos, y hizo pedazos una fragata de mas de doze mil arrobas de porte, que estava en el astillero casi acabada.
Donde la mar hizo mayor estrago, unel sus sus fuerços, fue en la ciudad, y puerto de Arica, cuya calamidad, y ruina escrivio el corregidor de aquella ciudad a la Real Audiencia de los charcas con la puntualidad, y sentimiento que el caso pedia, por lo qual me previno remitarle este capitulo con tu carta que dice asi. Mucho derozo señor: a los veynte y uno de Noviembre vispera de santa catalina, a las dos horas de la tarde comenzo a temblar en este puerto, al principio con poca furia, y menos ruido, y de alli aun poco

that land so subdued by it, that through the violence of two floods responding to it, this same one receded, and gathers with the other waters downward.
In the town of Camaná, in the district of Arequipa, the sea made its three advances and retreats, rising up the valley for more than half a league. It destroyed everything it found in those settlements, which were many vineyards, wine cellars, and sugar cane fields; it leveled the town, and in its retreat gathered forty drowned persons, and a mule train with its muleteers, and as if to return some of the much it had stolen, it left on its final retreat, tumbling down the valley, more than thirty thousand arrobas of fish, and among them species of exquisite fish never before seen in these valleys. In the valley and port of Ilo, the sea went almost half a league up the valley, uprooting many ancient trees and others, and broke to pieces a frigate of more than twelve thousand arrobas burden, which was in the shipyard nearly finished.
Where the sea did the greatest damage, joining all its forces, was in the city and port of Arica, whose calamity and ruin the corregidor of that city wrote to the Royal Audiencia of Charcas with the exactness and feeling that the occasion required, for which he sent me this chapter with his letter which reads thus: Most honored sir: on the twenty-first of November, the eve of Saint Catherine's day, at two in the afternoon it began to tremble in this port, at first with little fury and less noise, and from there a little more

translation:
History of the New World.

Further regarding the Indies, and continuing in this endeavor, and in the following sections of this first part, I set out to record the most notable and well-known things I have been able to learn about them — both those that are common to and of the same kind as those of Europe, as well as those particular and proper to this new world, of which, before it was discovered by us Spaniards, those of Europe had no knowledge. In order to proceed with clarity and distinction, it seemed right to me to divide them into four kinds and classes, following the division that philosophers make of all bodies composed of the four elements, which they call perfect mixed bodies: that is to say, the inanimate, such as metals, which are commonly generated in the bowels of the earth and lack life; the animated but insensible bodies, which include all the kinds of plants; the sensitive and irrational animate things, which encompass all the kinds of brute animals, whether of the land, water, or air; and finally the rational composite beings, who are the native peoples of these Western Indies and the New World. I follow in these ranks the order that nature observes in proceeding from the imperfect to the perfect. And I shall treat first in this book of the mixed bodies belonging to the first rank and member of the division, and in the following books, of the other three.

La comun patria de los cuerpos mixtos inanimados es el elemento de la tierra; adonde, dejadas aparte las que produce el criador al principio, quando dio ser, y perfeccion al mundo; es doctrina asentada de los filosofos que mediante la virtud de las causas generales, y las particulares qualidades de diversas tierras, se van siempre engendrando de nuevo en la misma materia otros muchos y de todos generos, y especies: los que los secan quasando, y endurieciendo unos con frio, y otros con calor; concurriendo a su generacion la virtud de la misma materia, y de los otros tres elementos: cuya diferencia especifica sigue la variedad de la mezcla, de que se forman, y la virtud del elemento que predomina en la tal generacion: y no menos la del astro que influye, y con quien tiene mas afinidad, y simpatia el cuerpo que se produce.
De manera que si en la mixtura concurren mayor porcion de tierra que de los otros elementos, engendrase ha un cuerpo grave, seco, duro, espeso, y escuro; qual es el hierro. y si sobre pesar aire el agua en la misma proporcion, producirse han minerales claros, y trasparentes, como los diamantes, zafiros, y demas piedras preciosas. De la misma forma si concurriere en la mixtion mayor copia de tierra, y agua que de aire, y fuego; y la tierra, y agua con iguales fuerzas, y facultades escurecieren notablemente los otros dos elementos; engendrase han minerales de naturaleza fluente, molicos, graves, y alguntanto claros, y relucientes, como lo
translation:

The common homeland of inanimate mixed bodies is the element of earth; where, setting aside those which the Creator produced at the beginning, when he gave being and perfection to the world, it is a settled doctrine among philosophers that through the power of general causes and the particular qualities of diverse soils, new ones are continually being generated afresh from the same matter, of all kinds and species: some drying and hardening, some by cold, others by heat; with the power of the matter itself and of the other three elements contributing to their generation. The specific difference follows the variety of the mixture from which they are formed, and the power of the element that predominates in such generation, and no less that of the star that exerts its influence, and with which the body produced has the greatest affinity and sympathy.
So that if in the mixture a greater portion of earth than of the other elements is present, a heavy, dry, hard, dense, and dark body will be generated, such as iron. And if air and water are present in the same proportion, clear and transparent minerals will be produced, such as diamonds, sapphires, and other precious stones. In the same way, if in the mixture there is a greater quantity of earth and water than of air and fire, and the earth and water with equal forces and faculties notably obscure the other two elements, minerals of a fluid nature will be generated, soft, heavy, and somewhat clear and lustrous, as

They are gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and mercury: always contributing to the generation of the most precious metals the most perfect, purest, and most refined matter; and on the contrary, the most foul or impure matter to that of the imperfect and base metals. Together with the mixture of the elements, the virtue of the celestial bodies influences them, as has been stated; without which nothing in this lower world can be born, live, or thrive. For this reason, both alchemists and astrologers assign to each species of metal its own planet, which presides over, guards, and generates it, and gives it all its activity and force. And in the generation of all kinds of stones, it is likewise a well-founded opinion that each species of stone inclines toward one of the fixed stars, which gives it its strength and vigor.

And no more nor less than the generation of inanimate things, which belong to the first order and class of natural bodies, the elementary forces combine with celestial influences; so too they concur in the production of those of other grades, each according to what its nature requires. Of the mixture of the four elements with the influences of the celestial bodies, which concur in the generation of natural bodies, the Indians had no knowledge, nor of the other uses pertaining to the natural sciences.

El ambar que se halla en muchos costos de la America es del genero de betun; aunque algunos han querido decir que es una que echade si la ballena, oermo excrementos suyos, obstaque como, y la umuerte crambav. lo qual tengo por falso; porque si asi fuera en todas los islas de los mares, en que se hallan vallenas, se hallara tambien el ambar; lo qual no vemos que pasa asi: porque en estos costos del Peru, ay innumerables ballenas, y muchas dellas suelen varar en tierra muertas, y nunca en mas de un quento anos he visto, ni oydo, que en toda la costa de sierra no se halle ambar. A black pitch is born among the rocks, which when solidified remains the color of liver; its powders, when drunk, are useful for coughs. In New Spain there is found an amber of this kind, which the Indians call Apozocalli; of which there are two species, one of which tends more toward a warm color; and the other they call chipaltetl; and it is understood that both have the same virtue as regular amber.

There is another pitch, which the Mexicans call Chapopotli, which flows liquid from the sea, and is found very solidified along the coasts of New Spain, where women buy it to carry it in their mouths and chew it; because it cleans and polishes the teeth and makes them white: it is black in color tending toward auburn, and thrown into graves as if alive.

In some places there is found stuck to the rocks that the sea beats a substance of yellow gum, very soft, which is good for coughs, and is of little use for the chest.

The amber found along many coasts of America is of the pitch family; although some have wanted to say that it is something expelled by the whale, or its excrement, though it is eaten, and the death crambav. I hold this to be false; because if it were so, in all the islands of the seas where whales are found, amber would also be found; which we do not see to be the case: because on these coasts of Peru there are innumerable whales, and many of them tend to wash up dead on shore, and never in more than a hundred years have I seen or heard that along the entire coast amber has been found. Chapter 3: On Sulfur Stone

The abundance of sulfur found throughout the Indies is very great, particularly in the Kingdom of Peru — not only in the volcanoes that spout fire, but also in innumerable mineral deposits; from these there commonly flow springs of hot water carrying the very smell of sulfur, whose water is for the most part chalky and whitish in taste, and which congeals into stone. One kind of sulfur stone is extracted mixed with earth, and requires refining in order to purify it; another vein of it occurs in entire masses, pure and refined, requiring no treatment at all — this second kind is golden in color, very lustrous, and almost transparent. Similar to this is the sulfur stone that forms from the waters of a spring that flows in the province of Collao. The Indians made use of sulfur stone, and by burning it they used it only to treat the mange of their llamas and sheep of the land. The Spaniards make from it a great deal of very fine gunpowder, and they put it to all the same uses as in Europe.

Chapter 4. On Salt.

Just as the kingdom of Peru is the most abundant in metals, chiefly silver, of any we know today in the world, so too it is rich in natural salt deposits; for it seems God provided them in such abundance in a place where salt is so often needed to process silver metals, consuming an incredible quantity of salt. And there is no province or city that lacks it; for from the great amounts extracted in some lands, it is distributed to others; and none is so distant from some salt works that it cannot easily be supplied by land or sea with what it needs.

Authors who write on the subject describe three kinds of salt: namely sea salt, mineral salt, and that which is made from the water of certain springs. All of these are found in these Indies in very great abundance. And of two of them — sea salt and salt from brackish springs — both natural and artificial forms are found. For beyond the sea salt made from seawater by human industry, in some places the sea overflows with its tides and floods, casting far beyond the limits of its shores a great quantity of water, which with the heat of the sun congeals into excellent salt. And in other places they extract it in large stones from beneath the water of the same sea, from a certain earth where it is found solidified.

Beyond this, there are three ways in which salt is made from spring water: two of them by human industry, collecting the said water in pools where it is evaporated by the heat of the sun, and the other by boiling it in pots over fire until it becomes recognizable; the third way is that the same brackish water from many springs and lakes evaporates on its own.

There are three other ways found in this land by which salt is made from water. One is that in certain places salt is made from fresh water, by boiling in it the saltpeter gathered from the surface of the earth that the sea once covered, and also by means of a certain herb that has this virtue. In the province of Venezuela, the Indians made salt from the ash of the shoots of certain palms, which, although it was very white, was sticky and bitter in the manner of saltpeter. In the province of Popayan, they boil the herb mentioned above, and from the water in which it was soaked they make salt by evaporating it over fire.

Of the other two methods, one involves rainwater that collects in pools, and by the particular quality of the soil where it settles, it is converted into salt by the heat of the sun. But the one that causes me the most wonder is that found in a river in the province of Tucuman, for although its water is fresh, from the riverbed they extract great slabs of very white and fine salt. All the different kinds of salt mentioned up to this point come from water, naturally, or through human skill; apart from those that yield mineral salt, of which there are many in the kingdom of Peru, both in the coastal lands and in the inland regions.
This salt is extracted by force of drill-bits, wedges, and sledgehammers of iron, and it comes in three varieties: one is granular salt, another is salt in stone form, and of this latter kind there is one they call "compass" salt, which is so smooth and transparent as crystal, while the other is less so, because it has some dark veins running through it.
The salt mines found in the coastal lands differ from those in the mountain ranges further inland, in that the coastal ones, being close to the sea, are ordinarily covered with sand, beneath which the salt lies not in veins, but rather like a continuous slab or flagstone forming a crust over the earth.
But the inland salt mines are enclosed in rugged mountain ranges, where between the earth and the crags run veins of salt, which continue unbroken, just like those of other metal-bearing minerals.

Al salitre llaman los Indios del Peru yn en la lengua
general, yuca; pero es el que se cria en la superficie de

To add to what we call it, having so few things to season it with: they could find the dried meat that they made, and the fish that they cured for keeping and carrying from one place to another, without a single grain of salt. They did this in the following way: if the meat or fish was to be kept for any length of time, they would roast it on a Barbacoa, and afterwards bind it with fibers and rushes in the hot lowlands. But those of Peru, both for short and long keeping, would dry and cure the meat and fish in the sun on the coast of the sea, and in the frost in the cold highlands. And even in the stews and dishes they ate, they did not always add salt to season them; instead, when they ate, they would place a lump of salt next to the plate, which served as their salt cellar, and from time to time they would lick it with their tongue, giving the flavor of salt to the palate rather than to the dish. And sometimes, when many were eating together and there was no more than one lump of salt on the table for everyone, it would go around from hand to hand, each one licking it in turn. Salt is called by two names in the two general languages of Peru: cachi in Quechua, and haque in Aymara.

Saltpeter is very harmful to buildings, particularly in coastal towns such as the ports of Callao and Pisco, because it eats away the foundations of houses unless they are built of hard stone. And for the properties that are near the sea, because if care is not taken to remove the saltpeter from them, they become barren. The Indians did not know of saltpeter for gunpowder, nor did they know how to process it; which the Spaniards do by distilling the water in which it appears, and letting it settle in clay vessels, at the bottom of which the saltpeter congeals like grains of transparent salt. It is found in many parts of this kingdom of Peru in no small abundance, from which very good gunpowder is made; particularly the finest comes from the provinces of Quito. In lands that lack snow, the Spaniards cool water with saltpeter.

Of alum stone there are found in these Indies four or five species. In New Spain they make it very white, bright, and transparent, which the dyers use in their dyes, and it serves for the cures for which it is said to be brought from Spain.

Chapter 6. On certain clays and potting earths from which pottery is made.

From the varied mixture of the elements and the influences of the heavens, so many diverse soils are formed, differing from one another in color and quality, as we observe: of which there are as many varieties in this New World as in the other parts of the Old. The best known of all are the earths from which pottery is made, and all manner of clay vessels, being so necessary for the use of the people. All manner of clay from which pottery is made is called by the Indians of this kingdom, in their language, saño; and all potting earth in general, llanta. Many varieties of clays and potting earths of all colors are found in this land, and in some places very precious ones, from which curious jars and other drinking vessels are made for holding water, as is the case in the city of Cuzco, in the province of Chuncito, from where they are carried to many places, being much esteemed as a very fine clay. In this archbishopric of Lima, the clays of the valley of Ica and of the valley of Jipi are held in no lesser esteem; from the latter, white vessels are made that keep the water cool.
But all those mentioned are surpassed by those from the Diocese of Natá in Panama, from where many are brought to this city of Lima, very finely made and of various shapes. However, of late there has been found in the kingdom of Chile

No tubieron los Indios muchos usos de vasos de barro, porque nunca supieron ladrillo, ni teja; niento das estas Indias ay noticia de auer auido jamas en este genero; ni en toda la tierra he hallo un canto de ladrillo, ni un caro de teja: ni en los rui nas de los edificios antiguos ay rastro de cal, ni a, ni memoria entre los Indios de que la aya auido. such fine clay that it surpasses that of Nata: jars made from it are brought to this city of Lima, which are so precious that they are sent from here as gifts to Spain, because they can compete with the best from there in smell, luster, and color of the clay.
The Indians did not make much use of clay vessels, because they never learned to make bricks or roof tiles; nor throughout all these Indies is there any record of there ever having been any of this kind; nor throughout all the land have I found a single piece of brick, nor a fragment of tile: nor among the ruins of ancient buildings is there any trace of mortar, nor any memory among the Indians that there ever was any. Nor did they make the varieties of earthenware that we use; but only pots and jugs different from one another in being larger or smaller, and in certain figures and decorations that they carved on them; and some small flat plates in the manner of patens. The other vessels that correspond to those which the Spaniards are accustomed to make from clay, they made from silver, gold, wood, and dried gourds: nor in their ancient tombs, where they buried with their dead all their foods and drinks, were any other vessels found beyond those mentioned. Nor did they arrive at the invention of glazing; all their clay vessels were unglazed, nor did they fire them as perfectly as we do, because they had no kilns for this purpose, nor for any other use: in the ground they made a hole, and in it they did not fire them except with dung and straw; and today they still fire them in this manner; although for this purpose the livestock brought from Spain helps them not a little, especially cattle, which the

It provides firewood, which they use in this ministry. The quantities of clay pots used by the Spaniards are excellent, since those made by Indians withstand fire. They also had neither a wheel nor any other instrument with which to make these vessels, other than their hands, which is why it took them a long time to form them evenly; and yet they still make them in their own way, and finish them just as well as if they had been made on a wheel.

After the Spaniards settled this land, everything that is made of clay in Spain is made here as well, including as much brick and tile as is needed for our buildings; many turned out a variety of vessels: particularly a great quantity of one-arroba jars in which wine is transported — it is estimated that five hundred thousand are newly made each year in the vineyards — and also a good number of half-arroba glazed small jars for oil, brandy, rose water, and other liquors that are stored in them.

As for small basins and large earthen jars, which in Spain are made of clay, they are little used in these Indies; in their place they use bateas, which are made of hard and valuable wood. The Spaniards have adopted this practice from the Indians, who — particularly those living in hot and mountainous lands — always used them. They make them from the trunks of very thick trees, most commonly cedar, and some are so large that they hold ten arrobas of water or more, and are big enough for a man to bathe in them.

Chapter 7. On Pasa, and other varieties.

Morada.
Casa is what the Indians of Peru call a certain kind of clay, which is white with some brownish spots, something like a flavor quality; it is cold in nature, and they use it because it is very pleasing to them, and dissolved in water they season their potatoes and other roots with it, dipping them in it as if it were a sauce. For this reason it is sold in the markets of all towns. Its powders, which are soft and gentle, applied to hemorrhoids are useful for drying them out and consuming them. Mixed with vinegar or quince juice they work against attacks of gout. They serve to remove stains, and are often used in place of soap, because the lather they raise cleans clothing. For this reason the Indians wash their hair with it, noting that it kills lice, and that if those who suffer from bloody dysentery eat it, it stops it.

Cap. 8. Del Millu.

Millu es una especie de tierra parecida en su stipticidad, y casi en el color al caparrosa; ay dos diferencias della, una con que tiñen las batas de aqui, y otra de colorado. es el millu un caudaloso de boca fuerte, porque demas de la stipticidad que tiene, es purgativo, y mordaz; a cuya causa sus polvos curan los lamparones. el que hubiere comido con esta tierra un tumponcito de azucar deseca las llagas de qualquiera parte del cuerpo: y finalmente con el millu, salitre, y alumbre se hace una agua fuerte muy medici nal. El nombre de millu es de la lengua Ay mara.

Cap. 9. Del Tacu.

Tacu llaman los Indios del Peru en la lengua Aymara a la tierra que propiamente es Bolo Armenico; y por tal se suele administrar: al qual podemos llamar con propiedad Bolo Indico. halla se el Tacu en el cerro rico de Potosi, y en otros minos de metales, en especial de hierro entre diferencias, la primera es una tierra colorara

for plastering and whitening walls. Carpa is another clay, or red-colored earth, used in torments and on the floors of houses. Chau is another clay from which roof tiles and bricks are made, and poto-colored things, which women are inclined to eat. All these names come from the Aymara language, which is the general language of the provinces of the Collao in the kingdom of Peru.

Chapter 8. On Millu.

Millu is a type of earth similar in its astringency, and almost in color, to copperas; there are two varieties of it, one with which they dye the garments here, and another that is red. Millu is a powerfully strong substance, because beyond its astringency, it is purgative and biting; for which reason its powders cure scrofula. Whoever has eaten a small lump of sugar with this earth will dry out sores on any part of the body; and finally, with millu, saltpeter, and alum, a very medicinal strong water is made. The name millu comes from the Aymara language.

Chapter 9. On Tacu.

Tacu is what the Indians of Peru call, in the Aymara language, the earth that is properly Armenian Bole; and it is commonly administered as such: which we may properly call Indian Bole. Tacu is found in the rich mountain of Potosí, and in other metal mines, especially iron mines, among different varieties; the first is a reddish earth

Chapter 11. On Tepetate

It is a kind of earth that seems half soil and half stone, because it is neither entirely soil nor entirely stone, though it shares properties of both: it is soft like earth, yet resists water, which never softens it the way it does rock. Some call it "female stone," and in New Spain they call it Tepetate, which makes up the greater part of the ground of that kingdom, both in the mountains and in many plains and low areas, though this does not always impede the fertility of the region; because where the tepetate is exposed, the soil is entirely unfruitful; and where it is covered with earth, if the tepetate beneath is thick, it ends up robbing the waters when the land is cultivated, as has happened on the heights and hillsides around Mexico City, or even diminishing what is sown. Tepetate comes in various colors; for the most part it is reddish, though it is also found very white. A tepetate surface makes good ground for roads that run over it, because no matter how much it rains it does not turn to mud, but rather hardens so that water does not seep through or penetrate it. It is also good for cutting irrigation channels, ditches, and millraces into it, because it saves on lime and stone; and whatever is built of this material is so firm and secure that it never collapses. There is one tepetate harder than others: in the valley of Piura near Lima there are small hills of nothing but very white tepetate, which when ground up is commonly used to clean silver plates, and for this purpose alone it is brought from that city of Lima.

Chapter 12. On Sand.

There are various kinds of sand found in Peru, found along the shores of the sea and the rivers, as well as in many other places on the surface and in the depths of the earth. In these things the variety shows itself mainly in the following ways: one is color, and another is whether the sand is finer or coarser; and for the smelted and washed silver metals there is, beyond that, a great quantity of sand. On the coast of the sea at Pisco and Callao there is much sand made of broken and ground shells; it is white and is mixed with salt for use in construction. Apart from this sand, there is found in many places a black and fine grit, which is commonly sprinkled over fresh writing instead of blotting sand; and there is so much of it in Peru that there is no place that lacks it for this purpose, since everyone can obtain this fine grit.

For the same purpose there serve two other types that we may call fine grit. One is marcasite, which is found in many rivers and which in color and brilliance resembles gold dust, and has deceived more than a few Indians into thinking it was gold. The others from Charcas resemble silver filings. From these last two, the sand used in inkwells and urinals is commonly supplied.

In the province of Florida there is a certain deposit of very fine, white sand that silversmiths in New Spain use for whitening silver. In a river of New Spain there is also found a white sand that is good for treating fevers.

Los usos en que gastamos la arena son en la me de la para los edificios de cal y canto: quanto se galla en esta ciudad de Lima para elle menester la sacandecurio; y la que se galla en el puerto del Callao recoge de la playa de la mar, que es mas gruesa; y por ida de los albañiles por mejor, de la qual regala toda la que entro en la fabrica de la muralla, y fortificaciones de aquel puerto. La arena nos menudita, y sutil sineparar el gods de ampolles asi: la ordinario no es tan gruesa para labrar mar moles, la mas gruesa para solar los cantones para evitar los lodos quando llueve; para elle hecho vi yo echar una cespada de arena en las calles, pena una huerta, con que se podian pasar por ellas en acabando de ello ver, sin que hubiese lido que lo impidiere.

Para ninguna de estos usos tubieron uso de arena los Indios, por que señalabarcon la me de la cal, y arena que hace para los edificios, ni se aprovecharon de ella para labrar marmoles, ni para hacer relojes, que nunca tubieron de arena, ni de ruedas, ni de sol; ni menos para echar sobre los escrituras que nunca supieron. Solo en una cosa hallo que los Indios de la costa del Peru se aprovechavan de la arena, que era para encalar el maíz por lo que lo hacían con gosto; y lo mantenían guardarla en latron revuelto con arena menuda; y de ellos lo aprendieron los españoles a encalar el trigo.

cap. 13. De las piedras comunes.

Entrando en el genero de canteras, minerales, y toda suerte de piedras, pongo en primer lugar las mas comunes, que general

The uses for which we employ sand are in the making of lime and stone buildings: all that is consumed in this city of Lima for this purpose is extracted from the area nearby; and that which is used in the port of Callao is gathered from the seashore, which is coarser, and is preferred by the masons, and all of it that went into the construction of the city wall and the fortifications of that port was of this kind. The fine and subtle sand, without separating the air bubbles: the ordinary kind is not coarse enough for working marble; the coarsest is used to pave the street corners to avoid mud when it rains; for this purpose I myself saw a layer of sand spread on the streets of a garden, so that one could walk through them right after a rainfall without anything hindering one.

For none of these uses did the Indians ever use sand, for they marked with lime and sand what they made for their buildings, nor did they make use of it to work marble, nor to make clocks, for they never had any of sand, nor of wheels, nor of sun; nor even less to sprinkle over writings, since they never had any. Only in one thing do I find that the Indians of the coast of Peru made use of sand, which was to preserve maize, keeping it stored mixed with fine sand; and from them the Spaniards learned to preserve wheat in this manner.

On many shores of the sea, and on most of the rivers, and also inland in places far from the coast and rivers, one finds in abundance the most common and ordinary stones, which are the smooth, flint-like ones, beautiful in all sizes. They tend to extract some from the larger rivers when they run swollen and muddy; although these are difficult to work because of their great hardness, they are very attractive and prized, particularly for decorative vessels. There are many coastal lands whose entire depth is made of stone of this kind, as we see in the high bluffs along rivers as well as along the seacoast, from which many stones are commonly broken loose by earthquakes and roll down to the bottom. The soil of this entire valley of Lima is composed of gravel, sand, and rubble, except for the surface layer, which is a little soil that tends to be from one to two varas thick, more or less. And so from the wells dug in this city, much of this stone is extracted, ranging in size from a hazelnut up to the size of a head, and some much larger, weighing three or four arrobas. The same is true of the stones from the rivers, which include very large and very small ones. The Spaniards make use of these kinds of stones to pave streets and the courtyards of houses; the large cobblestones are used in the foundations of buildings; the white ones are ground by potters to make the glaze for earthenware; and finally, in seaports the cobblestones serve as ballast for ships, and it is the best ballast of all.

The Indians did not have many uses for these pebbles, because they had no ships to ballast with them, nor did they know how to pave the streets and floors of the houses in their towns, since in the ruins of these we have found no such use: they only used the round stones as mortars and tools for working cut stone, and as ammunition in war to throw with their slings, at which they were very skilled. We can also include in this category of stones certain slabs as hard as the pebbles, which are commonly found loose, very flat and smooth, two to three palms in diameter, on which the Indians grind their maize and other things.

Chapter 14. On stones used in construction.

Every kind of freestone and granite, which is easy to work, is what we call suitable for ashlar buildings, and there are choice quarries of it throughout these Indies; some stones are found very light and porous, in the manner of pumice, or pumice stone, which does not sink in water, and which is marvelous for construction, not only for walls and fortresses: similar to it there are many other kinds of light and spongy stones of all colors.
In the city of Arequipa there is a quarry of stone

Chapter 15. On various flints.

In all places, particularly in the highlands and cold lands,
many kinds of fine flints are found;
these the Indians used very well and valued greatly, even
though not for striking fire, but used them instead of
knives and other tools. Flints of all colors are found,
and a kind of stone that looks like flint, as red as coral,
greatly esteemed by the Indians, which
they call Mullu, and from it they make strings of beads
that the Indian women wear around their necks as ornament. Among the gravel-
beds of rivers and along the seacoast many are found
that are perfect flints, such as certain pebbles
very hard that are brought from the river of Guayaquil, of a dark yellow
color. But where the greatest abundance of flints I
have ever seen is in the province of the Mixteca in New
Spain; in which nearly every stone encountered
along the road was choice flint. In the plaza of
Mexico some very fine white flints are sold, and
together with them a kind of tinder is sold, which
is the best I have ever seen in my life, which they extract
from the bark of certain trees.

The stone of the grape of Paraguay which is formed from earth
is so tough a flint that it greatly wears down the steel
striker. Also a fine flint is the wood found beneath the

Cap. 16. De la piedra de cal.

No se halla igualmente en todas partes canteros de piedra
de cal, ni en tierras calorcientas, y mas sino en lugares
redondos con alguna mas costa se sube de la falta de las que no la
tienen. En toda la sierra del Reyno del Peru se hallan dos
o quiera copiosas canteras de esta piedra, particularmente
en los terminos de la ciudad del Cuzco, adonde hasta los
pardos de los andenes de las chacras, y heredades hazian
los Indios de esta piedra.
Fuera de las canteras ordinarias que crian las tierras, ha-
llamos en esta tierra otros dos otros especies de piedra de cal
muy particulares. La una se saca en la diocesis de Arequipa,
la qual es una como corteza que la tierra cria en su sobre haz
de lo sor de un palmo poco mas o menos; hallase en terreno
llano, y en laderas, unas veces descubierta en la mis-
ma superficie de la tierra, y otras enterrada, y cubierta della
uno, o dos o todos por mas o menos, de modo que en limpi-
ando la tierra de encima se descubra esta corteza, y de
baxo de la qual bone se pone es tierra como sale en unas.
Y el cal que de esta piedra se hace el mui fuerte, aunque no
tan blanca.

Chapter 16. On limestone.

Limestone quarries are not found equally in all places, nor in warm lands, and more often only in certain areas where, with somewhat greater effort, one climbs from the lowlands where it is not found. Throughout the highlands of the Kingdom of Peru, one finds abundant quarries of this stone here and there, particularly in the territory of the city of Cuzco, where the Indians used to build even the terrace walls of the fields and estates from this stone.
Beyond the ordinary quarries that the land produces, we find in this land two other very particular kinds of limestone. One is extracted in the diocese of Arequipa; it is a kind of crust that the land produces on its surface, about a palm's width thick, more or less. It is found in flat terrain and on hillsides, sometimes exposed on the very surface of the ground, and other times buried and covered by one, two, or more spans of earth, so that by clearing away the soil above, this crust is uncovered. Beneath it the ground is as it comes in places. The lime made from this stone is very strong, though not so white.

Another type of limestone is found on some islands of the kingdom's seas, as in the valley of Pisa, and in other places. This kind does not form on land, but rather in the sea, and when the waves rage they cast it onto the shores in pieces of various sizes, from medium up to four arrobas and more in weight. Once dried out, and the foam having settled, it resembles pumice stone, tending toward an ashen color, and is so soft that it easily crumbles. It has a strange property, which is that it soaks up and drinks whatever water is poured on it. The lime made from it is very white, but not as strong as the first kind.
In the city of Puebla de los Angeles, in New Spain, lime is made from a certain stone that congeals from water; it is good and white. In the valley of Ichacay, near this city of Lima, there are two or three ravines close to the sea, from which a certain water runs that gradually turns into stone of a reddish color, well-formed, and almost transparent, from which a lime so white is made that it is brought to this city to whitewash buildings.

In the province of Nicaragua, and in other coastal lands where limestone is scarce, lime is made from seashells, and this can hold its own against all others. Even so, the best, strongest, and most abundantly produced lime comes from ordinary limestone, which is very hard, solid, and heavy, of which there is great abundance in the valley of Lima, in a small range of hills about a quarter of a league from the city, where the early settlers found it, to the

Since the city was founded, although in the early days they did not use as much lime in the buildings as they do now — for when I came to Lima some thirty-three years ago there was no more than one lime kiln, and at present there are forty — they can barely keep up with the construction work being done. And from this point forward we build at great expense, working with lime and stone, which we consider essential. Also, within the last twenty-five years, other quarries of this stone have been found in the hills near the town of la te, half a league from the city, and the lime from these quarries is considered better than that from the first ones.

The most useful method that has been found for cutting stone from these quarries is with powder charges: a small hole is made in a large stone, and into it are packed tightly about three or four pounds of gunpowder, and when it is lit, it produces a blast as great as that of an artillery piece, and the entire stone, even one as large as a room, cracks and breaks into many pieces. We have found in this city that the mortar made from this lime, when used in damp places such as irrigation channels or cisterns where water beats against it, becomes as hard as bronze; but in buildings in the dry inland areas where it does not rain, it does not set as well — so much so that when an old building is demolished, the lime is found to be almost as loose as ash. For this reason, in new construction using lime and stone, the work is continuously wetted and moistened so that it sets better, and experience has shown this method to be very beneficial. A fanega of lime sells in this city of Lima for eight reales, and in other parts of the kingdom the price is no more or less, depending on its abundance there.

cap. 17. de la piedra de yeso.

De piedra de yeso se hallan menos canteras que de cal, particular
mente en tierras calientes: en las sierras frias ay grandes cerros de
lla, y alguna mina de espejuelo, como son el del distrito de

Los Indios del reyno del Peru no alcancaron el uso

cla de cal, y arena, ni edificar de yeso, que cierto hubiera sido
de grandissima utilidad para ellos tiempos, y ahorraranlos
Espanoles de gran costa si hubieran conocido la cal, y usado de
lla en sus fabricas: porque todas las acequias, talamares,
puentes, y otras fabricas que en tiempo de su gentilidad hi
cieron de piedra seca las hubieran hecho con mezcla de cal
y arena, con lo qual hubieran sido de mas duracion, y nose
hubieran arruinado tan en breue; cuyo reparo cuesta mu
cho dinero, y trabajo. Los Indios Mexicanos alcancaron
el uso de la cal, si bien no la mezclaban con arena, sino con
una piedra molida, que llaman Tezonte; ni la cuaian sino
no sino hecho un monton de la piedra le dauan fuego.

Chapter 17. On gypsum stone.

Quarries of gypsum stone are found less commonly than those of lime, particularly in warm lands. In the cold highlands there are great hills of it, and some mines of selenite, such as those in the district of Guamanga and Cuzco. In the valleys of the lowlands a kind of gypsum is also found, particularly in those that are abundant in vineyards, such as the valley of Vitor in the diocese of Arequipa, and that of Pisco in the Archbishopric of Lima; it seems that God provided so far in advance for the need that those valleys would have for gypsum for the benefit of the great quantity of wine that is presently produced in them.

The Indians of the kingdom of Peru had not attained the use of lime and gypsum in their buildings; for they did not know how to make mortar from lime and sand, nor how to build with gypsum, which certainly would have been of the greatest utility for them in those times, and would have saved the Spaniards great expense had they known lime and used it in their constructions. For all the irrigation channels, sea walls, bridges, and other works that they built in the time of their paganism from dry stone could have been made with lime and sand mortar, which would have made them more durable and they would not have fallen into ruin so quickly; the repair of which costs much money and labor. The Mexican Indians did attain the use of lime, although they did not mix it with sand, but rather with a ground stone they call Tezonte; and they did not slake it, but instead piled up the stone and set it on fire.

Chapter 18. On the marbles and alabasters
found in the Indies.

In none of the ancient stone buildings that we see in this kingdom of Peru, made by the Inca kings, nor in those of New Spain built by the Mexican kings, has there ever been found anything carved from marble, alabaster, jasper, or porphyry, despite the fact that these Indies have many quarries of these kinds of stone. The Indians of this kingdom of Peru were accustomed only to making from stones some small vessels for everyday use, such as mortars and other things of that sort. The varieties of precious marbles found in this land are many, particularly in the cold highlands of this kingdom of Peru, where there are very rich quarries of marble of every color.

In the diocese of Chuquisaca there is extracted a kind of marble so excellent that a stonemason who worked in that Royal building of San Lorenzo in the Royal [Escorial] told me that no marble as fine as this one had been used in that precious edifice. It is white as snow, lustrous and almost transparent, without any stain or vein to mar it. And I saw in the city of Chuquisaca in the year sixteen hundred and [ten or fifteen], carved from this marble, a pillar of a fountain, almost as round and turned as the body of a man; it bore [illegible] in such a way that with the

Chapter 20. On stone that is formed by water.

In the town of Huancavelica, diocese of Guamanga, a hot spring flows forth in a quantity roughly equal to the body of a man, more or less. This water runs down to the river, and along the stretch where most of it passes, it turns earth into stone. Other springs of this kind are also found in other parts of the kingdom, and in New Spain. The stone produced by this water is whitish and porous, very good for construction, of which many buildings in the aforementioned town of Huancavelica are made; and the entire city of Puebla de los Angeles in New Spain is built of stone formed by water, from which salt is also made, by which it settles; and the limestone of the valley of Chancay, as already noted, was likewise formed by water; and in many other places similar springs are found, whose water ordinarily flows out hot, somewhat thick, and whitish. But one must note that it is not the substance of the water itself that turns to stone, but rather the matter that issues from it by nature

Chapter 22. On the stone that serves as firewood.

In the New Kingdom of Granada there is a hill of black and resinous stone, which burns in fire like wood, and people commonly use it for lime in the following manner: they place these stones in the kiln mixed together with limestone, and beneath them a small amount of firewood to start the fire, and once it begins to burn, these stones catch fire and gradually burn until they are consumed, the ash of which will be mixed in with the lime and serves blended with it, because it is a kind of lime.

Chapter 23. On the lodestone.

There are so many lodestone deposits in Peru that, due to their abundance, they have no value or esteem, for there are very large hills made entirely of this stone, from which pieces of whatever size one wishes are taken to carry to Spain and other places. Deltas dos proposiones a los dos polos que por diversas partes tiene esta piedra, nace la dificultad que se halla quando se labra de acertar con la parte que mira al Norte, y por la opuesta que mira al Sur. The power to attract iron is not with equal force, but rather on one side it tends to have greater ability than on the other. The second thing is that it does not face North from all sides, because in any of these stones, whatever their size, there are to be found a head and feet; one side faces North, and the opposite faces South. And it is very credible that this diversity arises from the position it held in the mine or quarry where it was formed: such that the part of the stone that while in the mine faced North always retains that inclination, and imparts it to the iron it touches; and the part that faced South retains its corresponding property, which it then imprints upon the iron that is touched by it.

From these two properties relating to the two poles that this stone possesses on its different sides, arises the difficulty in working it of determining which part faces North and which faces South. These stones are commonly worked into an oval shape, making one point at the part that inclines toward the North and the other at the part toward the South. And taking two such stones after they have been worked, one can test what I have described by tying each one by its middle to a thread and hanging them near one another: for when hung in this way at a proper distance, the points of each that face North will come together, attracting one to the other; and the same happens with the points that incline toward the South. And the same sympathy on one part, and antipathy on the other, that we experience in these stones among themselves, we also observe in the nautical compass needle, which is touched by them: for if one brings close to a needle that has been touched with the tip of the stone that inclines to the North, and applies the lodestone at the tip that faces North, it will attract the needle and draw it close to itself; but if one brings the lodestone close to the same needle from the other tip that faces South, it repels it. To such a degree that if one turns the stone around the needle, the needle likewise keeps turning, fleeing from the stone, because it was touched with the tip opposite to the one being applied. And so the lodestone, with its hidden virtue — one of which is iron, and the other the black sand used in sand-shakers — to clean this sand when it has mixed with earth, one need only pass the lodestone over it, because the sand immediately sticks to it, leaving behind the earth with which it was mixed. Chapter 29. On copaquira

Copaquiri is what the Indians of Peru call verdigris in the Aymara language. And because of the resemblance that the stone I describe here bears to it, they give it the same name, and the Spaniards, corrupting the word, call it copaquira, and piedra de los lipes, because it is found only in the province of the Lipes, which belongs to the Archbishopric of Charcas. Copaquira is a bluish-green stone, and transparent, which is extracted from a mineral deposit found in the said province of the Lipes, whose veins are no thicker than a finger, although some loose pockets of medium-sized stones of four, six, and more pounds are sometimes found. In the same mineral deposit one also finds alum stone, and the Indians who extract the copaquira affirm that upon deepening the veins two fathoms, they find rock salt of a very white and transparent kind.

This stone appears in all its properties to be the true copperas, or Roman Vitriol, which Doctor Laguna describes for us. It is so prized that it is not only distributed throughout all the Indies, but great quantities are also sent to Europe. Its temperament is so...

Chapter 25. On the Haquimasi.

The stone called in Peru Haquimasi resembles in some way what Dioscorides calls Budaypea, although it is whiter and without those small protuberances shaped like acorns with which the Judaic stone forms certain points. This stone is found in great abundance in many parts of Peru, because it is common there, and the Indians recognize it easily: running through it are many small fine wavy veins, somewhat split. cap. 26. de la corauari.

Los Indios del Peru llaman corauari a una piedra verde, que los Indios de la provincia de los lipez traen
translation:

Ground stone, taken in water or in chicha, serves to stop loose bowels and the excessive bleeding that occurs in women after childbirth, or on account of excess menstruation. It is also useful taken in the same way against blood that passes through the urine. Beyond this, its powders applied to fresh wounds have the power to close and dry them. Taken with the powders of bezoar stone and of contrajerva in orange-blossom water, they work against poison, heart ailments, melancholy, and all contagious illness, and thus the Indians of Peru use them. Furthermore, these powders ground very fine and taken on an empty stomach with a little wine and the juice of limes or small lemons dissolve stones in the bladder and kidneys; and mixed with those of the herb called chapichapi, which will be discussed later, they have the power to clean and smooth the teeth. Finally, there are many other cures performed with the powders of this stone, mixed with egg whites and applied from twenty-four to twenty-four hours, at night, to swollen parts of the head, or to recent tumors, and to the very great pains in it, and a great lack of sense — all these ailments are relieved with ease.

Chapter 27. On the Macay.

Macay is what the Indians of Peru call certain small loaves like two-real coins, though thicker, which they make from a stone resembling lime: they must knead them from the powder of said stone with putrid urine, and bake them in an oven, after which they quench them in urine mixed with compounds of sulfur stone, by which they acquire a very foul smell. The mixture is so strong that its powders easily cleanse any wound that may exist. Beyond this, they dissolve these powders with hot urine so that they remain in the form of a paste or porridge, which in Peru we call mazamorra, and anointing with

Chapter 28, on the stone of Buga.

In the province of Popayan, in a Spanish settlement called Buga, there are found some remarkable stones for many illnesses, to which we give the name of the land where they are found. The color of the good ones is like a dark olive tone with somewhat greener spots; these stones are very hard like flint, and their powders, drunk on an empty stomach in the quantity of one dram with water made from the bark or leaves of the guava tree, cure bloody dysentery. If taken in milk, these powders cleanse and heal all wounds, even those that are foul or malignant. Furthermore, mixed with egg white, they cause broken bones to knit and join together, and they serve for many other illnesses.

Chapter 29. On the Bezoar Stone.

The bezoar stone is formed from layers, or rinds, like the husks of acorns, one upon another; of which the outermost is very smooth and lustrous. These stones are found in different sizes, from as small as chickpeas up to the size of a hen's egg; and some (though rare) as large as a fist, weighing one pound or more. The shape they take is highly varied; for some are round, others oval, and flat, and of as many different forms as the pebbles of rivers. They likewise differ in color; some are found black, others brown, whitish, ash-colored, golden-blonde, olive-colored more or less dark, and eggplant-colored: and those most prized and considered most perfect are those of an olive color, or the color of an unripe eggplant. Among the Western Indians, and especially in the kingdom of Peru, where these stones are most widely used, they form in the stomach of three species of animals, all of which are ruminants: namely the vicuña, the deer, and the llama, or sheep of the land. The stones produced by vicuñas are held in the highest esteem, next come those of the deer, and lastly those of the llamas and guanacos; whose stones are very small, and tend toward a black color with some golden speckles. Usually one finds in the stomach of each of these animals one or more stones, and in some

Regarding the cause of these stones forming in the stomachs
of the aforementioned animals, I find great variety among the authors
who have written on this subject: I will say what I think, setting
aside the opinions of others. Two causes, primarily,
are those that contribute to the formation of these
stones: the one, which we may call the material cause, is the healthful
plant matter the animals eat, not as ordinary fodder,
but as medicine and antidote against venom, when
they find themselves wounded or harmed by something that aggravates
and distresses their stomachs. The other, which is the efficient cause, is the
natural constitution of the animals themselves. And what persuades
me that such an herb is the material cause of their production
is that the very same animals that produce them in some
lands do not produce them in others; and this occurs not in lands far
apart, but within the same province, as we
have experienced in the province of the Collao, which being
all of the same climate and weather, in some parts
a great quantity of bezoar stones is found, as in the
district of the Pacajes; and in other parts very few, and in
still other parts, none at all; even though the animals that produce them
are raised throughout all the Collao, and indeed throughout all of Peru.

If bezoar stones are generated from the herb that they call by that name, wherever the same pastures are found, one would expect to find the bezoar stones equally; which we do not see to be the case. And what I say here is also the opinion of the Indians themselves, paying attention to which herb it is that the bezoar animals eat, saying that a medium-sized shrub two or three feet tall called Tola in the Quechua language, and Sopo in another tongue, which is well known to all, is said to be a medicine and beneficial for this kind of livestock. And when we ask the Indians from some land where these stones are not produced for bezoar stones, they answer us that there are none there, because there is no Tola in that land. Whether they are right or not that this is the herb from which the bezoar stones are generated, I will not undertake to determine; but experience greatly supports it, for in all the places where Tola is found in abundance, many bezoar stones are produced, and where the herb does not grow, none are found.

The second point, that the natural constitution of the animal plays a part in generating these stones, I hold to be very certain and beyond doubt. Because we see that apart from the vicunas and the other animals mentioned, no other creature produces them, not even those that are native to this land, nor those brought from Castile, it being very probable that they sometimes eat the same herb. In this way it is proved that the constitution and nature of the animal greatly aids in the formation of the stones through the virtue that they possess; which does not appear to be solely

text:

La question es si la yerua, de que se engendran; porque quando ella y esta tuuiera muy grande virtud, lur tompi endose esta en el buche del animal, y conuirtiendose en otra sustancia, como se conuierte, la auia de perder, o por lo menos gran parte della. y asi me cayo que la virtud, y facultad, que tienen las piedras bezares, les viene de la yer ua de que se engendran, y de la que les comunica el animal, que con su virtud, y calor natural, fue causa eficiente de su produccion.

El principio, y fundamento, sobre que se forman todas las piedras bezares, grandes, y pequeñas, es qualquiera uso, que el animal siente lastimarse, o molestarle el estomago; lo con que le han herido; o lo que a vueltas de la yerua que pace, acaso el comio. Y adonde quando deshacemos estas piedras, hallamos dentro dellos, debaxo de la postrera capa algunos pelos, pajas, opalillos; alguna espino, o pedaço de clado, o alguna otra cosa semejante. Porque no induciendo todos los brutos animales en el instinto que les dio el autor de la naturaleza, lo que les puede a pro ue char, dañar, luego que se siente herido, o lastimado inte riormente el animal que cria las piedras bezares, busca remedio para su mal en la louna yerua contratodo veneno, que el conoce, y de la qual suele aprouecharse en sus nes sidades, comiendo della; y de donde les vienen a los pie dras bezares, que de la tal yerua se guarsan, el ser ellos an tidotos de los venenos. La qual yerua comida acude

The question is whether the herb from which they are formed matters; because when it and this had very great virtue, it being broken down in the animal's stomach, and being converted into another substance, as it is converted, it would have to lose it, or at least a great part of it. And so it occurred to me that the virtue and faculty that bezoar stones have come to them from the herb from which they are formed, and from what the animal communicates to them, which with its virtue and natural heat was the efficient cause of their production.

The principle and foundation upon which all bezoar stones are formed, large and small, is whatever the animal feels irritating or troubling its stomach; that which has wounded it, or what it happened to eat mixed in with the grass it grazes upon. And so when we break apart these stones, we find inside them, beneath the outermost layer, some hairs, straws, little stones; some thorn, or piece of a branch, or some other similar thing. For all brute animals being guided by the instinct given them by the Author of Nature toward what can help or harm them, as soon as the animal that produces bezoar stones feels itself wounded or inwardly hurt, it seeks a remedy for its ailment in some herb that counteracts all poison, which it knows, and from which it usually benefits in its times of need, eating of it; and it is from this that bezoar stones acquire, being formed from such herb, the property of being antidotes to poisons. Which herb, when eaten, comes to

dra; y come el animal va sufriendo mos, y mas

razas unas sobre otras, hasta que la piedra viene a al
car su grandeza, cuando el animal
muere, lo matan los cazadores.

No quiero de jar de hacer aqui memoria de la mas estraño,
y peregrina piedra bezaar que se ha hallado en el Peru; des
de que los Españoles los descubrieron; la qual se vendio en la
villa de Potosi en docientos y cinquenta pesos; y la

Chile: tenia de largo el piedra un dema; y era tuuaaos
