era de hueso con figura de harpon; y por la otra parte un
pedazo de la misma saeta. Era esta que causa mui grande
admiracion considerando que para que la saeta entrara
en el buche del animal, donde se formo esa piedra sobre
el pedazo que della quedo dentro, era fuerza romper
lo en gran cantidad; y que con todo eso no muriese el
animal, sino que viendose herido audiese a w

what wounds the stomach of the animal, wrapping around it and embracing it thus; and as it hardens with the warmth of the stomach, it comes to form the hook, or first layer of the stone; and as the animal goes on enduring more and more hardship; and as the healing herb works, layers form one upon another, until the stone reaches its full size, at which point the animal dies, and the hunters kill it.

I do not wish to fail to record here the memory of the most strange and remarkable bezoar stone that has been found in Peru since the Spaniards discovered those lands; which was sold in the town of Potosí for two hundred and fifty pesos; and it was acquired by don Pedro Sorelo de Ulloa, who was the magistrate of that town, and acting governor of the kingdom of Chile: the stone was about one span in length, and was as thick through the middle as a hen's egg; and it had running lengthwise through it a piece of an arrow, in such a manner that on one side the arrowhead protruded, which was made of bone in the shape of a harpoon; and on the other side a piece of the same arrow. This caused very great wonder, considering that for the arrow to have entered the stomach of the animal, where this stone formed around the piece that remained inside, it must necessarily have broken it into a great quantity; and that despite all this the animal did not die, but rather, finding itself wounded, proceeded to w

mer de la yerua saludable, y medicinal, con que tamo

piedra be zar tan rara, y admirable. De traso no menos

debajo de la primera capa una vala de arcabus, sobre
la qual se fue formando la piedra bezar.

No pocos han dudado si estas piedras bezares del Peru
tienen tanta virtud contra los venenos, y otros males,
como de ellas se fama publica; por lo qual me parecio
poner aqui una experiencia de la qual el virde de las ge

fue que tomo dos pollos iguales, y dio a uno cada uno

vel
translation:

of the healthy and medicinal herb, with which it so prevailed over the piece of earth that it had in its stomach, this bezoar stone so rare and admirable. Of no less marvelous origin I have news, affirmed to me by a trustworthy friar who saw it alive, which had at its center, beneath the first layer, a musket ball, over which the bezoar stone had formed.

Not a few have doubted whether these bezoar stones from Peru have such great virtue against poisons and other ailments, as is publicly claimed of them; for which reason it seemed good to me to record here an experiment performed by the viceroy of these lands, who was at that time governor of the province of Chucuito around the year sixteen hundred and some days, and what he did was take two equal chickens, and gave to each one an equal quantity of corrosive sublimate, and then made one of them drink powders of bezoar stone, of which that one survived, and the other soon died, upon whom the antidote had not been administered. By this experiment it was clearly shown how certain is the virtue of these bezoar stones; which, when good, serve as antidotes against all poisons, whether from the bites of vipers or other animals; and against typhus and plague-buboes. They also serve against all melancholy and afflictions of the heart, and for all pestilential fevers; and their powders are applied in poultices and cordials. And beyond this, whenever needed, no

Del Peru, como en la nueva España es mui usado tomar su

Indios del Peru la piedra bezoar illa, con la qual tenian
en su gentilidad algunas supersticiones, de la qual es era una
traer la siempre consigo para hacerse rico.

De las piedras beçares pequeños se hacen otras artificios
les, y contrahechos, y son de mas virtud que la natural, por
que fuera de la virtud destos, de que se componen los contrafe

y rosada, triaca Andromach, ambar, almizcle, perlas,

cap. 30. Del coco del Paraguay.

La piedra mas estraña de quantas han venido a mi noticio
es la que llamamos coco del Paraguay: hanle puesto este
translation:
First Part - Book 3.
173

In Peru, as in New Spain, it is very common to take the sweat with some powders of bezoar stone dissolved in a small bowl of atole, or corn porridge, or in some drink. The Indians of Peru call it the bezoar stone, with which they held certain superstitions in their heathen days, one of which was to always carry it with them in order to become rich.

From small bezoar stones, other artificial and counterfeit ones are made, and these are of greater virtue than the natural ones, because beyond the properties of those from which the counterfeits are composed, they add what the idols possess that are mixed with them, which are the following: aguardiente, rose water, theriac of Andromachus, amber, musk, pearls, hyacinths, emeralds, citron bark, red sandalwood, and powders of another herb; from all these mixtures the perfect artificial bezoar stones are composed. All of these, well ground and mixed, are combined with a little tar water mixed with egg white, so that the stones do not crack; these, once formed to whatever size and shape one wishes, and well polished, are placed in the sun or in a shaded spot.

Chapter 30. On the coconut of Paraguay.

The most remarkable stone of all those that have come to my attention is the one we call the coconut of Paraguay: it has been given this

text:
Historia del nuevo mundo

nombre los Españoles por tener figura de loo, y crianse en la
provincia del Paraguay. es por menor que la cabeza de
un hombre, aunque se hallan mayores, y menores; de fi
gura redondo, o alusada, de color pardo escuro, y por de dentro
hueca: tiene de grueso el casco como dos dedos a manera
de melon. El cual es de naturaleza de mui fuerte pedernal,
y por de dentro tiene todo el concavo empedrado de unas piedras
preciosas transparentes, que nacen del casco, del tamaño de
piedras medianas de anillo, puestas con tanto concierto, y
orden como estan entre si los granos de la granada: Por
estas piedras puntiagudas, y esquinadas de figura piramidal
mui duras, y relucientes, unas blancas, otras que tiran
a color amarillo, pero lo mas comun es ser de un color ti
rante a morado claro.

No es menos admirable el modo como ellos mismos se po
nen que los en ellos estan; crianse debajo de la tierra, y por
no se han acabado de formar, y endurecer; como se van
van, y aprietan los poros del casco de manera que el ayre
que queda encerrado dentro no puede comunicarse con el de
afuera, es fuerza que calentandose, o enfriandose con
la mudanza del tiempo, se dilate, o condense; y aunque pie
va alteracion de estas, que en si reciba, revienta el casco de
la piedra, o coco; aunque es tan duro, y fuerte, porque
translation:
History of the New World

the Spaniards named them for having the shape of a gourd, and they grow in the
province of Paraguay. It is smaller than the head of
a man, although larger and smaller ones can be found; of
round or elongated shape, dark brown in color, and hollow
inside: the shell is about two fingers thick, in the manner
of a melon. It is by nature of a very strong flint,
and on the inside the entire cavity is paved with precious
transparent stones, which grow from the shell, the size of
medium ring-stones, arranged with such order and
pattern as the seeds of a pomegranate among themselves: These
stones are pointed and cornered in pyramidal shape,
very hard and shining, some white, others tending
toward yellow, but the most common is to be of a color
inclining toward light purple.

No less admirable is the manner in which the stones themselves form
inside; they grow beneath the earth, and because
they have not finished forming and hardening; as they continue
and the pores of the shell tighten in such a way that the air
enclosed within cannot communicate with that
outside, it is inevitable that as it warms or cools with
the change of weather, it expands or condenses; and whatever
alteration it receives within itself, it causes the shell of
the stone, or coco, to burst; even though it is so hard and strong, because

Lobiernei estimadas estas piedras, y mas quando se ha

translation:

It would do the same even if it were harder than diamond. For when this stone bursts from beneath the ground, it flies out with such force and impulse that it breaks into two or three pieces, making a report louder than that of a musket; at the sound of which the Indians come running to find the stone, which they recognize by it.

These stones are greatly prized, and even more so when a large piece is found from which a drinking vessel can be made; for a whole one has never been found intact: and when they burst they tend to yield the greater part of the vessel whole; which can be presented to any great lord; and for this reason alone the inhabitants of Paraguay prize and seek out these stones so much: I saw one that had been worked only slightly at the foot to serve as a base, which was taken to the Kingdom of Peru in the year sixteen hundred and seven to be presented to the Pope, and it was a piece that well deserved to be placed in the hands of so great a monarch; which he esteemed greatly for its great antiquity. They say that these stones have the virtue, when one drinks from them, of relieving melancholy and sadness in a man; beyond this, the powders of these precious stones, given to drink in orange-blossom water, in addition to the effects already mentioned, are good against heart ailments, or epilepsy; and drunk with spirits, they have the power to restore the vital spirits.

cap. 31 de las esmeraldas.

Las esmeraldas mas finas que se han hallado a ceplos en America son las de la provincia de Puerto viejo, diocesi de quito, la qual cayo fuera del dominio de los incastros yes del Peru, por causa de las quales los primeros españoles que vinieron a la conquista de este reyno pusieron por nombre a aquella tierra la provincia de las esmeraldas. Pero estas fueron mui pocas por no auerse hallado hasta agora el mineral de donde los indios sacauan las que los españoles hallaron en si podos, y con que se adornaban, que aunque barbaros conocian, y preciaban por su hermosura, y resplandor estas ricas piedras. La tierra mas abundante dellas, y que ha henichido el mundo, y sido causa de que ayan perdido mucho del valor, y estima en que los hombres las tenian quando eran raras, es el nuevo reyno de Granada, donde ay una mina de perfectas, y excelentes esmeraldas, que ha muchos años se labra, y de ella se sacan las que se lleuan a españa, y reparten por todas estas Indias.

Nacen estas esmeraldas en mineral, como los metales, el qual esta en un cerro de la provincia de Muzo, a la veta seguida entre peña viua, que es la causa que lo mandan los que tratan de minas: salle de abajo como

Chapter 31: On Emeralds.

The finest emeralds that have been found in America are those from the province of Puerto Viejo, in the diocese of Quito, which fell outside the domain of the Inca kings of Peru. It was on account of these stones that the first Spaniards who came to the conquest of that kingdom gave the name "Province of the Emeralds" to that land. However, these were very few, because the mine from which the Indians extracted those that the Spaniards found on them and with which they adorned themselves has not been discovered to this day — although being barbarians, they knew and prized these rich stones for their beauty and brilliance. The land most abundant in them, and which has flooded the world with them and caused them to lose much of the value and esteem that people held them in when they were rare, is the New Kingdom of Granada, where there is a mine of perfect and excellent emeralds that has been worked for many years, from which are taken those that are sent to Spain and distributed throughout all these Indies.

These emeralds are born in mineral form, like metals, in a hill in the province of Muzo, running in a continuous vein through living rock, which is the reason those who deal in mines are ordered to follow it: it comes out from below like

text:
Primera parte. Libro 3. 175

tronco de arbol, y se va estendiendo en diuarsos ramos, que encajados en la peña hazen diuersas partes. son estos limos, y vetas del grosor de un dedo, mas y menos en partes, y no todos de esmeralda fina continuada, sino de la materia de que ella se engendra, que es piedra trasparente, y millo inas, entre la qual se topan pedazos de fino cristal. siguiendo los ramos, y vetas de la mina se hallan a trechos las esmeraldas finas contiguas a otras imperfectas, y vasas. y dellas se hallan muchas antes de dar con las finas: las quales se ven parece son de una mesma materia con las imperfectas. Porque dado que a munn mier to estan descontinuados las unas de las otras, a veces suele salir pegada con la esmeralda fina alguna parte que no lo es, la qual se le quita: son estas piedras imperfectas algo blanqueuznas, y no tan tersas, y trasparentes como las finas: lo qual muestra ser esta esmeralda imperfecta, o por no auer llegado a perfeccion aun, o por de fecto de la materia, que no la hallo alli el agente natural tan pura, y dispuesta. Dellas imperfectas, y viles unas se allegaron mas que otras a la fineza de las perfectas, y preciosas. Pero toda la veta que se compone de las unas, y las otras muestra una continua linea con la peña, en que nace encajada, sino contigua.

Asi mismo disergan entre si en perfeccion y fineca las esmeraldas que se sacan de una misma veta, ni mas ni menos difieren en la grandeza, y tamaño, porque las
translation:
First Part. Book 3. 175

the trunk of a tree, and it extends outward into various branches, which, set into the rock, form different sections. These seams and veins are roughly the width of a finger, more or less in places, and are not all of continuous fine emerald, but rather of the material from which it is formed, which is a transparent stone, and mixed with other matter, among which pieces of fine crystal are found. Following the branches and veins of the mine, fine emeralds are found at intervals alongside imperfect and base ones. Many of the latter are encountered before reaching the fine ones; and these fine ones appear to be of the same material as the imperfect ones. For, given that they are discontinuous from one another, it sometimes happens that a portion that is not fine emerald comes attached to a fine emerald, which must then be removed. These imperfect stones are somewhat whitish, and not as smooth and transparent as the fine ones; which shows that this imperfect emerald is so either because it has not yet reached perfection, or because of a defect in the material, which the natural agent did not find sufficiently pure and ready in that place. Among the imperfect and common ones, some come closer than others to the quality of the perfect and precious ones. But the entire vein, composed of both types, shows a continuous line within the rock in which it is embedded, rather than merely adjoining it.

Likewise, the emeralds taken from one and the same vein differ among themselves in perfection and quality, and they differ no less in size and dimension, because the

ay como avellanas, castaños, y nueces, y mas readas:
La mayor que se ha sacado de la mina fue una que hallo
un clerigo de la grandeca de la mano nueva al nivel, los
qual como rara, y exquisita presento a su Magestad. los
Indios del Peru llaman a la esmeralda en la lengua
general, Vmiña, que es argumento de que tubieron

cap. 32 de las perlas.

Los dos primeros descubridores de las mares, y costas de la
America fueron los que primero hallaron las perlas,
que en entrambos mares se miran: el Almirante don
Cristoval Colon en la bia de la mar del Norte: y el capi
tan Vasco nuñes de Balboa en la de la mar del Sur.
Porque la primera vez que vino el Almirante a Indias,
el año de mil y quatrocientos y noventa y nueve, vino
a costear la tierra firme, que en aquel viage descu
bio, y tomo tierra en la isla de cubagua, en la qual los que
de sus compañeros se desembarcaron vieron una India
con una sarta de perlas, e inquiriendo de donde las avia
avido, hallaron que los naturales de aquella isla las
pescauan con sus canoas. lo qual sabido por Colon rescato
algunos que lleuo a España para muestra. Posteriormente
despues hallo Balboa la mar del sur, y salio las juntas
a Panama, a las quales llamo el las de las perlas por
translation:
History of the New World

such as hazelnuts, chestnuts, and walnuts, and more mixed varieties:
The largest that has been extracted from the mine was one that a
clergyman found, of the size of the new hand to the level, which
as something rare and exquisite he presented to His Majesty. The
Indians of Peru call the emerald in the general
language, Vmiña, which is evidence that they had
knowledge and use of them.

Chapter 32, On Pearls.

The first two discoverers of the seas and coasts of
America were those who first found pearls,
which are seen in both seas: Admiral Don
Cristóbal Colón on the route of the North Sea, and Captain
Vasco Núñez de Balboa on that of the South Sea.
For the first time the Admiral came to the Indies,
in the year fourteen hundred and ninety-nine, he came
to coast along the mainland, which on that voyage he
discovered, and he landed on the island of Cubagua, where those
of his companions who disembarked saw an Indian woman
with a string of pearls, and inquiring where she had
obtained them, they found that the natives of that island
fished for them with their canoes. This being known to Colón, he traded
for some which he took to Spain as samples. Subsequently,
Balboa discovered the South Sea, and went out to the islands
near Panama, which he called the Pearl Islands because

text:
Primera parte. libro 3.
176
Las que hallo en ellas: las quales sacauan, y aproueachauan
sus Indios en los mismos usos que nosotros. Ainos uimulos hu
uieran en muega por carecer de instrumentos para ello, por
dian las perlas saluitre, y candides, y quedauan escuras,
y chamuscadas.
Criauan las perlas en unas conchas de lamar llamadas
hiifas, de la hechura de olmones, tan grandes como la mano
poco mas o menos, y casi redondas. Por la parte que esta a sido
la una concha con la otra como los olmones, que es como un
gonce, o quicio, conque se abre, y cierra el pescado que nace,
y biue dentro, sale fuera de conque estan pegados, y aidas a las
apeiras: y esvillos de la mar, que es un bulto negro, gredoso
como de puerto tan grueso como un dedo de la mano, el
qual sirua para arrancarlos. son las conchas de las per
las por de fuera tosca, y asperas ubiertas de una como corte
ca, o costra barda como los olmones, y por de dentro lisas, y blan
cas con un lustre como el de las por lo talgo mas duro, que
tira a color de cielo, gallardo en una piedra aspera la lustro
barda, que por de fuera tienen, que dan tan tersas, y lustrosas
como por de dentro, y casi trasparentes. De ellas se hacer
mui buenas cucharas, que llamamos de Nacar, las quales ver
den los negros pescadores de perlos, y son percanas mias, que
sus amos les permiten para aliuio del excesivo trabajo que
pasan en aquel oficio. Aunque el pescado que se halla dentro
de estas conchas tiene la carne tierna, y mas blanca que
translation:
First Part. Book 3.
176
Those he found there: which his Indians extracted and made use of in the same ways as we do. Had they not been so lacking in instruments for the purpose, they would have valued the pearls more, but they burned them with saltpeter, and they came out dark and scorched.

The pearls grew in certain sea shells called hiifas, shaped like olmones, about as large as a hand, a little more or less, and nearly round. On the side where one shell joins the other, as with olmones, there is something like a hinge or pivot, by which the creature that is born and lives inside opens and closes; it extends outward from where they are attached, clinging to the rocks, and sea urchins, which are a dark, clayish mass, as thick as a finger of the hand, serve to pry them loose. The outer surface of the pearl oysters is rough and coarse, covered with a kind of bark or dark crust like the olmones, while the inside is smooth and white, with a luster somewhat harder than nacre, tending toward a sky-blue color — a fine thing in a rough stone — and the lustrous dark exterior, once removed, leaves them as smooth and lustrous as the inside, and almost transparent. From them very fine spoons are made, which we call nacre spoons, and which the black pearl divers sell — a small privilege their masters allow them to ease the excessive toil they endure in that occupation. Although the flesh of the creature found inside these shells is tender and whiter than

text:
Historia del nuevo mundo

la de los ohtones, no es tan buena comida como ellos, y los otros generos de mariscos. Nacen las perlas encaspadas en la carne de los ostios como los nudos en la tabla, y en abriendo las se echa de ver si las ay ono, porque no todas las tienen.

Son las perlas muy diferentes unas de otras en el tamaño, figura, color, y lustre; y otras veces se hallan dos por rejas, yentos de mesones; y quando se acertan a hallar sobre muchas de valor vienen ellos el mas de baxo del agua desde quatro hasta doce braços en hondo, y aunque las ayan en mayor profundidad, no se pueden sacer. En la costa de Panama suelen de subir se algunas, y quedar en seo en vasamos, respeto de ser alta mai grandes las concientos y tenguantes; y entonces abren las machas para recebir los rayos del sol, como yo los he visto. Desde que los españoles empecaron en estas Indias la pesqueria de perlas, se hace en la mar del Norte en toda la costa de las provincias de Santa Marta, y Venezuela; y en la mar del Sur en la de Tierra Firme, e islas de las perlas. Es necesra gran granjeria principalmente los vecinos del rio de la hacha, y de la Margarita; es rica, y gruesa, y porque qui ere hombres de caudal; porque ha de tener quien la ha de embarcar con veynte o treynta esclavos buzos, y dos o tres españoles salariados, uno que haga oficio de mayordomo al diezero a los pescadores; y teniendo cuenta con lo que se saco y otro que sirva de arraez, y governar el barco. ver
translation:
History of the New World

that of the ohtones is not as good a food as they are, and the other kinds of seafood. Pearls grow embedded in the flesh of the oysters like knots in a board, and upon opening them one can tell whether they contain any or not, because not all of them do.

Pearls differ greatly from one another in size, shape, color, and luster; and sometimes two are found together, lodged in the same shell; and when they happen to find many of great value, the divers go down for them from four to twelve fathoms deep, and although there may be more at greater depth, they cannot be retrieved. On the coast of Panama some are known to surface and remain stranded on sandbars, owing to the very large tides and currents; and at such times the oysters open to receive the rays of the sun, as I myself have witnessed. Since the Spanish began the pearl fishery in these Indies, it is carried out in the North Sea along the entire coast of the provinces of Santa Marta and Venezuela, and in the South Sea along the coast of Tierra Firme and the Pearl Islands. It is a great and important enterprise above all for the residents of the Río de la Hacha and of Margarita; it is a rich and substantial trade, but one that requires men of means, for whoever undertakes it must outfit the venture with twenty or thirty slave divers and two or three salaried Spaniards — one to serve as steward and overseer of the fishermen, keeping account of what is brought up, and another to serve as coxswain and to pilot the vessel. Chapter 33. On other precious stones, of various colors, and virtues found in these Indies.

By precious stones I understand all those that are clear and shining, although many of them are not held in such high price by name, such as crystal, topaz, garnet, and others of this kind. Some are of the opinion that crystal is formed from water alone, frozen by excessive cold without any mixture of earth; which, if it were true, one would have to find in these Indies a greater supply of crystal than in any other part of the world, because there are lands so cold that they are always covered by many fathoms of snow, and where plains are discovered and caverns, and where it never rains water in its proper form, but rather when it falls upon the earth it is congealed into hail and snow. And I believe that those who held this opinion were led to it by seeing that crystal mines are ordinarily found in very cold places and lands, where that which is found in these Indies also occurs.

But I hold it as most probable that crystal, like the other transparent and clear stones, is produced like the others with a mixture of some portion of very clean and purified earth. In many parts of this America there are veins of very fine crystal, worth noting: in the province of Chachapoyas they say, in the diocese of Trujillo, certain small pieces are extracted of

It appeared to be crystal embedded or incorporated with all manner of precious stones of various and very vivid colors, and like a white band on the lower portions, which occupied a large part of the stone. The razors, knives, lancets, and all manner of tools that we brought from iron, the Indians of Peru as well as New Spain make from a certain stone, which the Mexicans call etzli, and those of Peru call itliltica. It is transparent like glass, and is found in three colors: white, black, and blue. There are many stonecutters of it both in Peru and in New Spain. It is cut into medium-sized stones, which naturally come out cornered, and they smooth them with rougher stones. From this, with great industry, they extract and split it without regard for its face in the middle, producing edges: they make them a third of a vara long, and in width one or two fingers thick, no thicker than our knives, and these edges are so sharp that they can shave a beard with them, but they are fragile and easily dulled and chip. And so their use is like that of very sharp razors, because after the second cut they are no longer useful. The Indians made swords from these stones, used one or two at a time, that with a single blow could cut a man in half, and they also armed the tips of their arrows with them. The fragments of this stone are useful for clearing clouding of the eyes and sharpening vision.
Stones of all colors for painting are found in many places, such as blue stone, very fine green, blue, and all colors.

Chapter 34. On Metals.

In such a manner did the sovereign Creator enrich and make fruitful our common mother the earth, that not only does she produce upon her surface innumerable kinds of herbs and plants for the nourishment of men and animals, but also within her bowels and deepest recesses she holds a great variety of metals, all ordered for the benefit of human life. For some are used by men to cure their illnesses, others to defend themselves from their enemies; others for vessels and all manner of tools and instruments that human ingenuity has invented; and others finally for the adornment and elegance of their persons and dwellings. Seven are the different species into which all kinds of metals are divided, namely: gold, silver, quicksilver, copper, iron, tin, and lead. In the formation of each one of these, its corresponding planet exerts its influence, communicating its force and affinity to each one or that metal with which it has the most analogy and affinity.

el oro recibedel sol todas las buenas calidades que tiene: sobre la plata predomina la luna: Mercurio, cuya naturaleza es instable y mudança, tiene especial cuidado del açogue, y asi entrambos son bulliçiosos, e inconstantes: Al cobre atiende Venus; al hierro Marte; al estaño Jupiter; y finalmente al plomo el pesado y frio Saturno.

Nacen generalmente los metales en tierras asperas, esteriles, infrututosas; en temples de sombrios, desapor habitables; pero la codicia del oro, y plata los puebla, y hace suaves, y abastecidos. Mas en tierras de buen temple, y abundantes de mantenimientos pocas veces se hallan minerales; repartiendo sus dones el autor de la naturaleza de modo que, mudando sus riquezas y frutos los unos con los otros, todos queden enriquecidos, y abastados. si bien es verdad que no deja de auer lugares apacibles, santos, y abundosos, que tambien crian metales; mas estos son mui pocos en comparacion de la gran riqueza que producen los esteriles, y fragosos. Por tener la mayor parte de las Indias occidentales la disposicion mas conveniente para que se engendren minerales, se hallan en ellas en mucho mayor cantidad que en otros regiones; particularmente en el Reyno del Peru, cuyas fragosas sierras, y despoblados paramos son tantos mas abundos de metales, quan to mas esteriles, y faltos de los frutos necesarios para el sustento de hombres, y animales. y lo principal por auer tenido por bien la sabiduria del eterno Señor por si al descanso
translation:
History of the New World.

Gold receives from the sun all the good qualities it possesses; over silver, the moon predominates. Mercury, whose nature is unstable and changeable, has special care over quicksilver, and thus both are restless and inconstant. Venus governs copper; Mars governs iron; Jupiter governs tin; and finally, heavy and cold Saturn governs lead.

Metals are generally born in rough, sterile, unfruitful lands; in gloomy, uninhabitable climates. Yet the greed for gold and silver populates them and makes them pleasant and well-supplied. But in lands of good climate, abundant in provisions, minerals are rarely found. The author of nature distributes his gifts in such a way that, by exchanging their riches and products with one another, all may be enriched and supplied. Although it is true that there are also pleasant, healthy, and abundant places that also produce metals, these are very few in comparison with the great wealth produced by the sterile and rugged lands. Because the greater part of the West Indies has the most favorable conditions for the generation of minerals, they are found there in much greater quantity than in other regions; particularly in the Kingdom of Peru, whose rugged mountains and desolate moors are all the more abundant in metals the more sterile they are and the more lacking in the fruits necessary for the sustenance of men and animals. And this is principally because the wisdom of the eternal Lord has seen fit to grant to rest

And once the royal fifths are paid to the King, the officials stamp them with the die and mark, without which no gold can be removed from the Indies, under penalty of forfeiture. The gold extracted in Peru in the province of Carabaya is of the finest grade, and the one that silversmiths most prefer to work. Also renowned is that of Chile, and that of Veragua, in the new kingdom of Granada, and in the province of Quito, where it is extracted in great quantities; but it is not of such high carats as that of Carabaya. In many other lands there are abundant mines and gold-washing sites, but no extraction takes place for lack of workers. The Indians of Peru call gold Cori in Quechua, and Chique in Aymara.

Chapter 37. On Silver.

Although gold is so excellent and precious that by quantity it far exceeds in value a great deal of silver, nevertheless the greatest wealth extracted from these Indies at present consists principally in silver, because the silver mines are far more numerous and incomparably more abundant than those of gold: for what is extracted each year from this metal, with all the wealth that comes from it, amounts to only a tenth part of the value that results from silver; because this exceeds twelve million pesos, and at most one million in gold, more or less, throughout all of America. Por ordinario mas, los mineros de hierros, y humedad tal que los de los bajos, por estar mas lejos de dar en agua. Todas las tierras frias, y sierras y altos del Peru, estan empedradas de plata, porque apenas ay por ellas cerro, que en poca, o mucha cantidad no la tenga. Descubriense cada dia, y labran se tantas, que con cuidado tan grande el tiempo, en el mundo de la extraordinaria riqueza del Peru, luego que fue descu-bierto, no era la plata que se sacaua entonces la quarta par-te de la que oy se saca.

Silver was used primarily among the Peruvians, and was so common among them that nobles and commoners alike had many pieces, vessels, and jewelry of silver, and they even combined it with other metals — the place that silver now holds suits it well, ranking it above all others except gold.

It is ordinarily found in rough and barren lands, in cold high plains, in hills, ridges, and snowy mountain ranges, in rocky, scrubby, and rugged terrain, and some also in small hillocks and flat ground. Ordinarily more so in iron-bearing and humid areas than in lowlands, being farther from water. Ordinarily all the mining hills are barren of trees, not entirely of earth nor of bare rock, but partly of earth and partly of stone, of reddish, brown, or whitish color; those that have some of these characteristics are called by miners hills of good cloth, because mines are usually found in them. All the cold lands, mountain ranges, and highlands of Peru are paved with silver, for there is scarcely a hill anywhere that does not contain it in some quantity, large or small. From now until the end of the world, the inhabitants will not lack for mines to work. New ones are discovered every day, and so many are worked, that despite the great attention given at the time to the extraordinary wealth of Peru after it was discovered, the silver then extracted was not even a quarter of what is extracted today.

As stated in the preceding chapter, pure and clean silver is so rare that no great account is made of it, and most of what is extracted comes from ore. Even so, some clean and refined silver is occasionally found that requires no processing, which is called hammered silver. To separate it from the earth and dross with which it is mixed, nothing more is needed than to shake it and give it a few blows with a hammer. Most of the time it appears like frost, and other times it is wrapped in the manner of a thin thread of fine silver, coiling around many turns as if it had been wound through it, passing through many parts. Likewise, large and small points of perfect and pure silver are found embedded and clustered within the very same stones. Other pieces of silver are found the size of a hand, in the form of plumes, and others that look like nothing so much as a honeycomb after the honey has been removed, and I found there, along with many other shapes, many that I myself have seen. This hammered silver is not found in fixed veins, but rather in loose formations within the earth and low-grade ore of the mines.

The silver that is born in mineral deposits incorporated within rocks, although it is all one and the same, when it comes to refining and improving it, yields its full grade; and it is worthy of wonder to see how many are the ores in which it is produced. For some are black, others yellow, brown, chestnut-colored, ruddy, and of every color; some extremely hard and famously flinty, and others soft, tender, and very brittle. Some are smooth and sticky, and others on the contrary dry, clean, and crumbly. Some minerals are lustrous, others [illegible], others [illegible], and others have [illegible]

The mines of continuous and consistent metals are always

Although the ore of continuous mines tends to vary greatly

nonetheless the inequality is not as great as in the case of the non-fixed mines.

that the metal is stone, and in parts as hard or harder than the building stone of a house, and it differs from it so much in color and other properties that any miner could distinguish it. Wherever fixed veins are discovered, it is certain that others lie nearby, because they are born from one another, like branches of a tree. And not infrequently, when two veins are encountered at great depth, which at the surface had been very far apart, one is found to have merged with the other, or to have given out, each continuing on its own course — which tends to cause miners many disputes. Some veins emerge above the ground, raising up a crag or ridge of the same thickness, and yield good metal, just as what lies deep within. Others are covered by one fathom more or less, and these are called capped veins. Some have their richness near the surface of the earth and as they go deeper they thin out and are lost, already much diminished in grade. These are called head mines. Others — and these are the hardest — yield rich metal at thirty and forty fathoms depth, even though at the surface they may appear poor.

The mines that run shallow, along the openings of the earth, are usually worked by open-cut, making a trench the width of the vein. Although these are very few compared to those that descend into the abyss, which are the most difficult to work, because as one follows the metals, the earth must be broken and drilled

The rock that lies across from it they call "cajas" [wall-rock], which commonly contains no silver. Going deep into the mines, they set up supports at intervals so that the walls do not give way, and these supports are pieces of the hardest wood they leave unbroken, so that they serve them as props. They reinforce the ore body as the mine progresses, making recesses, which are dry-stone walls from one side to the other, as bracing against the force of the mine.
The tools with which they break and extract the ores are iron bars of thirty to forty pounds in weight, tipped with steel; they also use certain chisels or long nails, about a third of a vara more or less, likewise steel-tipped, which they call "fámulos," with which, together with a hammer, they dislodge the ore that remains stuck to the walls, which they call "respaldos"; and they also shape the chimneys. When ore so hard is encountered that the bars cannot break it, they use wedges, and a mallet, or hardwood. When the vein is worked straight down, plumb toward the bottom, it is called "labor de apoyo"; and if it is worked level, that is, directly in front of the worker, it is called "labor de frontón"; a chimney that goes straight upward is called so; and one that goes at an angle, like a millstone groove, they call "labor de chiflón." The most useful of all these works is that of the chimney shaft, because it rises perpendicularly, and has platforms built along its way, or barbacoas, where the drilling workers climb up to work.
In the main ore-bodies of many hills they cut passages called socavones that run through the veins, and through them one enters to cross into the mines, and extracts the metals; of which the owner of the socavon takes a certain portion, when it is used to cross into the mines of others.
These socavones are passages cut through the hills at level grade, going in straight, like a street, more than one man's height tall, and two varas wide: they are cut through solid rock, and go into the innards of a hill two hundred paces and more, as was said above; when they are very long, air-shafts are made in them, because without these the candles go out inside, and the men run short of air: the making of one of the longest socavones, when it is cut through rock, can cost from twenty to thirty thousand pesos; and it happens that after a miner has spent all that money, he gets nothing of value from it.
In these socavones and in the deep mines, one does not feel the storms of heaven with their thunder and lightning; for which reason miners usually take shelter in them as a safe refuge in such storms. When the mines are deep and go straight down, one descends into them by means of ladders made of leather ropes.

The hills are riddled and full of holes, like caves and lairs of wild beasts, which descend to the depths of the abyss, one hundred, two hundred, and more fathoms deep: where those who work cutting and processing the metals never come out whether it is day or night, lighting themselves with tallow candles, never ceasing that labor, relieving one another so that some may rest while others work. Once the metals are brought to the surface, they are placed in small
enclosures, which are made at the mouth of the mine, in the manner of troughs,
which they call canchos; and there in the sunlight they go about
breaking them with a hammer, and sorting, and separating those that
are of the ore veins, from the useless stones. All the work
comes back to breaking them apart, and drawing from the deep recesses of
the earth the rough metals, and crude stones; in which is found
the treasure so precious as silver: without which, until
it is brought out clean and refined, there are no few torments
and transformations that men must put it through
before giving it its final form.

Chapter 38. On the processing of silver by
smelting.

From the mines the ores are carried in llama trains,

(Los que llamamos carneros de la tierra) al llegar los de su planta beneficiar, y beneficiante unos con la lengua, y otros por fundicion. Y el beneficio con fuego es de dos maneras: una en Guayrás, y otra en hornos de reberueracion. Purifianse solamente los metales mas ricos, por ser los otros diprimidos, es si son, con alguna liga que les haga de rentable y unidos. A y metale dellos tan poros pero y gruos, que sue len a cinquenta pesos, a ciento, y a docientos por quintal.

Para derretirlos ponen en los collados, y laderas, donde con mas fuerso se plantan los vientos, unos braseros grandes de barro, que llaman guayrás, con carbon encendido, y el metal dentro: y como se van derritiendo, va consumiendo el fuego la escoria, y purificando la plata. Todos lo que sacauán los Indios del Perú antiguamente era por este modo de fundicion, porque nunca supieron otro beneficio; y estos cauanos aprouechauan sin lirbo los metales mui ricos: y por muchos años no usaron los Españoles otro beneficio en ellos y es por ha cer que siendo Virrey don Francisco de Toledo se dio con ella de avogue.

Y la fundicion de reberueracion se hace echando los metales al horno unos hornos de hechura de los de cocer pan, saluo que la boca por donde se da fuego esta pero no mas de un medio alto del suelo del horno, y hecho en ella un pequeño hornillo abrazado, donde se echa la leña, y se da fuego, cuya llama es trando por la boca del horno adentro, batia todo su techo, y bo beda; y cuyo calor se derriten los metales que dan en el
translation:

Those that we call llamas of the land, when they arrive to benefit their plant, some are processed with mercury and others by smelting. The processing with fire is of two kinds: one in Guayrás, and the other in reverberatory furnaces. Only the richest ores are purified in this way, since the others are too base, and if they are mixed with some alloy that makes them profitable and combined. And there are ores among them so porous but coarse, that they often yield fifty pesos, a hundred, or two hundred per hundredweight.

To smelt them, they are placed on hillsides and slopes, where the winds blow most strongly, in large clay braziers called guayrás, with burning charcoal and the ore inside; and as they melt, the fire consumes the slag and purifies the silver. Everything that the Indians of Peru extracted in ancient times was done by this method of smelting, because they never knew any other process; and in this way they made use without trouble of the very rich ores. And for many years the Spaniards used no other process there, until it was that during the viceroyalty of Don Francisco de Toledo the mercury amalgamation method was introduced.

The reverberatory smelting is done by placing the ores in furnaces shaped like bread ovens, except that the opening through which the fire is fed is no more than half a man's height from the floor of the furnace, and built into it is a small enclosed firebox where the firewood is placed and lit, whose flame, entering through the mouth of the furnace, strikes the entire vault and ceiling; and by this heat the ores are melted within it.

When they are already well melted, in such a way that one can stir and turn them with a thick iron rod — set there as a stone to break them apart — an opening is made on one side of the furnace level with the surface of the metals, a small mouth through which there exits and flows for a good distance, after falling to the ground, the metal from above, which contains no silver, but is entirely slag and a mixture of various metals. And this opening or gap is scraped downward until the refiners can see that all the slag has come out — in which matter they have such great skill that if a single drop of silver should begin to come out mixed with the slag, they recognize it and stop it. This slag that rises to the top of the molten metal is tough and black, with a slight reddish tinge; and upon cooling, which happens very quickly, it becomes so glassy that it breaks easily, and is heavy and shiny. Once the slag has been removed in this way, they attend to the silver metal, which is still mixed with lead and other compounds, and they draw it out in the same manner as the slag, opening the mouth of the furnace down to its floor, through which it flows out melted and falls to the ground. The miners call this metal from the first smelting "crude": from this crude metal there comes out, from six to ten quintals out of the hundred that were put into the furnace, and the rest was lost to smoke and slag.

In the second smelting and fusion they load the furnace with another fifty quintals of crude metal: which amounts to five or six batches from the first: and they smelt this second batch in the same manner as the first, and those who do it give it fire for no more than thirty hours, more or less: after it is well melted, the chiuia is drawn off as in the first time; which is of the same color and qualities as the first, except that it somewhat resembles tin in color. This second fusion they call adulterating the crude metal: from it a sheet is extracted composed of lead and silver with very little ore and slag. The less lead it contains, the more silver it has, and vice versa. To then separate the silver from the lead, and finish purifying it, a third smelting or fusion is given, for a period of twelve hours more or less, according to what the metal requires: which metal is smelted in the third and final smelting in a furnace somewhat smaller than the first, of the same shape: and when everything is well melted, a small crack and opening is made in the furnace, through which flows

With this process, the silver that is contained in all kinds of ores — rich, poor, coarse, and hard — is given its value, without losing a whit. And in order that they melt and flow easily, care is taken to mix with the ores a seventieth part of what is a lead-like metal; which, although it tends to be poor and of low grade, still serves mixed in with the others to make them run. The quantity of silver extracted by this process varies depending on whether the ores are rich or poor. From a single furnace load at the smelting works that I was able to observe in Oruro in the year sixteen hundred and six or eight, in which entered a considerable quantity from the first melt and smelting, amounting to some fifty quintals, that is to say two hundred and fifty of crude ore, there were extracted six hundred and fifty marks of silver.

Of pure silver. The ores from which silver was extracted were chaplato, broche, and negrillo; the latter was very rich, but harder to work, as all negrillos are. And the poroche was so poor that when refined, it yielded barely a pestle per quintal in the smelting process that I describe — one fifth of the negrillo ore; and the other four parts went to poroche. And although in terms of noise and labor the smelting process is similar to that using mercury, since it is not necessary to grind the ores, they weigh the same without mercury: even so it has its drawbacks, and the profit is not very great; since it is necessary to rebuild the furnaces almost entirely for each smelting, and so much firewood is consumed, that a refiner in Oruro certified to me that he spent six thousand pesos on firewood each year; and that those who made a profit from it earned one hundred pesos per week.

Chapter 39. On the mercury refining process.

The mercury refining process yields much greater wealth than smelting, because it is more abundant and universal; through it all the silver is extracted from the ores however low-grade and poor they may be. When the ore yields two ounces or more per quintal, a profit can be made from refining it; and below this there is very little or no profit, particularly in the mining settlements that do not have assigned Indians under royal warrant and repartimiento, or mita as they call it in Peru. A reasonable yield is four ounces; and those that yield

From this point upward they are considered rich metals, and the more they yield, the richer they are. When I was living in Oruro in the year sixteen hundred and eighteen, many ores were being processed at eight ounces per quintal; and some of the richest yielded as much as thirty marks per quintal: these were extracted in small quantities from very narrow veins. The greatest richness that has been drawn from the said mines of Oruro has been half silver, so that from one quintal of metal it has happened that twenty marks of pure, clean silver were obtained. At other times metals have been found that yielded a third, or a quarter part silver; and more commonly one comes across two, three, and four marks. But the most common are those of about four ounces per quintal, more or less.

In order for the mercury to bond with and separate the silver from the waste, the ores are first ground in certain mills, or water-driven mills in the manner of fulling mills, in the following way. The water for one mill is of greater volume than what a single millstone requires; it strikes with a drop of thirty to forty feet, and thus rushes with great force upon the wheel, which is set up like that of a fulling mill, and is so large that it measures twenty-two feet in diameter if it has one axle-head, and twenty-six if it has two; and because a very thick beam is called a single-headed mill, when the axle of it

A wheel on one side alone raises a row of stamps and grinds; and with two heads, when grinding on both sides, each one raising its own row of stamps. The number of stamps on each head runs from six to ten. These stamps are made of very hard and heavy wood, squared off to two palms in circumference, and nine to ten feet in length. Each one has at its end an iron striking-plate with which it crushes the ore. One stamp weighs several arrobas, and the largest may weigh four or five, so that each stamp comes to weigh ten or twelve arrobas in total. The stamps are arranged in a row, together and raised upright. They rest upon a great beam called the mortar, which is covered with thick iron plates called tejos. The axle of the wheel lifts these stamps one after another to a height of three or four palms, and as they fall they deliver a terrible blow upon the ore. On each side of the mortar stand two or three Indians who do not stop feeding ore into the mortar while the stamps rise; and even though some of these ores are stones as hard as flint, the heavy blow of the stamps breaks them down and grinds them like flour. A mill of one head can grind in a natural day from one hundred and fifty to two hundred quintals of ore; and double that if the mill has two heads.

When the owner of a mill grinds metals belonging to others, the cost for each mill of thirty to forty thousand pesos — this being for a single-head mill — and if it has two heads, sixty thousand. But if he grinds his own metals, combining the costs of the mine work with those of the mill, it comes to double. If the metals are not very poor, but of middling quality, the owner of a two-headed mill saves from twenty to thirty thousand pesos per year, and half that if the mill has only one head. In each mill there is a very large house with many rooms and quarters, both for offices and for lodging all the people who work there, so that each mill looks like a small town.

The sifted powder of the metals is placed in stone-built bins, raised like small granaries, holding about four hundredweight each, with as much water as is needed until it forms a soft mud that can be stirred and kneaded easily. The treatment given to the metals in these bins varies according to their properties. But all of them generally receive salt and mercury; and beyond that, some are also given copper metal, others processed iron, tin, lime, magistral, and other materials. Into each bin, six hundredweight of salt and from one and a half to two hundredweight of mercury are added. In Oruro they further add from two to twenty pounds of tin; and in Potosí they use iron and copper. Once this mixture is made, prepared in the manner described, they turn it over and work it through four to six times, kneading it very well with their feet; and each day lifting

from four to six passes until the mercury is fully incorporated with the silver: this is achieved through the heat of the sun. For this reason, depending on different times of the year, the process takes more or fewer days, and to check its progress, the refiner tests it several times a day, carrying with him whatever tools he needs. The time commonly spent on this process is from eight to fifteen days. Some mercury is consumed in the process, and the more so the richer the ores are. It is ordinary to lose as much mercury as the pure silver extracted — four to six pounds more or less, depending on the quality of the ores.

After the mercury has been incorporated with the metal, they remove it from the bins and place it in large wooden vats, where it is washed. A pipe of water enters the vat, and as much flows out as enters, carrying with it the finer earthy particles, while the coarser and heavier material sinks to the bottom together with the mercury and silver. The water in the vat is stirred by a paddle shaped like a wheel spoke, which they call a molinete, with arms at the end like a cart wheel, driven by the flow of water. This, with its rapid motion, swirls the metal around and dissolves it, causing the earth and slag to separate, while the mass of mercury and silver settles to the bottom of the vat. Other washing stations are smaller; in them three bins are washed each day, and half a bin is placed in each vat. Those using wheels and running water wash more gently, and each vat takes one bin of metal. To better collect the silver, more mercury is added to the vat while washing the metals. Types of metals called lamas, relave, and relavillo.
The lamas and relavillo are the finest and most delicate parts of the metal, and the water it carries with it runs off as described above. These are collected in large pools, the relavillo in some smaller basins where it settles. There is a channel through which the bars enter the basins. The relave is the coarser metal, like grains. It remains on the floor of the amalgamation vat and on top of the amalgam, and because it comes out very clean and washed, these different types of metals resulting from the washing still retain some silver, and for this reason they are collected to extract it through various processes.

For the relave and relavillo, a person goes along throwing handfuls into the sluices, which are small channels made in the style of gutters lined with coarse cloth or old pieces of fabric. When the water carries the earth through, the amalgam of mercury and silver remains stuck to the cloth, and by gently washing it, it is gathered up.

The lamas are burned in small furnaces made of clay vessels called caperucas, and each furnace holds thirty caperucas. Twenty or more furnaces are placed together in a row, in which two cajones are burned at once. They are fired for six hours, and the mercury that had combined with the lamas is found stuck to the lids of the caperucas. The lamas that come out poorly processed are re-treated in vats with mercury, and the lamas that come out of these are called relamos. Some of these are burned in large reverberatory furnaces, where two fires keep them for two nights and days. They reduce by a quarter, which is the impure material and the mercury that was in them, which the fire consumes; that

Chapter 40. Of the piñas and bars of silver.

The metal having been washed, and the mercury that has bonded with the silver — which they call pella — separated from the earth and dross: they pour it into coarse linen cloths, and by pressing the pella they beat out a portion of the mercury with blows: because there now remains no other task to be done with the silver than to separate it from its most intimate companion, the mercury. Once pressed in this manner, the pella is left loose and soft, and very similar to the touch of sieved ash or condensed snow. From it they form the piñas, pouring it into molds shaped like pine cones or small sugar loaves, and pressing it into them: the piñas come out of the mold still somewhat soft, because the pella is pliable and soft, with a hole in the middle so that the mercury can escape more easily. For this purpose they place them in small furnaces, each one over its hole, covered with a clay cap made in the shape of a sugar loaf mold or a still: there they apply fire with charcoal, by means of which the mercury exits through a tube like that of an alembic, which the covers have: and each piña uses two arrobas of charcoal to de-mercurize: which, once de-mercurized, is left free and solid, but very spongy, and so much so, if they weigh them, that before de-mercurizing, what it has is no more than one fifth, or thereabouts, of the weight it had with the mercury. Afterward they are given another round of fire to refine them further, re-burning every ten piñas with four arrobas of charcoal, with which the processing of

Desde que los metales se cortan de la lamina hasta dar a la plata la perfeccion que hemos visto, tiene tantos enemigos, y galfanos, o por mejor decir codiciosos, y aficionados, que apellos un sello han la mejor parte, que pone admiracion. Porque los Indios que brefean en la mina, en viendo la corpa (asilla man a la piedra de metal rico) la apartan, fueltan para; los que los sacan fuera de la mina echan tambien el ojo a los mejores, y si pueden a su salvo los hurtan: al acarrear lo al ingenio tienen los mismas avecias. Pues los Indios que trabajan en los ingenios no se duermen: y despues de lavado el metal, y sacada la pella, es de tanto malcodicia, quanto lo que entonces se usa, es bocado de mes sustancia, y menor precio. De suerte que quando el minero viene a sacar en limpio su plata, y la tienen bien quintada aquellos por cuyas manos pasa: y son hurtos hasta entonces tan disimulados que no se pueden echar de ver en el menoscabo de la hacienda.
El modo que se tiene en ensayar, y quintar la plata es, que el dueño entrega la piños al ensayador, el qual las funde, y hace barras: y para ensayarlas barras, y ponerles la ley que tienen, saca de cada una un bocado con un formol de acero a manera de uña, que segun la ordenanza ha de ser de dos tomines, aunque siempre se alariga amos, sinque los dueños lo hagan caso del exceso, por la gordad, y riqueza de la tierra. Aquel bocado, o pedazo de plata van ante las, y despues de purarlo, y refinarlo al fuego, y por el peso, y

the silver, and it remains pure and refined, made into ingots of thirty, forty, and more marks each.
From the time the metals are cut from the vein until the silver reaches the perfection we have described, it has so many enemies and thieves — or better said, greedy and eager ones — that by one means or another they take the better part of it, which is astonishing. For the Indians who work in the mine, upon seeing the ore (which they call the rich metal stone) set it aside and steal it; those who carry it out of the mine also cast their eye on the best pieces, and if they can do so safely, they steal them; those who transport it to the mill have the same bad habits. And the Indians who work in the mills do not sleep either: and after the metal is washed and the amalgam extracted, so much is lost through greed, since what is used at that point is a morsel of greater substance and lesser cost. So that when the mine owner comes to collect his silver in the clear, it has already been well skimmed by all those through whose hands it passes; and these thefts are so cleverly concealed up to that point that no loss can be detected in the estate's accounts.
The manner of assaying and taxing the silver is as follows: the owner delivers the ingots to the assayer, who melts them and makes bars; and in order to assay the bars and determine their fineness, he takes from each one a small piece with a steel punch shaped like a fingernail, which according to the ordinance must weigh two tomines, although it always runs over, and the owners make nothing of the excess, given the abundance and richness of the land. Chapter 42. On Mercury.

The mercury mines of this kingdom of Peru are held to be of equal importance to those of silver, because these mercury mines serve without being worked, and if some had not been worked, so great a quantity of silver as is now extracted could not have been obtained. In various parts of the Indies, mercury ores have been found, but not rich enough to be profitably processed. Above all, in the town of Huancavelica, in the diocese of Huamanga, the richest deposits of this ore were found, and because they have been worked for many years now, they have yielded endless riches, and for their sake that town was populated, whose residents have no other trade or livelihood than the working of these mines. The hill from which these ores are extracted is adjacent to the town, and in it each miner has built his hut where they process the ores, and there are many groups of Indians who come by mita to work in these mines, and they rotate every two months. Once the ores are removed from the mines to these camps, they are carried from there on trains of llamas or local sheep to the smelting settlements to be stored.

The mining settlement is located about one league, give or take, from the mountain, in the most convenient and sheltered areas, chosen because water was found there in abundance, and close to said place fuel for the smelting works: the discovery of which was the principal cause of all this wealth, because had God not provided such an abundance of ichu grass throughout the surrounding highlands, the mercury ores could not have been processed, since there is no firewood for many leagues around these mines with which to smelt them.

For the processing of this metal, each miner has his own smelting site, with its furnaces and necessary equipment. The method of processing and smelting these metals has changed several times; the one used before the current method was adopted was called de jabetas: whereby the metal, broken into small pieces, was smelted in certain clay pots or vessels. But the present process is much easier, more manageable, and more refined — it consists of placing the metals just as they come from the mine, without breaking them up, into furnaces of a particular design. This method was discovered during the time of the Viceroy, the Count of Chinchon, and its inventor was well rewarded with a generous income granted to him by the Viceroy.

The mercury ore that the Peruvian Indians call llimpi is the finest from which they extract vermilion. And although the Indians made use of llimpi for paint

Chapter 42. On Copper.

There are found greater quantities of copper mines in this kingdom, and in many other parts of the Indies, than of silver or other metals. The Indians extracted it in great quantities in ancient times; for which reason many mines worked long ago can still be seen today. Because as they lacked iron, they forged from this metal their weapons, tools, and instruments for agriculture, and for some other trades; and they made no less use of it in certain medicinal applications. At present, the Spaniards work some of these mines, extracting from them all the copper consumed in the Indies, and some that is sent to Spain. All the copper of the kingdom of Peru is of very fine quality, most notably that which is taken from the province of the city of Los Charcos, and that of the kingdom of Chile, from where all that is spent in the City of Lima is brought, to cast artillery, bells, and for all the other uses it serves, both as instruments and in medicine.

Almost all the copper of the kingdom ordinarily has some mixture of gold, and more than any other metal it is very easy to refine, because at the first smelting it comes out pure and perfect. To process it they place the raw metal in a furnace just as it comes from the mine, often in small pieces, alternating a layer of charcoal and a layer of metal; they then apply fire until it melts, the dross separates and rises to the top, and the copper sinks to the bottom. They draw off all the slag through a channel, and after it the clean copper by itself, which upon falling to the ground and meeting the air forms into large sheets. Only the river metal mines are worked; and from the combined ores one gets a fifth part of pure copper, others a quarter, and those that go to refining get as much as half — these are considered very prosperous. In the New Kingdom of Granada there are mines where pure copper is found already calcined, so that it need not be passed through fire to be refined. The metals from the mines of Paria yield a quarter part of clean, already calcined copper. The Indians of the kingdom call copper in the general language Anca.

Chapter 43. On Iron

It is a remarkable thing that, although the nations of the New World knew the mines of most metals, worked them, and made use of them in many ways, none has been found that had any use of iron or knew of it; nor do we find among the Indians any memory of or name for this metal — even though there are as many mineral deposits of it throughout the mountains as anywhere. In place of iron for their weapons and tools they used wood

Chapter 45. On Lead.

Lead is found together with silver, as these two metals are commonly mixed, and for this reason I can truthfully say that wherever there are silver mines, there are also lead mines. And so they usually extract it from the silver ores that are processed by smelting, it being the slag that is finally separated from the silver. There are also many mines of lead alone, which is processed by smelting it by itself; and some are very rich, notably one in the town of Juli, diocese of Chuquiabo, and another in the province of Sonqo, archdiocese of Guamanga. Because of this there is great abundance of lead throughout this entire kingdom; although

History of the New World: First Part, Book Four.

Chapter 1. On how the native plants of this New World are to be distinguished from those that have been brought from Spain and from other regions.

Among the mixed things composed of corruptible matter and form, the family of plants holds second place in order. This will be treated in this book and in the following ones. Regarding what presents itself here, there is a considerable difficulty, which although it did not arise in the preceding book — where bitumen and animate things were discussed — it does arise in what is to be noted from here forward; which is the need to distinguish the plants that were found in this New World from those that the Spaniards have brought from the lands that settled it, whether from Spain or from other foreign lands. This difficulty arises, first, from the abundance with which these foreign plants have taken hold and spread throughout this land, now growing in many places across the fields and wastelands without any cultivation by men. Wherefore

Para salir de la duda, la averiguar esta dificultad se ofrecen dos caminos: el primero es ver si la cosa de que se duda tiene nombre propio en las lenguas de sus naturales; porque siendo ellos tan curiosos, e inteligentes en la agricultura, y conocimiento de plantas, que no ay yerva ni por pequeña, y deshechado que pro voca, a quien no tengan puesto nombre, como la natural de esta tierra: indicio manifiesto parece no ser de las Indias la planta que entre ellos careciere de nombre; y por el contrario, ser natural de aca la que en sus lenguas lo tuviere.

Some have come to us as strangers or pilgrims, as much as the natives of the land: and regarding the many herbs and other plants that are found in these Indies, which being common and of the same species as those of Spain, one may doubt whether they were found here or were brought to them from others, of which there is no doubt that they came from Europe. To resolve the doubt and clarify this difficulty, two paths present themselves: the first is to see whether the thing in question has its own name in the languages of its native peoples; for since they are so curious and knowledgeable in agriculture and the knowledge of plants, that there is no herb, however small, nor however undesirable it may be, to which they have not given a name, as is natural to this land — it seems a clear indication that any plant which lacks a name among them is not native to the Indies; and on the contrary, that which has a name in their languages is native to here.

To make this as generally true as possible, certain warnings are added: the first is that not every word found with a proper name in the natural language of some Indian nation should straightforwardly be taken as an indication that it is native to the land, as it may be that the Indians gave it such a name based on some resemblance. And the second is that such a word must carry the meaning that properly signifies that name; as we see in this kingdom of Peru, where certain words from the general language are known to have not existed in this land before the Spaniards settled it — such as the word for hen, Atamalpa; for mirror, quilpi; and for shears, quelcani: which words primarily signify other things, for the first signifies an Inca king; the second

Therefore, in order to resolve this difficulty, one must look at whether the thing in question has its own proper name in the language of the Indians.
Because since the languages of the native peoples are so many that almost every town speaks its own, and even among those, each one has as many languages as there are factions and lineages living among them; and the topic of which there is doubt; had its name in this land before the Spaniards came to it, in each of its languages its most proper name: and if in other places only a single name is found taken from some Indian language, it is clear evidence that the Indians applied it to it by transference, as can be seen in the three names mentioned, and in many others that could be brought forward to confirm this truth. Sometimes I was led and helped to ascertain some things about which there could be doubt.

The second thing to be noted is that just because one does not find the proper name in the province where one happens to be, it should not therefore be inferred that it did not exist in the Indies: because there are many cases in which the Spaniards have carried things from one province to another within the same Indies, renaming in the lands to which they were transplanted things with the names those same things had in the provinces from which they are native, going by the names of the lands from which they were transplanted — something about which I could bring much evidence here, which I omit to avoid prolixity: where it is to be noted that just as it is not a certain argument to find a given name in one of the languages of the Indians in order to infer that such a thing is native to the Indies, in the same way it is likewise not sufficient proof to affirm

Beyond this I managed to know and speak with some old Spaniards among the first settlers of the land, and with nearly all the sons of the conquerors; who have such knowledge of the plants and products brought from Spain that they take pride in those which their forebears brought, keeping the information in their memory.

It is worth noting here that since Spaniards commonly give to the plants, fruits, and other natural things of America the names that the Indians of the provinces where they reside had given them; and many of these are general and common throughout all the Indies, it comes from this that one and the same fruit has many different names in various lands; which tends to cause great confusion for those who in Europe read accounts of the natural things of the New World: because it happens that when the same thing is set down in various accounts written in different provinces many times under different names, one who has no knowledge of what I am explaining here will be misled, thinking that things written with different words are distinct things. El que viere la descripcion que yo hago de cada cosa

Chuquiabo had been named twice before under different names, an error I must not fail to point out as I go along, because as it became customary to name that city by three names — which are Chuquiabo, Pueblonuevo, and La Paz — whoever encountered two of them, thinking that each signified a different city, came to make three cities out of one, led astray by the variety of names. This example being set out, one can see how easy it is to fall into the same error in other matters.

In order to remove the occasion and stumbling block of falling into such a mistake for whoever reads this history, we shall observe two or three precautions. The first is that for each plant and animal I shall give a brief description, portraying with the greatest accuracy possible both the parts of the plant and its fruit, so that by the description given for each thing one may distinguish one from another, without being confused and misled by the variety of names that would otherwise lead one astray. In providing this description I shall not trouble myself with determining whether the thing in question is the same as what the ancient authors describe, such as Pliny, Dioscorides, and others, because I judge that endeavor to be beyond reach given the difficulty we find in ascertaining which species of plants those authors are depicting, even though some of them are well known to all. Whoever reads the description I give of each thing

The second observation is that one and the same plant, in different lands, owing to the various climates thereof, has great diversity within itself in the size of the plant itself, its leaf, and its fruit; in the time of fruiting, and in other qualities. And such diversity is at times so great that it has happened to me almost not to recognize plants I had known, upon seeing them in different lands and climates. For which reason I will describe each plant according to the most common form it takes in this kingdom of Peru.

Every sort of plant is divided among genera or classes: the first in herbs and vegetables, which shall comprise all those plants that complete their course in one year, and whose stalks and branches are tender and not of woody matter; then shrubs and small trees, to which genus belong all those plants that in duration and nature are of hard, woody material comparable to trees, yet do not rise from the ground as high, nor form a trunk as thick and tall as they; and finally, in all the lineages of trees, in whose class fall all those plants that form a tall and strong trunk, whose timbers serve most notably against fire, and are used in the framing of buildings, in the construction of ships, and in other uses of the like kind. Each of the three classes and ranks of plants will have its own book, as follows.

In all parts of the world there is the rush, which grows two or ten years on the banks of lagoons, rivers, marshes, and swamps, in many varieties, all of which produce the totora abundantly. The first and largest species of rush is the cattail; the Indians of Peru call it totora, as do the Spaniards; and the Mexicans call it Tale. In the provinces of the Collao that lie along the shores of the great lake of Chucuito, where it grows abundantly, it serves as fodder for cattle, particularly a certain variety of it that is triangular in shape, and whose roots, which are white and tender, the Colla Indians eat; they call this root couri, and they display many bundles of them in the plazas of their towns for this purpose, as they do with other foodstuffs. From the cattail, the Indians of Peru make mats and rafts, not only to cross rivers but also to go out to sea in them; especially from the totora, which they call l'amo, or the large and triangular rush. The ash of the cattail helps them with all flows of blood and to dry wounds. There are many other varieties of rushes; some are shorter and thinner than totora, from which grows a great bulrush in the lake of Mexico, and they serve in that city in place of paper for animals, and they call it there zacate. Others are round, called min min in Peru. Among them are found large and small ones of all the varieties that grow in Spain. The sea rush, so called by the Indians, and by Garcia, has a square stem.

In some places the Indians make curious mats of thin, long rushes, especially in this city of Lima and in the town of Lambayeque, in the diocese of Trujillo. These mats are called here petates, which is a Mexican name; and they make them in all sizes, as rugs are made, and they serve the same purpose as rugs on the pedestals of altars and on the platforms where women sit. They are also placed underneath small rugs, and travelers use them to cover their saddlebags and the loads of their animals, because they protect them from the rain. In short, rush mats are better than those made in New Spain from palm leaves, because they are more durable, and even when folded like a rug they do not break.

In the province of Chachapoyas, in the diocese of Trujillo, there grows in the countryside a species of rush no larger than an asparagus, called in that land sipanti. Although it is always green, it does not give off its scent until split down the middle, at which point it smells as fragrant as a pastille. It is placed among clothes so that they take on its scent. There is also another three-sided rush of aromatic scent, though not very strong, called by the Indians vermilcu or ayaras; swallowed it is harmful, but used in tobacco it removes the bad smell of it and refreshes the brain.
