Plant of the spark: Espadaña: cortateras: a plant with very slender stems, and very small leaves. What the Spaniards call: thorns.

Grama grass grows in such abundance in the valleys of the coast of Peru that it costs the farmers a great deal of money, especially the wine producers, to clear it from their fields; it grows in parts two to three nodes high, and it serves to melt the glass that is prepared for carrying from one place to another. The plant called Mugo, which grows on rocks, and on the trunks and branches of trees, hanging from them like hair, or more like sheets of lichen in great quantity; the Indians, when they feel tired and weak in their muscles, tend to bathe in the decoction of this plant, which they say makes them feel well.

Also the plant from which glass is made, which grows ordinarily on the sea floor; the Indians had no use for it because they did not know how to make glass, nor was any such thing found anywhere in the New World; and it was one of the things that most amazed them when the Spaniards brought it; and even more so when they saw a small glass full of rich, golden wine. Today in Peru glass is found, not much, but of very fine quality; and in New Spain as well.

The holy thistle, called caribcho by the Indians, grows in all temperate lands; it has a yellow flower and a new seed resembling that of the radish, which serves everyone here as a safe purgative. Wherever one wishes, one can find grasses among them. The plant called rabo del lobo grows abundantly in swamps and humid places. The plant called bola grows in cultivated lands, and it bears a yellow flower; the juice of this plant is used to cure the sickness of the valley. Sarsaparilla; horehound; all kinds of mushrooms, large and small, among which some are poisonous and not edible.

All these plants are well known to the Indians, and they have given them names in their language; it is not surprising that all of them are wild and uncultivated, since they had no inclination to make gardens and transplant them by planting them in their fields; yet they made use of all of them for their sustenance, as well as for curing their illnesses and ailments. Another very common one is artemisia, which common people usually call altomisa; it grows in such great quantities on the estates of this valley of Lima that they burn it in the lime and brick kilns. Of wild mallows there are two species; not those we call locas, which bear large flowers, white and purple, for these are garden

Chapter 3. On Maize.

Thus I found throughout all these Indies no wheat, nor any other kind of grain of those that grow in ears in Europe. The Creator gave only three kinds of seeds to the natives of this land to serve them as bread, which are maize, quinoa, and chia.
Of these, maize is so widespread throughout all of America, both on the mainland and on the islands adjacent to it, just as wheat is in Europe. The maize plant is already well known in Spain under the name of Indian wheat. Its leaves resemble those of cane, except that they are wider and not as rough. The stalk — the cane of maize — rises most commonly to about one estado in height, and grows as thick as a thumb, more or less. It has, at equal intervals, knots like common cane. It is tender and weak, and breaks easily. Between the leaves it puts forth ears or plumes of a color between white and red, with many small filaments. It produces its fruit not at the top, as most other plants do, but around the stalk, and each plant or cane yields from one

Esta cubierto el choclo con unas tunicas, o capas de hojas, asperas, y correosas; y entre ellas, vel grano ay muchos hilos como cabellos del color del maiz, que sobrepasando a la longitud del chodo, sale por la punta del ur marogito dellos, tan grueso como un dedo. One finds four choclos (this is what they call in Peru the ears or cobs of maize) — each cob, after being husked, is as thick as a wrist, and some are of extraordinary length, ordinarily quite long, and from here on down. The cob is covered with husks or layers of leaves, rough and leathery; and between them and the grain there are many threads like hairs the color of maize, which, surpassing the length of the cob, emerge from its tip in a bundle as thick as a finger. The grains of maize are the size of chickpeas, not perfectly round; they are arranged on the cob in rows lengthwise, in great order like the seeds of a pomegranate, and so tightly packed together that to shell a cob the labor is to pry out one grain, since once one is removed it makes room for the rest.

Maize is a crop so versatile that it grows not only in temperate lands, but also in many others of various climates, such as cold and hot lands, dry and humid ones, in mountains and in plains, in winter and in summer, under irrigation and dependent on rainfall. Between it and wheat there is this difference: all lands that bear wheat also bear maize, but those that are too cold to produce wheat will likewise not produce maize. Though in this respect wheat has an advantage over maize in tolerating cold better; because in temperate lands that lean more toward cold than heat, sowing

There are many varieties of maize, because first of all it comes in all colors: light, dark, yellow, purple, light red, dirty, and mixed with various colors. It also differs in flavor and in the size of the kernels; the largest ones found are somewhat smaller than broad beans. One kind is very tender, with very white flour, and mild; another is very hard, which the Indians call muruchi, and the Spaniards call morocho, which is the one that the canalizaduras ordinarily use. Given these differences, the Indians have their own names for each.

Maize is the most suitable grain-bread that has been found for these people of such limited industry, because of the little effort it requires to prepare it to the point where it can serve as sustenance, not having the trouble that wheat requires — reaping, threshing, milling, and all the other labors that men must go through before it reaches the goodness of bread. For from the moment the ear of corn is in milk it serves as nourishment for days; and they eat maize in many ways, either as whole grain or ground: as whole grain, they eat it green while still in milk, before it dries, or roasted in the embers, or boiled in water, and in both ways it is tasty; and together with any kind of fruit, green ears of corn are sold in the plazas, some raw and others cooked. In New Spain they boil the maize in lime or lye to hull it, and then, as soon as it is done boiling, they grind it on a Metate, which is an instrument made of two stones, one long one about half a vara, and another about a third of that, and another small, round, and long one like a German rolling pin. In this way thin little rounds are made, which are toasted or cooked on clay dishes placed over the fire. This is the most prized bread the Indians make from maize; in Peru it is called tanta, and in New Spain Tlascale. These tortillas are not made the same way everywhere: in New Spain they are made thin, the width of a horseshoe's edge; in Tierra Firme, as large as what they call Arepas; those found in Peru were like those of New Spain. They must be eaten hot, because when they cool they become tough like wet leather and lose their flavor. On one occasion when in an Indian village of Beneyu we ran out of bread, the priest ordered the Indian women to make us maize tortillas as they used to make them in the old days for their chiefs. And they made them so delicious and fine that they seemed like pan-fried pastries, because they had kneaded the maize flour with eggs and lard. In the port of Santa Elena, diocese of Quito, the best are made

The other way of grinding the corn to make it into flour is to place it dry on a large flat stone, and grind it with another medium stone, which goes from one person to two mills. At present much is ground in our wheat mills; since the Indians in ancient times had no sieves, they sifted the flour only for people of distinction, such as the Caciques, using a cotton cloth, in which the fine flour or flower of the flour would stick, and the coarse part was separated from it by hand; but now they use our sieves. They also make from corn flour, besides the bread called torta, or rough pieces they call Yanos: porridges, or maçamuría, which in New Spain they call Atole, and other uses.

y patos; y engordan con ella los capones mejor que con
bellota. Y si aun su caña deja de ser provechosa, porque
verde la chupan los Indios como si fuera caña dulce; y en
algunas partes, hacen de su zumo miel, y vino; y si hoja
verde, y seca es maravilloso pasto para las caualgaturas:
y en la nueva España hacen de estas cañas secas vistosisimas
gines de vulto, que salen aunque sean muy grandes, muy
liuianas.

Demas desto es el maiz muy medicinal, porque el
zumo de su hoja verde junta las heridas frescas:
y tostado el grano, y tocado con vino aplicado caliente
en la quijada resuelue el dolor ventoso, y quita la inter
perecia pla. Mezclada su harina con zumo de hojas de
rabanos, quita los cardenales. finalmente el atolede,
o atole que se hace della un azucar o comida mui rago
cada, saludable, y facil de digestir, y que seda a los

The Spaniards likewise make use of maize in many
ways, for from it they make starch, and Surbio, afrancoyllo,
which serves in place of rice, and sometimes with milk and sug
ar, and other times with fat, small pastries, porridges, paboles, ro
poles of sweet with sugar, and other dishes and other preparations
that are healthy and wholesome. In short, this grain is of such
great usefulness that, beyond being sustenance for
men, it is also for animals,
for it is given in place of barley to riding animals; it is the grain
that birds eat, such as hens, turkeys, doves,
and ducks; and with it capons fatten better than on
acorns. And even its stalk is not without use, because
when green the Indians suck it as if it were sugar cane; and in
some places they make from its juice honey and wine; and its leaf
both green and dry is a wonderful fodder for riding animals:
and in New Spain they make from these dry stalks the most striking
figures in the round, which turn out, even when very large, extremely
light.

Beyond this, maize is very medicinal, for the
juice of its green leaf closes fresh wounds:
and the grain, toasted and applied with wine warm
to the jaw, relieves wind pain, and cures intemperate ills. Its flour mixed with the juice of radish leaves
removes bruises. Finally the atolede,
or atole made from it is a sweet or very substantial food,
healthy and easy to digest, and which is given to the sick

de maiz es de la lengua de los Indios de la isla española.
Los Mexicanos lo llaman Tlaolli; y los del Peru, para,
en la lengua quichua; y en la Aymara, Tona; y a la mag-

Cap. 4. de la chicha de Maiz.

Debaxo del nombre de chicha se comprehenden todas
las bebidas que usan los naturales del nuevo mun-
do en lugar de vino; y porque mui frecuentemente se
embriagan; al qual vicio son tan inclinados, que ni lo
aprovechado auerle combertido a nuestra santa fe; ni el
trato, y comunicacion con los Españoles; ni los castigos que
hacen en ellos sus amas; y las Justicias, para que se apar-
ten del; ndo que en algunas provincias tiene alguna
enmienda; y en general en todas partes no son menos
tanomanos, y frequentes los borracheros, como en
tiempo de la gentilidad. Hacese la chicha de muchos semi-
acomodandose cada nacion a aquellas semillas, y fru-
tos, que mas en abundancia produce su tierra, para
hacer chicha dellas; unas chitas se hacen de Oca, y yucas

wounded, like those sick with fever. The name
maize comes from the language of the Indians of the island of Hispaniola.
The Mexicans call it Tlaolli; and those of Peru call it para,
in the Quechua language; and in Aymara, Tona; and the masa
of maize the Indians of New Spain call elo-
and the Peruvians call it choclo; and its juice, the masa without grai-

useful to the muleteers, because they stuff the pack-

Chapter 4. On chicha made from Maize.

Under the name chicha are included all
the drinks that the native people of the New World
use in place of wine; and because they get drunk very frequently,
a vice to which they are so inclined that neither
the benefit of having been converted to our holy faith, nor their
dealings and communication with the Spaniards, nor the punishments
inflicted upon them by their masters and the Justices, to make them
give it up; although in some provinces there has been some
improvement; in general, in all places they are no less
given to drinking and frequent drunkenness than in
the time of their paganism. Chicha is made from many seeds,
each nation adapting to those seeds and fruits
which their land produces most abundantly, to
make chicha from them; some chichas are made from oca and yuca

Primera parte libro 4. 215
y de otras raices: otras de quinua, y del fruto del mulle: las In
dios de Tucuman la hacen de algarrobas; las de Chile de
peses; las de Tierra firme de pinas: los Mexicanos de
Maguey, el vine que ellos llaman Pulque: y el llamado
en diferentes provincias de diversas frutas, y legu
bres, que parece que en inspirado todos los moradores
de la America contra el agua, segun rehusam de beber
la pura. Pero la mejor chicha de todas, y que mas gene
ralmente se bebe en esta tierra; la qual como vino prec io
so tiene el primer lugar entre todas las demas bebidas
de los Indios, es la que se hace de maiz.
Esta se hace de muchas maneras, y en lo que se di
fervcian unas de otras, es en ser unas chichas mas fuer
tes que otras, y de diferentes colores: porque se hace chi
cha colorada, blanca, amarilla, cenicienta, y de
otros colores. Una muy fuerte llamada Sora, que
hacen de maiz, que primero esta algunos dias enterra
do hasta que se tostece: otra de maiz tostado: otra
de maiz mascado, y de otras maneras. La mas ordi
naria que beben los Indios del Peru es la que se ha
ce de maiz mascado; para la qual seven no solo en
sus pueblos, sino tambien en muchos de los españoles,
donde ay concurso de Indios; como en Potosi, Oruro,
y otros; hechos urinales en las plazas de badian viejas,
translation:
First part, book 4. 215
and from other roots: others from quinoa, and from the fruit of the molle tree: the Indians of Tucuman make it from carob; those of Chile from fish; those of Tierra Firme from pineapples; the Mexicans from Maguey, the wine they call Pulque; and that called in different provinces by various fruits and vegetables, which seems as if all the inhabitants of America were inspired against water, given how they refuse to drink it pure. But the best chicha of all, and the one most generally drunk in this land, which like a precious wine holds first place among all other drinks of the Indians, is that which is made from maize.
This is made in many ways, and what differentiates one from another is that some chichas are stronger than others, and of different colors: for chicha is made that is red, white, yellow, ash-colored, and other colors. One very strong kind called Sora is made from maize that is first buried for several days until it ferments; another from roasted maize; another from chewed maize, and in other ways. The most ordinary kind that the Indians of Peru drink is that made from chewed maize; for which one sees not only in their own towns, but also in many Spanish ones where there is a gathering of Indians, such as Potosí, Oruro, and others, vessels set out in the plazas made from old jars,

text:

y muchachos sentados mascan de maiz: que no pouras to causa alos españoles solo verlo; sin que lo causa alos Indios el bebar un brebaje pecho tan suciamente. No mascan todo el maiz desde se hace la chicha; sino par te del, que mesclado con lo demas sirve como de la bradura. La qual tienen los Indios por tan necesaria para darla al punto a la chicha, que quando el maiz se muele para este efeto en nuestros molinos de a gua; mascan la harina hasta humedecerla en la boca; y hacerla masa: y llenan su poca a lo que se an pan en este o zenduo de mascarma iz, y harina, fue ra de lo que interesan tragando lo que quieren p aro matar la hambre.

Los españoles tambien suelen hacer chicha de ma iz por regalo, pero hacenlo con mas limpieza, y avi o lidad que los Indios: la qual es una bebida saladable, fresca, y de buen gusto: y se hace desta manera. Cuesto se un almud de maiz (mas o menos segun la canti dad de chicha que se hade hacer) y de que se muele; y cierne su harina; la qual se amasa con un poco de agua tibia, y no caliente, que llene un poco de sal: hase desbarmu bien la masa desta manera que ni quede rala, ni aguanosa, ni mezdura; sino que haga algun poco de corra. hecho esto se le sala masa por una noche; y por la mañana se echa en uno
translation:

and boys sitting chew maize: which alone is enough to disgust the Spaniards just by watching it; no less so does it disgust the Indians to drink a beverage made in such an unclean manner. They do not chew all of the maize from which the chicha is made; only a portion of it, which mixed with the rest serves as a kind of leavening. This the Indians consider so necessary to give the chicha its proper quality, that when the maize is ground for this purpose in our water mills, they chew the flour until it is moistened in the mouth and formed into a dough; and they fill their small portion of this mixture of chewed maize and flour, apart from what they gain by swallowing whatever they wish to satisfy their hunger.

The Spaniards also are accustomed to making chicha from maize as a treat, but they do it with more cleanliness and skill than the Indians: it is a wholesome, fresh, and pleasant drink, and it is made in the following way. One almud of maize is taken (more or less according to the quantity of chicha to be made) and it is ground and its flour sifted; this flour is then kneaded with a little warm, not hot, water, adding a little salt: the dough must be worked very well in such a way that it is neither too thin, nor watery, nor too dry; but rather that it holds together somewhat. Once this is done, the dough is left to stand overnight; and in the morning it is placed into

Toda suerte de chicha mas bebida aprovecha contra
el mal, y detencion de orina; y contra las arenas, y pie-

Indios asi viejos como nuevos se hallan estas enferme-

medio quartillo della en ayunas, aunque ayuntado
en remojo por espacio de una noche los casos de media
cebolla blanca, y un poco de azucar, quita la pringacion

a vessel that can hold one arroba of water; and into it shall be poured about six quartillos of very boiling water, and with a large spoon it shall be stirred so that the dough and water become lukewarm; and then successively lukewarm water is added until it reaches a full arroba, and it is stirred again so that everything combines. Then the vessel is covered, and left like that for twenty-four hours; once these have passed, the water that has settled and become clear is drawn off and poured into another vessel, from which about six quartillos of it are taken; this, with a pound and a half of sugar, must boil a little, and this sugared water is mixed back in with the rest, and after it has become lukewarm it must be quickly poured into the vessel from which it is to be served for drinking, covering it with a cloth so that the foam that must come out does not obstruct the serving of the chicha. If the vessel into which the new fermented batch of the drink is poured already has some chicha in it, it will be ready to drink within two days, and if not, it will take seven or eight days to ferment and mature.
Every type of chicha as a beverage is beneficial against illness and retention of urine; and against gravel and stones in the kidneys and bladder: for which reason these ailments are never found among the Indians, both old and new converts, because of their custom of drinking chicha. Taking half a quartillo of it on an empty stomach, even steeped overnight with pieces of half a white onion and a little sugar, it removes the burning sensation

De rinones, o quando menos la templa, y apoca para que no desuelle, y haze llagas en la via de la orina. Stomando de esta bebida quando no esta mui agria, o madura, medio quartillo caliente en ayunas aprovecha contra la ulcepa sion, y contra todo detenimiento de orina, y mal de ijada. Tambien sirve el wncho, o siento de la masa que hace la chicha, porque aplicado sobre los pies gotosos, les quita el ardor, y mitiga el dolor. El nombre de chicha no es del reyno, pienso que lo tomaron los españoles de la lengua de la isla española; llamase en la lengua Cuithua del Peru, Aca; y en la Aymara, Chila.

cap. 5. De la quinua.

La quinua es una planta mui parecida a los bledos, crece dos tercias en alto por mas o menos, su hoja es como la de los bledos salvo que junto al peon es mas ancha, y no tan puntiaguda, produce la semilla en el remate del tallo en unos racimillos como los de los bledos: la qual es del tamaño de granos de mostaza, tanto quanto mayor, no redonda perfectamente, sino algo chata. Es esta semilla la que sufre mas el frio de quantos nacen en estas Indias, asi de las naturales de aca, como de las traydas de España; porque se da en tierras tan frios donde las demas se yelan hasta la cebada. Ay dos especies de quinua ni mas ni menos que de bledos, una blanca, y otra dorada: quando esto
translation:
History of the New World.

Of the kidneys, or at least it tempers and reduces so that it does not chafe or cause sores in the urinary tract. Taking half a quartillo of this beverage warm on an empty stomach, when it is not too sour or unripe, is beneficial against ulceration and against all retention of urine and pain in the side. The sediment or lees of the dough used to make chicha also serves a purpose, because when applied to gouty feet, it removes the burning and eases the pain. The name chicha does not come from this kingdom; I believe the Spaniards took it from the language of the island of Hispaniola. In the Quechua language of Peru it is called Aca, and in Aymara, Chila.

Chapter 5. On Quinoa.

Quinoa is a plant very similar to pigweed. It grows about two thirds of a vara in height, more or less. Its leaf is like that of pigweed, except that near the stem it is wider and not as pointed. It produces its seed at the top of the stalk in small clusters like those of pigweed. The seed is about the size of mustard grains, or somewhat larger, not perfectly round but rather somewhat flat. This seed tolerates cold better than any other plant grown in these Indies, whether those native to this land or those brought from Spain, because it grows in lands so cold that all other plants, even barley, freeze. There are two species of quinoa, no more and no less than those of pigweed: one white and one golden. When this

text:
Primera parte. Libro 4. 217

tierna esta yerua antes de espigar, se come guisada como las acelgas, y espinacas, aunque solamente la blanca, y no la colorada, porque su comida causa mal de orina.
La semilla de la quinua es de tan diferentes colores como el maíz, porque ay quinua blanca, amarilla, morada, colorada, y cenicienta: una silvestre, y otra domestica, y que tiñada. La mejor de todas es la blanca, y ella y los granos finos sircula como arroz, y molida en polvo empleadas, también hacen de su harina pan como las arepas de maíz. De las otras quinuas de colores hacen chicha, señalada mente de la cenicienta llamada cañahua, cuya chicha es mui recia en el embriago, y alov agria quando da muísmo cura. Los tallos, y hojas de la quinua cocidas, y comidos con aceyte, y vinagre, y azúcar tienen facultad de ablandar el vientre: su zumo, o como con unos gotas de vinagre es contra las inflamaciones, y añadiendo azúcar es un buen gargarismo para inflamaciones de la gota. La simiente de la yerua cocida en agua con leche, o grasada de la olla aumenta la leche en las paridas, y se ha hallado por esperiencia, y así lo he visto yo usar, ser muy prouechoso para qualquiera caída tomar una escudilla de polenta caliente, o de su simiente de la semilla de la quinua, aunque se mita el daño que de las caídas podría resultar. De la caña, o tallo de la quinua quemado hacen los Indios una ceniza que llaman
translation:
First Part. Book 4. 217

This herb while tender, before it goes to seed, is eaten cooked like chard and spinach, though only the white variety and not the red, because eating the red causes urinary problems.
The seed of quinoa comes in as many different colors as maize, for there is white, yellow, purple, red, and ash-colored quinoa: one wild variety and one domestic, and one that dyes. The best of all is the white, and it and the fine grains are used like rice, and ground into flour they make bread like maize arepas. From the other colored quinoas they make chicha, most notably from the ash-colored one called cañahua, whose chicha is very potent in causing intoxication, and turns sour when it has gone too far. The stalks and leaves of quinoa, cooked and eaten with oil, vinegar, and sugar, have the property of softening the bowels. Its juice, or taken with a few drops of vinegar, is good against inflammations, and with the addition of sugar it makes a good gargle for inflammations of the gout. The seed of the herb cooked in water with milk, or with pot drippings, increases milk in new mothers, and it has been found by experience — and I have seen it used myself — that it is very beneficial for any kind of fall or injury to take a bowl of warm polenta, or of the seed of quinoa, so as to lessen the harm that could result from such falls. Chapter 6. On chia.

Chia is native to New Spain. The plant
is very similar to that of quinoa, and its leaves are seen
dried. It puts out a spike similar to that of quinoa, and on
it the seed, which is very similar in shape to sesame,
except that it is smaller and black in color. The Indians of
New Spain grind this seed and add it to atole, or ma-
camorra, and it gives it a good flavor.

Chapter 7. On yuca.

Since all of America was a land lacking the grain
species and seeds of Europe, from which their settlers drew sustenance,
as well as the meat of domestic animals, until the Spaniards
brought to it wheat, and all manner of vegetables, and
domestic livestock from Spain: God supplied the lack of these
things by endowing this new world with many and diverse
fruits and vegetables, principally an infinite variety
of roots, which served as sustenance for the Indians.
Of these, the most widespread, and that which sustains a great
part of the Indies, is yuca, which the natives of warm
lands have never ceased to call cacabi: because

Not a few parts of it are eaten by the Spaniards. Yuca is a plant that grows two estados tall, more or less, and sends up a stalk, or straight rod, round, solid, and as thick as a finger of the hand. From the ground all the way up to the crown it is covered with leaves, which do not weigh it down, and it is made all the more beautiful and handsome by these leaves being very fine to look at. They are attached to the stalk by a long stem, very similar to that of a grapevine leaf — very red in color, round, smooth, and no thicker than a slender reed. The leaf itself closely resembles that of hemp; it has the shape of a star with seven or nine points, cleft down to the stem and nearly equal, making it round overall. Each point resembles in shape and width the leaf of a peach tree, except that it is not so channeled. They have a deep green color that is quite striking. When the plant is covered with leaves, since they are all so equal, it ends up being as broad in circumference as the width of a man's body from top to bottom, which makes it so pleasing in appearance that, for its good looks, people often plant it in gardens. The leaves fall off over time, beginning from the lowest ones, and where they were attached to the stalk they leave small knobs or nodes, which is why the stalk is very knotted in those places.
The way it is sown or planted is by sticking into the ground pieces of the stalk from those that have been uprooted. These pieces soon take root, each one sending out two or three shoots, and as they grow upward, they spread out and

From each plant one can take four to eight roots, more or less, depending on the fertility of the soil that produces them; they take a year to ripen, and they become much better if left for a year and a half.

There are two kinds of yuca, one sweet and one bitter; the sweet one is eaten like sweet potatoes, boiled or roasted, and is often put into the pot in place of turnips, and in any form it has a good flavor, and even if eaten raw it does no harm. This kind is called on the island of Española "Boniata," meaning without poison, in contrast to the other kind, which is so poisonous that any animal that eats it before it is pressed out will die without remedy; and the same fate befalls whoever drinks the juice that comes out when it is pressed. From this poisonous yuca cassava bread is generally made, and they make it in the following way: after these yucas are ground up they are grated on rough stones, and then, once grated, they are placed in a long, narrow sack about the width of a thigh called a cibucan, made from soft tree bark, in the manner of a press; and then

So, placing it [the yuca], one puts it in this tall bag, and at the other end a great weight is placed, which causes it to spread and compress the yuca. And after it has been pressed down for as long as it takes to be well squeezed, so that all that poisonous juice, which is like whey, comes out, they remove it, and what remains looks like squeezed almonds. These they place in the buren, which is a flat earthenware pan as large as a sieve, set over the fire and sealed with clay so that no flame escapes. And although when it is poured in it is loose and moist like wet bran, it curdles together, and they turn it so that it cooks better. In the time it takes to fry an egg, each cake of it is well formed. These cakes they then put out in the sun for one or two days to dry out, and they end up as stiff as a board, even though when taken off the fire they were soft and greasy. These cazabi cakes keep without spoiling, as if new, for more than a year, and at sea they make up for the lack of hardtack. Two kinds of cazabi are made: one very thin one called jaujau for refined people, which is very white, tender, and crumbles easily; and another thicker and more compact one for common people. And speaking of the cakes of one and the other, it seems to me that the saying is verified here: "for want of bread, cakes will do," because in lands where wheat bread cannot be had it cannot really be eaten with pleasure, nor is it appetizing, no matter how much some may wish to praise it.

Chapter 8. On the Sweet Potato.

The sweet potato is a root very well known not only throughout the Indies,
but also in Spain; and it is among the most prized
foods that the Indians had. The plant is small, and its
branches spread out over the ground without rising very high;
each plant produces many shoots or stems, which are
round, smooth, and purple; and they grow like tendrils
spread out over the ground. The leaf of the shoot
grows on a stalk as long as that of a vine leaf,
but more slender, tender, and purple in color; the leaf is
wider near the stem than at the other end, and ends in

Sacase de cada mata de quatro a doze rayes, mas o menos segun la tierra es mas o menos fertil. Los batatas se diferencian entre si en el tamaño, y forma, lo mas comunmente son por en medio algo mas gruesas que por las puntas; y algunas ay prolongadas, y para los por todas partes, otras redondas, joaldas, o a hutadas; ay las tan gruelas a vno el braso, y de media vara de largo, y de aqui para abajo: son muy tiernas, y harinosas, y se hallan tan bien de diferentes colores, moradas, amarillas, blancas, rojas, y jaspeadas.

Son entre diferencios, la una que retiene el nombre comun de batata; la qual se aventaja a las otras como la camuesa a los manzanas: la segunda es de las que dan en el Peru, que llamamos camotes, que tiene el segundo lugar en bondad: si bien en algunas partes son tan buenos los camotes, que no deven nada a las mejores batatas, quales son los de Payta dio ese de [ilegible], y del valle de la misma ciudad de Trugillo. La tercera es peor de batatas, es de aquellas que en la isla española la llamar Ages, y los españoles las nombran ñames: crecen los ages en muy breve tiempo, y por elo los suelen sembrar muchos para sustento de sus esclauos, y gente de seruio. From each plant one can extract four to twelve roots, more or less depending on how fertile the soil is. Sweet potatoes differ from one another in size and shape; most commonly they are somewhat thicker in the middle than at the tips; some are elongated and tapered at both ends, others are round, oval, or flattened; some are as thick as a man's arm and half a yard long, and from there downward. They are very tender and floury, and they also come in different colors: purple, yellow, white, red, and mottled.

There are among them different varieties: the first retains the common name of batata, and it surpasses the others just as the camuesa apple surpasses other apples. The second is the kind found in Peru, which we call camotes, and which holds second place in quality; although in some places the camotes are so good that they are in no way inferior to the best batatas, such as those from Payta in the diocese of [illegible], and from the valley of the same city of Trujillo. The third kind of sweet potato is inferior; it is the one that on the island of Hispaniola they call ages, and the Spaniards name them ñames. The ages grow in a very short time, and for that reason they are commonly planted in large quantities to feed slaves and servants. It grows as large as a medium-sized turnip, which can sit upright: on the outside it is earth-colored, and when the skin is removed it remains white, with some purple spots, like jasper.

The sweet potatoes are eaten boiled and roasted over coals, and they taste like roasted chestnuts; they are also used to make delicious stews and fritters. Although this plant's root resembles a turnip or radish, forming a head where the root meets the leaves, from each node there grow and extend underground many small tendrils or thin threads, resembling the plant's rootlets, and at the tip of each one of these a root grows. In this same manner grow almost all the edible roots found in the Indies, such as yuca, potatoes, ocas, peanuts, and many others. The green leaf of the sweet potato, or camote, mashed and mixed with lard without salt and placed on chiggers, kills them and relieves the pain and discomfort they cause. This root is called batata in the language of Hispaniola; in Peru it is called Apichu in the Quechua language; and in Aymara, sutucu. The Spaniards call it camote, which is a name from the Mexican language.
